## Dīgha Nikāya
## Commentary on the Mahāvagga
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta
## Discourse Related to the Recollection of Former Habitations

The text beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and ending with "karerikuṭikāyaṃ" is the Mahāpadāna Sutta. In this sutta, this is the commentary on the new (not previously explained) terms. Regarding "karerikuṭikāyaṃ": Karerī is the name of a Varuṇa tree. A pavilion made of those Karerī trees stood at the door of that dwelling; therefore, it is called the "Karerī Hut" (Karerikuṭi). This is just as it is called the "Kosamba Hut" (Kosambakuṭi) because a Kosamba tree stood at its door. It is said that within the Jetavana Monastery, there are four great buildings: the Karerī Hut, the Kosamba Hut, the Fragrant Hut (Gandhakuṭi), and the Salala Hall (Salalāgāra). Each was completed at an expense of one hundred thousand [coins]. Among these dwellings, King Pasenadi of Kosala had the Salala Hall built and donated it; the remaining dwellings were built and donated by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika. Thus, the Blessed One dwells in the Karerī Hut, which was built upon pillars by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika and is like a celestial mansion.

Regarding "pacchābhattaṃ": For those who observe the ascetic practice of eating at one sitting (ekāsanika), even if they have eaten in the morning and it is still within mid-day, it is still "after the meal" (pacchābhatta). However, in this context, "pacchābhatta" is intended to mean after the regular meal. "Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṃ" means those who have returned from the alms-round, having finished their meal and risen from their seats.

Regarding "karerimaṇḍalamāဠေ": This refers to a sitting hall built not far from that Karerī pavilion. That Karerī pavilion was [situated] between the Fragrant Hut and the hall...
3:
When the sectarians (titthiyas) recollect their former habitations, they can only recollect what they themselves have seen, done, or heard. Likewise, the disciples (sāvakas) and the Private Buddhas (paccekabuddhas) [can only recollect what they have seen, done, or heard]. The Buddhas, however, can recollect everything that was seen, done, or heard by themselves or by others.

The knowledge of former habitations of the sectarians is like the light of a firefly. The knowledge of the disciples is like the light of a lamp. The knowledge of the Chief Disciples is like the light of the morning star (Venus). The knowledge of the Private Buddhas is like the light of the moon. But the knowledge of the Buddhas is like the light of the autumn sun's orb. For the Buddha, there is no limit such as "this many hundreds of births, thousands of births, or hundreds of thousands of births," or "this many hundreds of aeons, thousands of aeons, or hundreds of thousands of aeons." When he recollects anything, there is neither stumbling nor obstruction; it is connected directly with the advertence (āvajjana), and is connected directly with the desired attention (manasikāra) and the arising of the thought. It proceeds without snagging, like a bolt shot with force through a weak bundle of leaves, or like the thunderbolt (vajira) of Sakka released upon the peak of Mount Sineru. "Oh, how great is the Blessed One's knowledge of former habitations!"—thus the conversation arose, was born, and proceeded concerning the Blessed One himself. To show all of that in brief, only this much was said in the Pāḷi: "Thus also is the recollection of former habitations, thus also is the recollection of former habitations." Therein, "iti pi" means "in this way also."

2-3. "Assosi kho...pe... atha bhagavā anuppatto": The explanation for this passage is exactly as stated in the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta. This, however, is the distinction: in that Brahmajāla Sutta, he heard by means of his omniscient knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa); in this sutta, however, he heard by means of the divine ear (dibba-sota). In that sutta, the talk concerning praise and dispraise was interrupted before completion; in this sutta, it is the talk concerning former habitations. Therefore, the Blessed One thought: "These monks are praising the qualities [of my knowledge] by referring to my knowledge of former habitations, but they do not know the attainment of my knowledge of former habitations. Come, I shall tell and show them its attainment." Having come, he sat upon the noble Buddha-seat which was dusted and spread by the monks at that moment—a seat normally reserved only for the Buddhas to sit and deliver a Dhamma discourse. At the conclusion of his question, "Monks, for what talk are you now gathered?" and at the conclusion of their reply, "Here, Bhante..." and so on, he said, "Would you like [to hear]..." and so forth, desiring to give them a Dhamma talk related to former habitations. Therein, "iccheyyātha no" means "would you like?" Then the monks, with joyful minds, requested him, saying, "This is the Blessed One's..." and so on. Therein, "etassa" means "of the giving of this Dhamma talk."

## Explanation of the Determination of the Bodhi Tree

In the determination of the Bodhi tree, the phrase *pāṭaliyā mūle* means at the foot of the Pāṭali tree. On that day, the trunk of that Pāṭali tree rose to a height of fifty cubits, and its branches extended fifty cubits; thus, it was one hundred cubits in height. On that day, that Pāṭali tree was entirely covered with flowers from its base upwards, as if bound by floral crests, and a divine fragrance wafted forth. At that time, it was not only this single tree that bloomed; all the Pāṭali trees in the ten thousand universes bloomed. Not only the Pāṭali trees, but in all the trees of the ten thousand universes, trunk-lotuses bloomed on the trunks, branch-lotuses on the branches, creeper-lotuses on the creepers, and sky-lotuses in the sky; even great lotuses burst through the surface of the earth and emerged. The great ocean was also covered with lotuses of five colors, as well as blue lotuses and red lotuses.

The entire ten thousand universes were crowded with banners and streamers, pervaded by hanging garlands, flower clusters, and floral globes tied here and there, and resplendent with flowers of various colors, resembling the Nandana Grove, the Cittalatā Grove, the Missaka Grove, and the Phārusaka Grove. Banners hoisted at the edge of the eastern universe touched the edge of the western universe. Banners hoisted at the edges of the western, southern, and northern universes touched the edge of the southern universe. In this way, the universes were endowed with mutual glory. The term *abhisambuddho* means that, having penetrated the entire majesty, power, and glory of the Buddha's qualities, he fully realized the Four Noble Truths.

In passages such as "Monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, attained Enlightenment at the foot of a Puṇḍarīka tree," the explanation of the terms should be understood in this same manner. Here, however, *puṇḍarīka* refers to a white mango tree. The dimensions of that tree were also the same. On that day, that tree was also well-covered with flowers possessing a divine fragrance. It was covered not only with flowers but also with fruits. On one side of that tree hung tender fruits, on another side middle-aged fruits, on another side partially ripe fruits, and on another side fully ripe fruits, which were delicious as if infused with divine essence. Just like that tree, in all the ten thousand universes, the flowering trees were adorned with flowers and the fruiting trees were adorned with fruits.

*Sālo* refers to the Sāla tree. The dimensions of that tree were also the same, and the majesty and glory of its flowers should be understood in the same way. This same method applies to the Sirīsa tree. As for the Udumbara tree...
10:
...there were no flowers, but the abundance of its fruit should be understood according to the method stated for the mango tree; likewise for the Nigrodha tree and the Assattha tree. Thus, for all Buddhas, the seat (pallaṅka) is one and the same, but the trees are different. Among those trees, whatever tree a Buddha sits under to penetrate the Enlightenment known as the Knowledge of the Four Paths, that particular tree is called a Bodhi tree. This is the Determination of the Bodhi Tree.

## Explanation of the Determination of the Pair of Disciples

In the determination of the pair of disciples, *Khaṇḍatissaṃ* refers to Khaṇḍa and Tissa. Among them, Khaṇḍa was the younger brother of the same father, and Tissa was the son of the royal chaplain. Khaṇḍa reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom, while Tissa reached the pinnacle of the perfection of concentration. The term *aggaṃ* (chief) means they were supreme because their qualities were incomparable to others, excluding the Blessed One Vipassī. *Bhaddayugaṃ* (auspicious pair) means they were an auspicious pair precisely because they were the chief ones. *Abhibhūsambhavaṃ* refers to Abhibhū and Sambhava. Among them, Abhibhū reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom. Having gone from the city of Aruṇavatī to the Brahma world together with the Blessed One Sikhī, he displayed various miracles to the assembly of Brahmas; while preaching the Dhamma, he covered the ten thousand world-systems with darkness, and then radiated light for those who were struck with religious urgency, wondering "What is this?" Having made the resolution, "May all see my form and hear my voice," he made his voice heard while reciting the two verses beginning with *Ārambhatha*. Sambhava reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom.

*Soṇuttaraṃ* refers to Soṇa and Uttara. Among them, Soṇa reached the perfection of wisdom, and Uttara reached the perfection of concentration. *Vidhurasanjīvaṃ* refers to Vidhura and Sanjīva. Among them, Vidhura reached the perfection of wisdom, and Sanjīva reached the perfection of concentration. This Sanjīva, who frequently entered meditative attainments, was meditating through the power of attainment in night quarters, day quarters, monasteries, caves, pavilions, and so on; one day, he entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) in the forest. Then, woodcutters and others, noticing him and thinking "He is dead," cremated him. He emerged from the attainment at the predetermined time, shook out his robes, and entered the village for alms. From that event onwards, they knew him as "Sanjīva" (The Living One). *Bhiyyosuttaraṃ* refers to Bhiyyosa and Uttara. Among them, Bhiyyosa was superior in wisdom, and Uttara was chief in concentration. *Tissabhāradvājaṃ* refers to Tissa and Bhāradvāja. Among them, Tissa reached the perfection of wisdom, and Bhāradvāja reached the perfection of concentration...
11:
It happened. "Sāriputta-Moggallāna" refers to Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Among those two, Sāriputta was the foremost in the field of wisdom, and Moggallāna was the foremost in the field of concentration. This is called the Definition of the Pair of Disciples (Sāvaka-yuga-pariccheda).

## Explanation of the Definition of the Assembly of Disciples

In the Definition of the Assembly of Disciples, the first assembly of disciples of the Blessed One Vipassī was endowed with four factors: all were "Ehi Bhikkhu" monks, all possessed miraculous bowls and robes, all arrived without being invited, and they arrived on the fifteenth-day Uposatha. Then the Teacher, holding a fan and being seated, recited the Pātimokkha. The same method applies to the second and third times. It is the same for all assemblies of the remaining Buddhas. However, since for our Blessed One, the assembly occurred only during the first period of enlightenment, and this sutta was spoken at a later time, He did not conclude with "Monks, now there is only one assembly of my disciples," but rather said, "There was [an assembly]."

In that context, "twelve hundred and fifty monks" refers to the one thousand former matted-hair ascetics (Jaṭilas) and the two hundred and fifty followers of the two chief disciples, totaling twelve hundred and fifty monks. In this regard, the story should be told starting from the aspiration of the two chief disciples to show their ordination. Among those who were ordained, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reached Arahantship on the seventh day. The General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, on the fifteenth day, while the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta was being preached to his nephew, the wandering ascetic Dīghanakha, at the Sūkarakhata cave in the middle of Mount Gijjhakūṭa, followed the teaching with his insight and attained the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection (Sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa). The Blessed One, knowing the Elder's attainment of Arahantship, ascended into the air and descended at the Veḷuvana Monastery itself. The Elder, reflecting, "Where has the Blessed One gone?" and knowing He was at Veḷuvana, also ascended into the air and descended at Veḷuvana. Then the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha. Referring to that assembly, the Blessed One said, "twelve hundred and fifty monks." This is called the Definition of the Assembly of Disciples (Sāvaka-sannipāta-pariccheda).
14:
Having said, "I will serve the Blessed One," and when asked, "Ānanda, what benefit do you see in such service?", he replied: "Venerable Sir, in this Dispensation, there are sons of good family with faith who, not getting an opportunity to approach the Blessed One, say to me: 'Venerable Ānanda, please accept alms at our house tomorrow together with the Blessed One.' Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One does not go there, I will not have the opportunity to show the assembly at the desired moment or to dispel their doubts. There will be critics saying: 'Why does Ānanda serve the Ten-Powered One? The Blessed One does not even grant him this much favor.' Also, in the absence of the Blessed One, people will ask me: 'Friend Ānanda, where was this verse, this sutta, this Jātaka preached?' If I cannot fulfill that request, there will be critics saying: 'Friend, do you not even know this much? Why do you wander for a long time following the Blessed One like a shadow?' Therefore, I desire the re-preaching of the Dhamma that was taught in your absence." Thus he made these four requests. The Blessed One granted them to him.

In this way, having taken these eight boons, he became the permanent attendant. For that position, he attained the fruit of the perfections (pāramīs) fulfilled for a hundred thousand aeons. Referring to this status of permanent attendant, He said: "Monks, now my attendant monk is Ānanda, the foremost attendant." This is called the Definition of the Attendant (Upaṭṭhāka-pariccheda).

The Definition of the Father (Piti-pariccheda) is clear in its meaning.

Regarding the phrase "He entered the monastery," why did He enter the monastery? It is said that the Blessed One, having spoken this much, thought: "I have not yet preached the lineage of the seven Buddhas continuously to the end. Today, when I enter the monastery, these monks will speak of my virtues even more extensively, based on the Knowledge of Past Lives (Pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). Then I will come and preach the Buddhavaṃsa continuously and show it to the end." Thus, giving the monks an opportunity for discussion, He rose from His seat and entered the monastery.

In the text that the Blessed One preached, these nine turns (vāra) appear: the Definition of the Aeon (Kappa-pariccheda), the Definition of Birth (Jāti-pariccheda), the Definition of Clan (Gotta-pariccheda), the Definition of Lifespan (Āyu-pariccheda), the Definition of Enlightenment (Bodhi-pariccheda), the Definition of the Pair of Disciples (Sāvaka-yuga-pariccheda), the Definition of the Assembly of Disciples (Sāvaka-sannipāta-pariccheda), the Definition of the Attendant (Upaṭṭhāka-pariccheda), and the Definition of the Father (Piti-pariccheda). The Section on the Many (Sambahulavāra) has not yet come; it should be brought forward and shown.
16:
Sutanā, Sabbakāmā, Sucittā, Rocinī, Rucaggatī, Sunandā, and the seventh, Bimbā.

These were the mothers of the sons of those seven Buddhas. However, Bimbādevī became known as Rāhulamātā (Mother of Rāhula) when Prince Rāhula was born. This is the Bhariyapariccheda (Classification of Wives).

These two Bodhisattas, Vipassī and Kakusandha, departed for the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana) riding a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses. These two, Sikhī and Koṇāgamana, departed having mounted the back of a noble elephant. Vessabhū departed while seated in a golden palanquin. Kassapa, while still seated on the great upper floor of the palace, produced the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna); emerging from that jhāna and using it as a basis, he resolved: "May the palace fly up and descend at the terrace of enlightenment (Bodhimanda)." The palace traveled through the air and descended at the terrace of enlightenment. The Great Being (Mahāpurisa) also descended from there, and standing on the ground, he thought: "May the palace stand in its original place." That palace stood in its original place. The Great Being, having exerted himself in meditation for seven days, attained omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) while seated on the throne of enlightenment (Bodhipallaṅka). Our Bodhisatta, however, departed riding the noble horse Kanthaka. This is the Yānapariccheda (Classification of Vehicles).

For the Blessed One Vipassī, the monastery was established in an area measuring one yojana; for Sikhī, three gāvutas; for Vessabhū, half a yojana; for Kakusandha, one gāvuta; for Koṇāgamana, half a gāvuta; for Kassapa, twenty usabhas. For our Blessed One, the monastery was established in an area measuring sixteen karīsas by standard measure, and eight karīsas by royal measure (rājamāna). This is the Vihārapariccheda (Classification of Monasteries).

For the Blessed One Vipassī, they had golden bricks made—one cubit in length, one span in width, and eight finger-breadths in height—and having laid them edge to edge, they purchased the site for the monastery. For Sikhī, they purchased it by covering the ground with the tips of golden spikes. For Vessabhū, they had golden elephant feet made, and having laid them edge to edge, they purchased it. For Kakusandha, they purchased it by covering the ground with golden bricks in the same manner as mentioned. For Koṇāgamana, they purchased it by covering the ground with golden tortoises in the same manner as mentioned.
18:
Difference in lineage (Kulavematta) means that some Buddhas are born in the Khattiya (warrior-noble) lineage, while some Buddhas are born in the Brāhmaṇa (brahmin) lineage. Difference in exertion (Padhānavematta) means that for some Buddhas, the period of exertion is only a short time, as it was for the Blessed One Kassapa. For some Buddhas, it is for a long time, as it was for our Blessed One. Difference in radiance (Rassivematta) means that the bodily radiance of the Blessed One Maṅgala extended to ten thousand world systems. The radiance of our Blessed One was only about one fathom around him. That difference in radiance is connected to the inclination (ajjhāsaya); for whomsoever desires a certain amount, for that person the bodily radiance spreads to that extent. For the Blessed One Maṅgala, however, there was the inclination: "May it always spread to ten thousand world systems." But regarding the qualities that are penetrated (paṭividdhaguṇa), there is no difference whatsoever among any of the Buddhas.

Furthermore, they showed the classification of the co-natals (sahajāta) and the classification of the constellations (nakkhatta) of our Blessed One. It is said that together with the Omniscient Bodhisatta, these seven co-natals came into existence: the mother of Rāhula, the Elder Ānanda, the minister Channa, the horse Kanthaka, the four great pots of treasure, the Great Bodhi tree, and the minister Kāḷudāyī. The Great Being descended into his mother's womb under the constellation of Uttarāsāḷha, departed for the Great Renunciation, preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, and performed the Twin Miracle (Yamakapāṭihāriya). He was born, attained enlightenment, and entered Parinibbāna under the constellation of Visākhā. The assembly of disciples took place and he relinquished the life-force under the constellation of Māgha. He descended from the celestial realm under the constellation of Assayuza. These matters should be brought forth and shown. This is called the Sambahulapariccheda (Classification of Various Matters).

Now, in the sentences beginning with 'Atha kho tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ', those monks said: "Friends, this is the destination of the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa), namely, the ascending to rebirth starting from death. But this matter of sending the knowledge backward starting from rebirth to reach death is extremely difficult. The Blessed One spoke as if showing footprints in the sky." Thus, being filled with great wonder, they said, "It is wonderful, friends," and so on. Then, wishing to show another reason, they said, "Yatra hi nāma tathāgato," and so on. Therein, 'yatra hi nāma' is a particle in the sense of wonder; the meaning is 'such a Tathāgata.' In the word 'chinnapapañca', the obsessions (papañca) are these three defilements: craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and views (diṭṭhi). In the word 'chinnavaṭuma', 'vaṭuma' refers to the round of wholesome and unwholesome kamma. 'Pariyādinnavaṭṭa' is a synonym for that same round; the meaning is that the entire round of kamma has been exhausted. 'Sabbadukkhavītivatta' means one who has transcended the suffering known as the entire round of results (vipākavaṭṭa)...
22:
(Old age, sickness, and death) are not apparent. There is no Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas that is devoid of the Three Characteristics. When they preach 'Anicca, Dukkha, and Anatta,' people do not think to listen or believe, wondering, 'What are these people talking about?' Because of this, the realization of the Dhamma (abhisamaya) cannot occur. In the absence of such realization, the Dispensation (Sāsana) cannot be a means of deliverance from the cycle of rebirth. Therefore, that period is not the proper time (for a Buddha to arise). A period when the lifespan is less than a hundred years is also not the proper time. Why? Because at that time, beings have excessive defilements (kilesas), and the advice given to those with excessive defilements does not remain in the place of advice; it disappears quickly like a line drawn on water with a stick. Therefore, that period is also not the proper time. Only the period when the lifespan is between one hundred thousand and one hundred years is called the proper time. At that time, the human lifespan was eighty thousand years. Then the Great Being (Mahāsatta) observed the time, thinking, 'It is the time to be reborn.'

Then, while observing the island, he looked at the four great islands along with their surrounding islands and saw, 'Buddhas are not born in the three islands; they are born only in Jambudīpa.' Thus he observed the island.

Then, thinking, 'Jambudīpa is indeed large, measuring ten thousand yojanas; in which region are Buddhas born?' he observed the region and saw the Majjhimadesa (Middle Country). The Majjhimadesa is indeed described in the Vinaya texts in this manner: 'In the eastern direction, there is a market town named Gajaṅgala,' and so on. That Majjhimadesa is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty in width, and nine hundred in circumference. In this region alone, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Disciples, Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti), and other powerful Khattiyas, Brahmins, and wealthy householders (Mahāsāla) are born. 'In this region, there is a city named Bandhumatī; I must be reborn there,' he reached this conclusion.

Then, while observing the family, he thought, 'Buddhas are born in a family esteemed by the world. At present, the Khattiya (warrior-noble) family is the one esteemed by the world; I will be born in that family. King Bandhumā will be my father.' Thus he observed the family.

Then, while observing the mother, he thought, 'The mother of a Buddha must not be flighty or addicted to intoxicants. She must have fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for a hundred thousand aeons and must have kept the five precepts (pañcasīla) unbroken since birth. This Queen named Bandhumatī is such a person; she shall be my mother...'
23:
When he reflected on how long her lifespan would be, he saw, 'Ten months and seven days.'

Having thus conducted these Five Great Observations, he gave his word, accepting the request of the deities, saying, 'Friends, the time has come for me to become a Buddha.' He then dismissed those deities, saying, 'You may go,' and surrounded by the deities of Tusita, he entered the Nandana Grove in the city of Tusita. Indeed, there is a Nandana Grove in every celestial realm. There, the deities wander about, reminding him of his previously performed meritorious deeds, saying, 'Pass away from here and go to a happy destination.' While wandering there, surrounded by deities reminding him of his merit, the Bodhisatta passed away.

When he thus passed away, he knew, 'I am passing away,' but he did not know the death-consciousness (cuti-citta). Even after taking rebirth, he knew it, but he did not know the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) itself. However, he did know, 'I have taken rebirth in this place.' Some elders say, 'He ought to obtain the sequence of reflection (āvajjana-pariyāya), and will know only at the second or third thought-moment.' But the Tipitaka Mahāsīva Thera said, 'The rebirth of Great Beings is not like the rebirth of others; their mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) reach the highest point. However, because that consciousness cannot be known by that same consciousness, he does not know the death-consciousness. Even at the moment of death, he knows, "I am passing away." Although he does not know the rebirth-linking consciousness, he knows, "I have taken rebirth in such a place." At that time, the ten thousand world systems tremble.' Thus, descending into his mother's womb with mindfulness and clear comprehension, among the nineteen types of rebirth-linking consciousness, he took rebirth with a Great Resultant (Mahā-vipāka) consciousness similar to the unprompted wholesome consciousness associated with joy and knowledge (somanassa-sahagata ñāṇa-sampayutta asaṅkhārika) preceded by loving-kindness. Mahāsīva Thera, however, said it was with a consciousness associated with equanimity (upekkhā-sahagata). Just as our Buddha took rebirth on the full moon day of Āsāḷha under the constellation of Uttarāsaḷha, so did this Bodhisatta.

At that time, it is said that in the city, starting from seven days before the full moon, people celebrated a festival of constellations, free from intoxicants and magnificent with flowers and perfumes. On the seventh day, the Bodhisatta's mother rose early, bathed in scented water, adorned herself with all ornaments, and ate excellent food. Having undertaken the Uposatha vows, she entered the state chamber (siri-gabbha) and, while falling asleep on the auspicious couch (siri-sayana), she saw this dream: 'Four...'
24:
It is said that the Great Kings lifted her up along with her bed and took her to Lake Anotatta. Having bathed her, they dressed her in divine garments, anointed her with divine scents, and adorned her with divine flowers. Not far from there was a silver mountain, inside of which was a golden mansion. They laid her down there with her head towards the east. Then the Bodhisatta, having become a noble white elephant, wandered on a golden mountain nearby. Descending from there, he ascended the silver mountain, entered the golden mansion, and having circumambulated his mother three times, he seemed to enter her womb through her right side.

Then the Queen, having awakened, reported the dream to the King. When the night had turned to dawn, the King summoned sixty-four eminent Brahmins. On a ground prepared with auspicious offerings such as parched grain and smeared with green cow-dung, he had costly seats arranged. To the Brahmins seated there, he offered excellent milk-rice prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar, served in gold and silver bowls, and covered with gold and silver lids. He also satisfied them with other gifts such as new clothes and tawny cows. Having thus satisfied them with all their desires, he related the dream and asked, "What will happen?" The Brahmins said, "Do not worry, Great King. A conception has taken place in the Queen's womb. It is a male child, not a female. You will have a noble son. If he lives the household life, he will become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). If he leaves the household life and goes forth into homelessness, he will surely become a Buddha, the one who draws away the veil from the world." This is the explanation of the phrase "He descended into his mother's womb."

"Ayamettha dhammatā" means this is the nature (niyāma) of descending into the mother's womb in this context. It is said that this is the natural way, this is the fixed law. This fixed law (niyāma) is fivefold: the law of kamma (kamma-niyāma), the law of seasons (utu-niyāma), the law of seeds (bīja-niyāma), the law of mind (citta-niyāma), and the law of nature (dhamma-niyāma).

Among them, the law of kamma is the giving of pleasant results by wholesome kamma and unpleasant results by unwholesome kamma. To illustrate this, the stories of the verses beginning with "Na antalikkhe" should be told. In brief, a certain woman, having quarreled with her husband and wishing to die by hanging, placed a noose around her neck.
25:
Wishing to die, she placed her neck in the noose. A certain man, while sharpening a knife, saw the woman's action and ran towards her to comfort her, wishing to cut the rope, saying, "Do not be afraid, do not be afraid!" At that moment, the rope turned into a cobra and stood there. The man, being terrified, fled. The woman died right there. Such stories should be shown here.

The law of seasons (utu-niyāma) refers to such things as the simultaneous blooming and fruiting of trees in various regions at various times, the blowing or non-blowing of the wind, the intensity or mildness of the sun's heat, the falling or non-falling of rain, and the blooming of lotuses by day and their closing by night.

The law of seeds (bīja-niyāma) is that from a rice seed only rice fruit is produced, from a sweet seed only a sweet taste, and from a bitter seed only a bitter taste.

The law of mind (citta-niyāma) is the arising of receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana) and so forth immediately after eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa), due to the preceding mental states (citta-cetasika) assisting the succeeding mental states by way of the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya).

The law of nature (dhamma-niyāma) is the occurrence of events such as the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system when the Bodhisattas descend into their mother's womb. In this context, the law of nature is intended. Therefore, to show this meaning, the Buddha said, "This, monks, is the nature (dhammatā)," and so forth.

In that passage, "kucchiṃ okkamati" (descends into the womb) means he has already descended into the womb. This happens only when he has already descended, not while he is descending. "Appamāṇo" means exceeding any measure. "Vipulo" means vast. "Uḷāro" is a synonym for that same vastness. In passages such as "they eat sublime (uḷāra) foods," "uḷāra" is said to mean delicious. In passages such as "the venerable Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with sublime (uḷāra) praise," "uḷāra" is said to mean excellent. However, in this context, it is intended to mean vast. "Devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ" (the divine majesty of the gods) means surpassing the majesty of the gods, whose radiance from their clothes, bodies, ornaments, and mansions spreads for twelve yojanas.
26:
Lokantarika means the occurrence of a Lokantarika hell in the space between every three world systems (Cakkavāḷas), just like the empty space in the middle when three cartwheels or three alms-bowls are placed touching one another. This Lokantarika hell is eight thousand yojanas in extent. Because it is always open, it is unobstructed (agha); it also has no foundation at the bottom (asaṃvuta). It is enveloped in a great mass of darkness. It is endowed with a blinding gloom because it prevents the arising of visual consciousness. It is said that visual consciousness does not arise in that hell. The moon and the sun are so powerful that they appear simultaneously in three continents. They dispel the darkness and show light over an area of nine hundred thousand yojanas in each direction; such is their great majesty. When it is said that they cannot overwhelm it with their light, it means that those moons and suns travel in the middle of the Cakkavāḷa mountains, whereas the Lokantarika hells are located outside the Cakkavāḷa mountains. Therefore, those moons and suns cannot overwhelm that place with their light.

'The beings who are there' refers to the beings who are born in that Lokantarika Great Hell. As for what kind of kamma they performed to be born there—they are born there due to committing grave and cruel offenses against their parents and against virtuous ascetics (samaṇas) and brahmins, and for performing cruel deeds such as killing living beings daily. They are like the thieves Abhaya and Nāga on the island of Tambapaṇṇi. The bodies of those beings are three gāvutas in size, and they have long nails like bats. They cling to the Cakkavāḷa mountains with their nails like bats on a tree. While crawling, when they touch each other's hands, they think, "We have found food," and as they struggle there, they flip over and fall into the water that supports the world. When the wind blows, they break off and fall into the water like Madhuka fruits falling. As soon as they fall, they dissolve like a lump of flour in the extremely salty water.

When they say, "O friends, there are other beings as well," it means that on that day, they see and think, "O friends, just as we are experiencing great suffering, other beings have also been born here to experience this suffering." This light does not last even for the duration of drinking a single cup of gruel (yāgu). It emerges for only a moment, like a flash of lightning or the snap of a finger, and vanishes even while they are saying, "What is this?" 'Trembled' means shaking all around. The other two terms are merely synonyms for the first term. Furthermore, the statement beginning with "immeasurable" is said for the purpose of conclusion.
32:
It should be understood. These turns (vāra) appear in the Pali text. However, many turns do not appear; those turns should be brought in and explained.

On the day the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) was born, the ten-thousandfold world system (lokadhātu) trembled. Deities and Brahmas from the ten-thousandfold world system assembled in a single world system (Cakkavāḷa). First, the deities received him, and later, humans received him. Harps bound with strings and drums bound with skin sounded by themselves without anyone playing them. The shackles and bonds of humans were broken into pieces. All diseases were calmed; they became pure like copper rust washed away by an acidic liquid. Those born blind saw forms. Those born deaf heard sounds. The lame became endowed with speed. Even those born dull-witted, mute, or deaf gained mindfulness. Ships that had set out to sea reached good ports. Treasures situated in the sky and on the earth shone with their own power. Those with enmity attained a mind of loving-kindness. The fire in the Avīci hell was extinguished. Light appeared in the Lokantarika hells. Water in the rivers ceased to flow. The water in the great ocean became sweet in taste. The wind stopped blowing. Birds in the sky, on mountains, and in trees descended to the ground. The moon shone exceedingly bright. The sun was neither too hot nor too cold, and the season became pure and perfect. Deities, standing at the doors of their own celestial mansions, celebrated a great festival by clapping their hands, shouting, and waving their garments. A great rain fell over all four great islands. The great masses of people were no longer oppressed by hunger or thirst. Door-leaves opened by themselves. Trees that bear flowers and fruits took on flowers and fruits. The ten-thousandfold world system became like a single mass of banners and garlands.

Among those events, the trembling of the ten-thousandfold world system is the omen (pubbanimitta) for the attainment of Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). The assembly of deities in a single world system is the omen for their assembling all at once to listen to the Dhamma when the Wheel of Dhamma is set in motion. The deities receiving him first is the omen for the attainment of the four fine-material sphere jhānas (rūpāvacara jhāna). The humans receiving him later is the omen for the attainment of the four immaterial sphere jhānas (arūpāvacara jhāna). The harps with strings sounding by themselves is the omen for the attainment of the successive attainments (anupubbavihāra). The sounding of the skin-bound drums is the omen for the sounding of the great drum of Dhamma. The breaking of bonds is the omen for the total eradication of the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna). The cessation of diseases for the great masses is the omen for the realization of the Four Truths. The blind seeing forms is the omen for the attainment of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu)...
34:
"...did he go, or did he go as an elderly person? Later on, did he remain like that, or did he become a young child again?" they asked. This question arose at the lower Lohapāsāda monastery and was answered by the Elder Tipiṭakacūḷābhaya. The Elder, having spoken much regarding the doctrines of fatalism (niyativāda), past actions (pubbekatakammavāda), and creation by a supreme lord (issaranimmānavāda), finally explained: "The Great Being walked on the ground, but to the great multitude, it appeared as if he were traveling through the sky. He walked while clearly visible, but to the great multitude, it appeared as if he were invisible. He walked without clothes, but to the great multitude, he appeared as if adorned and well-dressed. He walked as a mere child, but to the great multitude, he appeared like a youth of sixteen years. Afterwards, however, he was just a young child; he was not like that [the appearance] anymore." The assembly was delighted, saying, "The Elder has answered the question as if he were the Buddha himself." The section on the Lokantarika hell is as previously described.

It should be understood that all these natural occurrences (dhammatā) mentioned from the beginning happen to all Bodhisattas.

## Description of the Thirty-Two Marks of a Great Man

"He saw" means he saw the Great Being who had been brought and laid down on a coil made of silk. "Of the Great Man" (Mahāpurisassa) refers to a man who is great by way of birth, lineage, family, region, and so on. "Two destinies" (dve gatiyo) means two ends, two fulfillments. For this word gati—in the passage "Sāriputta, there are these five destinies" (M. i. 153)—it refers to the destination to be reached by beings, such as hell and so on. In the passage "I do not know the coming or going (gati) of these virtuous monks of good character" (M. i. 508), it refers to intention (ajjhāsaya). In the passage "Nirvana is the destination (gati) of the Arahant" (Pari. 339), it refers to the refuge (paṭissaraṇa). In the passage "Moreover, Brahma, I know your destination (gati) and I know your splendor, Baka Brahma of such great power" (M. i. 503), it refers to fulfillment (nipphatti). It should be understood that here too, it refers to fulfillment. "No other" means there is no other destiny or fulfillment.

"Righteous" (dhammiko) means one endowed with the ten wholesome courses of action, free from following the four wrong paths (agati). "King of Righteousness" (dhammarājā) is just a synonym for the preceding term. Or, he is called "King of Righteousness" because he obtained kingship through righteousness.
35:
"Cāturanto" means the ruler of the earth bounded by the four oceans, such as the eastern ocean. "Vijitāvī" means a conqueror of battles. "Janapadatthāvariyappatto" means one who has attained stability and firmness in this country. For when a fierce king oppresses the world with taxes and punishments, people abandon the middle country and live in the border regions, relying on mountains and seashores. Under an excessively soft king, people oppressed by the violent plundering of wealth by thieves abandon the border regions and live in the middle of the country. Under such kings, the country does not attain stability. However, to show that when this prince rules, this country will be as firm as if placed on a stone slab and encircled with iron bands, they said, "Janapadatthāvariyappatto."

In the term "Sattaratana-samannāgato" (endowed with the seven treasures), it is called a "treasure" (ratana) because it produces delight. Furthermore:

"Because it is cherished, of great value, incomparable, rare to see, and used by noble beings, it is called a treasure."

From the time the Wheel Treasure appears, there are no other shrines (devaṭṭhāna); everyone honors and pays homage to that Wheel Treasure with scents, flowers, and so on; thus it is a treasure in the sense of being cherished. No price can be set on the Wheel Treasure, saying it is worth this much wealth; thus it is a treasure also in the sense of being of great value. The Wheel Treasure is unlike other treasures existing in the world; thus it is a treasure also in the sense of being incomparable. Since Wheel-turning Monarchs appear only in the same aeons (kappa) in which Buddhas arise, and Buddhas arise only once in a while, it is a treasure also in the sense of being rare to see. That treasure arises only for a noble being (uḷārasatta) who is distinguished by birth, appearance, family, and power, and not for anyone else; thus it is a treasure also in the sense of being used by noble beings. As with the Wheel Treasure, so it is with the remaining treasures. Because he is endowed with these seven treasures as a retinue and as all means of enjoyment, he is called "Sattaratana-samannāgato."

Now, to show them individually, the passage beginning with "Tassimāni" is stated. Therein, among the Wheel Treasure and so on, this is the summary of the meaning: The Wheel Treasure appears, capable of taking and giving the glory and wealth of the four great islands surrounded by two thousand small islands. Likewise, the Elephant Treasure appears, capable of traveling around the earth bounded by the ocean in just one morning, able to go through the sky. Likewise the Horse Treasure. Endowed with the four factors...
36:
The Gem Treasure (Maṇiratana) appears, which is capable of dispelling darkness for the distance of a league and enabling the seeing of light. The Woman Treasure (Itthiratana) appears, who is free from the six faults and pleasing to the heart. The Householder Treasure (Gahapatiratana) appears, who is capable of seeing hidden treasures buried within the earth for the distance of a league. The Counselor Treasure (Pariṇāyakaratana) appears, who is the eldest son born from the womb of the chief queen and is capable of advising the entire kingdom.

'Parosahassaṃ' means more than a thousand (sons). 'Sūrā' means those who are free from fear. 'Vīraṅgarūpā': the limb of a hero is called 'vīraṅga', which is a name for energy (vīriya); because they have a physical form endowed with that energy, they are called 'vīraṅgarūpā'. They are of an energetic nature, energetic by character, made of energy, and free from lethargy. It means they do not get tired even if they fight all day. 'Sāgarapariyantaṃ' means the earth bounded by the ocean, with the Cakkavāḷa mountains as its limit. 'Adaṇḍena': those who rule by punishing beings who have committed offenses with fines of a hundred or a thousand rule by the rod of wealth. Some advise by cutting or breaking; they rule by the rod of weapons. But this king, renouncing both types of punishment, dwells without a rod. 'Asatthena': those who rule by harming others with weapons such as single-edged swords rule by the weapon. But this king, without causing even as much blood as a small fly might drink to flow by a weapon, conquers and dwells over the aforementioned earth righteously, accepted and welcomed by rival kings with the words 'Come, Great King'; he dwells as the master, having overcome it.

Having thus spoken of one accomplishment, to speak of the second, the passage beginning with 'Sace kho pana' is stated. Therein, 'vivaṭacchado' means one for whom the covering or veil consisting of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, wrong view, defilements, and craving has been opened and destroyed. There is also a variant reading 'vivaṭṭacchadā', but the meaning is the same.

Having thus spoken of the second accomplishment, to show the signs that are the causes of those accomplishments, the passage beginning with 'Ayañhi, deva, kumာro' is stated. Therein, 'suppatiṭṭhitapādo' (well-planted feet) means that while for others, when placing the foot on the ground, the forefoot, the heel, or the side touches first, or there is a gap in the middle, and when lifting the foot, only one part like the forefoot rises first, it is not so for him. His entire sole touches the ground all at once, like the surface of a golden sandal, and rises from the ground all at once. Therefore, he is called 'suppatiṭṭhitapādo'.
47:
'Tena hi' means: 'If I too must have such hair and such a body, then, friend charioteer, (let us return).' 'Alaṃ dānajja uyyānabhūmiyā' means: having set out saying 'Today we shall go and see the pleasure garden,' he speaks in accordance with his spiritual urgency (saṃvega), having a dismayed heart, thinking that there is no more use for that pleasure garden. Upon reaching the palace, he dismissed the women and sat alone in the auspicious chamber. 'Yatra hi nāma' means: where there is birth (jāti), old age (jarā) is manifest; that birth is truly loathsome and contemptible. Viewing this birth as something disgusting, he sat as if digging up the root of birth, like one pierced in the heart by the first arrow.

'Sārathiṃ āmantāpetvā' means: the King, from the time the omen-readers spoke, had been listening watchfully. Hearing that 'the Prince, while going to the garden, turned back midway,' he had the charioteer summoned. In the passage beginning with 'Mā heva kho', it means he thought: 'Let him only rule the kingdom, let him not go forth into homelessness, let the words of the Brahmins not be true.'

## Description of the Sick Man (Byādhipurisa-vaṇṇanā)

'Addasa kho' means he saw (the sick man) shown by the devas of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), just as described previously. 'Ābādhikaṃ' means one who is pained by an uneven affliction that breaks the physical postures. 'Dukkhitaṃ' means one suffering from the pain of disease. 'Bāḷhagilānaṃ' means one who is excessively ill. 'Palipannaṃ' means one wallowing (in his own excrement and urine). 'Jarā paññāyissati byādhi paññāyissati' means: here too, where there is birth, these two are manifest; that birth is truly contemptible, and only non-birth is safety. Thus he sat as if digging up the root of birth, like one pierced by a second arrow.

## Description of the Dead Man (Kālaṅkatapurisa-vaṇṇanā)

'Vilātaṃ' means a litter (palanquin). 'Petaṃ' means one who has passed away from this life. 'Kālaṅkataṃ' means one who has reached the end of his time; it means one who has died after completing and finishing whatever span of time he was meant to live. The Brahmas also showed this person in the same manner as before. 'Yatra hi nāma' means: here too, where there is birth, these three are manifest; that birth is truly contemptible, and only non-birth is safety. Thus he sat as if digging up the root of birth, like one pierced by a third arrow.
49:
Anupabbajitāni. Why is it not stated here, as it is in the later account of the renunciation of Khaṇḍa and Tissa, "having departed from the royal city of Bandhumatī"? It is because they heard the news only after they had already left the city. All of them were attendants of Prince Vipassī. They came to serve him in the early morning, but not finding the Prince, they went to eat breakfast. After eating, they returned and asked, "Where is the Prince?" Hearing that he had gone to the park, they set out thinking, "We shall see him there." While leaving the city, they met the returning charioteer. Upon hearing his words, "The Prince has gone forth," they removed all their ornaments right where they heard the news, sent for dyed robes from the shops, shaved their hair and beards, and went forth. Thus, because they heard the news outside the city after having already departed, it is not stated here "having departed from the royal city of Bandhumatī."

Cārikaṃ carati — Wandering on tour: This means that in every place he reached, a great pavilion was constructed and offerings were prepared. He wandered for four months, accepting only the alms-food requested by the people who had invited him for the following day.

Ākiṇṇo — Crowded: Surrounded by this group. When did this thought arise in the Bodhisatta? It was on the fourteenth day, thinking, "Tomorrow will be the full moon of Visākhā." At that time, the Bodhisatta, becoming weary of the crowd, thought: "These people surround and follow me now just as they did before when I was a layman; what is the use of this crowd?" He thought, "I will go this very day," but then reconsidered, "Today is not the right time; if I go now, everyone will know; I will go only tomorrow."

On that day, in a village similar to Uruvelā, the villagers invited him for the next day. They prepared only milk-rice for the eighty-four thousand renunciants and the Great Being (the Bodhisatta). Then, on the following day, after finishing the meal in that village with those monks, the Great Being went to his usual dwelling. There, those monks performed their duties for the Great Being and then entered their respective places for the night and day. The Bodhisatta also entered the leaf-hut (dwelling) and sat down.

"When the sun stands still at the hour of midday, and the birds are silent, the great forest seems to roar; that fearsome state appears to me" (as found in the Saṃyutta Nikāya).
56:
It is the name for ignorance (avijjā) and so on, which are the causes of formations (saṅkhāra) and so forth. "Sabbasaṅkhārasamatha" and the following terms all refer to Nibbāna. Because all the agitations of formations are stilled and calmed upon reaching that Nibbāna, it is called "Sabbasaṅkhārasamatha" (the stilling of all formations). And because all acquisitions (upadhi) are relinquished, all craving (taṇhā) is exhausted, all lust of the defilements (kilesa-rāga) fades away, and all suffering (dukkha) ceases upon reaching that Nibbāna, it is called "Sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodho."

That craving is called "vāna" because it weaves or sews together existence with existence, or action with its fruit. Because of the departure from that "vāna," it is called "Nibbāna."

"That task would be wearying to me" means that teaching the Dhamma to those who do not know would be a weariness and a vexation to me. It refers to physical weariness and physical vexation; however, in the mind, neither of these exists for the Buddhas.

"Apissu" is a particle used in the sense of augmentation. It shows: "Not only did this thought occur, but these verses also became clear." In the passage beginning with "Vipassinti," it refers to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. "Anacchariyā" means wonderful or unprecedented. "Paṭibhaṃsu" means they became objects of the knowledge known as intuition (paṭibhāna); they reached the state of being contemplated.

"Kicchena" means with difficulty (attained), but not through a painful practice (dukkhā paṭipadā). For the Buddhas, all four paths are pleasant practices (sukhā paṭipadā). However, this is said in reference to the "attainment-practice" (āgamanīya-paṭipadā) during the time of fulfilling perfections. At that time, while still possessing lust, hatred, and delusion, he gave his decorated head, drew blood from his throat, plucked out his well-anointed eyes for any beggars who came, and gave away his son, the light of the lineage, and his devoted wife, and underwent cutting and breaking of the body in lives such as the Preacher of Patience (Khantivādī). It is with reference to this that it is so stated.

In the word "Halaṃ," the letter "ha" is merely a particle; it means "Alaṃ" (enough/sufficient). "Pakāsituṃ" means to teach. It means: "Enough of teaching this Dhamma attained with such difficulty; what is the use of teaching it?"

"Rāgadosaparetehi" means those touched by lust and hatred, or those followed by lust and hatred.

"Paṭisotagāmiṃ" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Truths that goes against the stream of views such as permanence (nicca), etc., as impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), non-self (anatta), and foulness (asubha). "Rāgarattā" means those infatuated with sensual lust, lust for existence, and lust for views. "Na dakkhanti" means they cannot see through this nature of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness.
62:
He should be known as 'Vijitasaṅgāma' (Conqueror of the Battle) because he has conquered the defilements; as 'Satthavāha' (Caravan Leader) because of his ability to lead venayyas (beings to be tamed) across the difficult journey of rebirth and so forth; and as 'Aṇaṇa' (Debtless) because he is free from the debt of sensual desire.

'Apārutā' means opened. 'Amatassa dvārā' refers to the Noble Path. Indeed, that Path is the door to Nibbāna, which is called the Deathless. He shows that 'I have opened that door and left it so.' 'Pamuñcantu saddhaṃ' means let all people release their faith. In the last two padas, this is the meaning: 'I remained without teaching this sublime and supreme Dhamma, which I have mastered and well-developed, thinking that it would be a weariness to my body and speech; but now, let the multitude of people bring forth the vessel of faith, and I shall fulfill their aspirations.'

## Description of the Pair of Chief Disciples

'Bodhirukkhamūle' means he disappeared (returned to the celestial realm) at the Ajapāla Banyan tree, which is not far from the Bodhi tree. 'Kheme Migadāye' means that at that time, Isipatana was a park named Khema; it is called Migadāya (Deer Park) because it was given as a sanctuary for deer. Referring to that, it is said, 'Kheme Migadāye.' Just like the Buddha Vipassī, other Buddhas also, when going for the first time to teach the Dhamma, travel through the air and descend at that very spot. However, our Blessed One, seeing the potential (upanissaya) of the Ājīvaka Upaka, and knowing that 'Upaka is traveling on this road; he will see me, converse with me, and then go; later, becoming disenchanted, he will return and realize the fruit of Arahantship,' traveled the eighteen-yojana journey on foot. 'Dāyapālaṃ āmantesi' means that as soon as he saw him, he looked at him repeatedly and called out to the one who approached, saying, 'Venerable sir, our master has arrived.'

75-6. 'Anupubbī kathaṃ' means he taught the discourse in gradual order: the discourse on giving (dāna), followed by virtue (sīla), followed by heaven (sagga), and followed by the path (magga). Therein, 'Dāna-kathā' means this giving is the source of happiness, the foundation of prosperity, the basis of wealth, and the protection, refuge, destination, and final resort for one who has gone astray. In this world and the next, there is no support, foundation, object, protection, refuge, destination, or final resort equal to giving. In the sense of being a support, it is like a jeweled lion-throne; in the sense of being a foundation, it is like the great earth.
63:
In the sense of being an object of focus, it is like a rope to be grasped. This giving is like a boat in the sense of crossing over suffering; like a hero on the battlefield in the sense of providing relief; like a well-fortified city in the sense of protecting from danger; like a lotus in the sense of being unstained by the impurities of stinginess and so forth; like fire in the sense of burning those defilements; like a cobra in the sense of being difficult to approach; like a lion in the sense of being fearless; like a bull-elephant in the sense of being endowed with strength; like a white auspicious bull in the sense of being considered highly auspicious; and like the horse-king Valāhaka in the sense of bringing one to the land of safety. Indeed, giving bestows in this world the prosperity of Sakka, the prosperity of Māra, the prosperity of Brahmā, the prosperity of a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch), the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, and the knowledge of Supreme Enlightenment—thus is the discourse connected with the virtues of giving.

Because one who gives is able to undertake the precepts of virtue, he taught the discourse on virtue (sīla-kathā) immediately after that. 'Sīla-kathā' means: this virtue is a support, foundation, object, protection, refuge, destination, and final resort. For the prosperities of this world and the next, there is no support, foundation, object, protection, refuge, destination, or final resort equal to virtue. There is no ornament like virtue, no flower like the flower of virtue, and no fragrance like the fragrance of virtue. Indeed, even the world with its devas, looking upon one adorned with the ornament of virtue, wearing the flower of virtue, and anointed with the fragrance of virtue, never tires of the sight—thus is the discourse connected with the virtues of virtue.

To show that this heaven can be obtained by depending on this virtue, he taught the discourse on heaven (sagga-kathā) immediately after virtue. 'Sagga-kathā' means: this heaven is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; there is constant play there, and prosperities are constantly obtained. The devas of the Realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) enjoy divine happiness and divine prosperity for nine million years; the Tāvatiṃsa devas for thirty crores and six million years—thus is the discourse connected with the virtues of heaven. Indeed, the mouths of the Buddhas are not sufficient to describe the prosperity of heaven. It has also been said: 'Monks, I could speak the discourse on heaven in many ways,' and so forth.

Having thus attracted them with the discourse on heaven, then, like one who decorates an elephant and then cuts off its trunk, he showed: 'This heaven is also impermanent and unstable; one should not form desire and lust for it.' To demonstrate this, he taught the faults of sensual pleasures (kāmānaṃ ādīnava) in this manner: 'Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger in them is even greater,' and so forth.
67:
“Your Majesty, I am unable,” he replied. Then the King, realizing that “The citizens are powerful, and the general is also on their side,” said, “Grant me the opportunity to offer alms to the Saṅgha for another seven years and seven months.” The citizens did not accept. The King reduced his request to “six years, five, four, three, two, and one year.” Even with these reductions, they did not accept. He then requested another seven days. The citizens, thinking, “It is not proper to be so harsh with the King now,” granted his request.

The King distributed in just seven days the alms that had been prepared for seven years and seven months. For six days, he gave alms without letting anyone else see. On the seventh day, he summoned the citizens and asked, “Friends, will you be able to give such an offering?” They replied, “Was it not because of us that this offering became possible for Your Majesty? We shall be able to do so.” The King, wiping away tears with the back of his hand, paid homage to the Blessed One and said, “Venerable Sir, I intended to serve six million eight hundred thousand monks with the four requisites for the rest of my life without giving a turn to anyone else. Now the citizens do not grant me permission; they are angry, saying, ‘We do not get the chance to give alms.’ May the Blessed One show favor to them starting from tomorrow.”

Then, on the second day, the General prepared a great offering and stationed men all around, saying, “Guard the area so that no one else can give even a single spoonful of alms today.” On that day, the Treasurer’s wife, weeping, said to her daughter, “Dear daughter, if your father were alive, I would have been the first to offer alms to the Dasabala (the Buddha) today.” The daughter said to her mother, “Mother, do not worry. I will act so that the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, will partake of our alms first.” Then, she filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand with milk-rice prepared without water, seasoned it with ghee, honey, sugar, and so on, covered it with another bowl, and surrounded it with jasmine garlands to make it look like a ball of flowers. When the Blessed One was about to enter the village, she carried it herself and left the city surrounded by a group of maidservants. Along the way, the General’s attendants said, “Mother, do not go this way.” One of great merit (Mahāpuññā) is one who speaks pleasant words, and they were unable to reject her words even as she spoke repeatedly. She asked, “Uncles and brothers, why do you not let me pass?” They replied, “Mother, it is because the General has ordered us not to allow anyone else to give food.” “Do you see food in my hands? Do you not see a ball of flowers?”
68:
“We see it,” they said. She asked, “Does your General not even allow the offering of a ball of flowers?” They replied, “Mother, he allows it.” “In that case, move aside, move aside!” she said. Approaching the Blessed One, she said, “Venerable Sir, please accept this ball of flowers.” The Blessed One, looking at one of the General’s attendants, accepted the ball of flowers. The woman paid homage to the Blessed One and made a wish: “Venerable Sir, in whatever life I am born, may I never have a livelihood of anxiety. Like this jasmine flower, may I be beloved in every place I am born, and may my name be Sumanā.” The Teacher said, “May you be happy.” She paid homage, circumambulated him, and departed.

The Blessed One went to the General’s house and sat on the prepared seat. When the General approached with gruel, the Teacher covered his bowl. “Venerable Sir, the Saṅgha is seated,” he said. “We have already received one portion of alms on the way,” the Teacher replied. The General removed the flowers and saw the alms-food. The young attendant said, “Master, the woman deceived me by saying it was flowers.” The milk-rice was sufficient for all the monks, headed by the Buddha. The General also gave his own offerings. After the Teacher had finished his meal and spoken words of blessing, he departed. The General asked, “Who was it that gave that alms-food?” “It was the Treasurer’s daughter, Master,” they replied. “That woman is wise; for a man who has such a woman living in his house, the attainment of heavenly fortune is not difficult,” he said, and he brought her to his home and placed her in the position of chief wife.

The next day, the citizens gave alms; the day after that, the King gave alms. Thus, they began to give alms on alternate days. The King stationed spies and gave offerings that surpassed those given by the citizens. The citizens did the same, giving offerings that surpassed those given by the King. The dancing women in the palace said to the young novices, “Friends, take this; this offering was not made by hands that have wiped the clothes of householders or washed the mucus and saliva of children; it is prepared purely and excellently.” The next day, the citizens, while giving alms, said, “Friends, take this; this offering was not made with rice, milk, curd, or ghee collected from towns and villages, nor was it brought by beating the legs, heads, or backs of others; it is made only with pure ghee and milk.” In this way, seven years, seven months, and seven days passed. Then, this thought arose to the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said, “It arose after seven years, seven months, and seven days had passed since his Enlightenment.”
69:
"Another Great Brahmā" refers to the very Brahmā who requested the preaching of the Dhamma.

"Eighty-four thousand dwellings" refers to eighty-four thousand monasteries (vihāras). All of them were great monasteries, similar to Abhayagiri, Cetiyapabbata, and Cittalapabbata Mahāvihāras, which could each accommodate twelve thousand monks.

"Patience is the highest austerity (tapo)" means that what is called patient endurance (adhivāsana-khanti) is the highest austerity. "Titikkhā" is a synonym for khanti. The meaning is that patient endurance, known as titikkhā, is the supreme austerity. "Nirvana is supreme" means the Buddhas declare that Nirvana is supreme in every way. "He who harms others is not a recluse (pabbajita)" means that one who, due to a lack of patient endurance, harms, oppresses, or hurts others is not called a recluse. The fourth line is a synonym for that same meaning. "Not a recluse (pabbajita)" is synonymous with "not a samana (ascetic)." "One who harms others" is synonymous with "one who oppresses others." Alternatively, "parūpaghātī" means one who destroys virtue (sīla). Virtue is called "para" (the highest) because of its supreme nature. The meaning is that any ascetic who, by oppressing any living being, becomes a harmer of others and a destroyer of his own virtue, is not called a recluse. Alternatively, one who, due to the absence of patient endurance, becomes a harmer of others and intentionally takes the life of even a gadfly or a mosquito, is not a recluse. Why? Because he has not cast out his defilements. "He casts out his own defilements (mala), therefore he is called a recluse (pabbajita)"—this is the characteristic of a recluse. Even if one does not harm or kill but oppresses others with sticks, weapons, etc., that person who oppresses others is not a samana. Why? Because his cruelty (vihesā) has not been calmed. "Because of the calming of evils, one is called a samana"—this is the characteristic of a samana.

In the second verse, "all evil" refers to all unwholesome states (akusala). "Not doing" means not giving rise to them. "Of the wholesome" refers to the wholesome states of the four planes. "Fulfillment" means attainment. "Purifying one's own mind" means brightening one's own mind; such purification occurs through the path of Arahantship (arahatta). Thus, by abandoning all evil through the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara), fulfilling the wholesome through tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā), and purifying the mind through the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala)—this is the teaching, the advice, the instruction of the Buddhas.
105: ...reached. Upon hearing this, a certain monk, a pupil of the Elder at Girivihāra, heard that question from the mouth of a monk on alms round and said: "Friend, while our teacher was praising the Dhamma at the lower Lohapāsāda, he preached a Dhamma that no one had ever heard before." When asked, "Venerable sir, what did the Elder say?", (he replied): Although the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere has two factors and is accompanied by equanimity, it only suppresses the defilements; however, defilements still occur in the close vicinity where they tend to grow. These defilements, in the five-constituent existence, arise depending on one of the objects such as blue, etc., and the fine-material sphere jhāna does not transcend that object. Therefore, only the one who, having turned away from all form, suppresses the defilements by the power of the formless jhāna and reaches the fruit of Arahantship, is called "one liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta). Thus, friend, did the Elder speak. Having said this, he cited this sutta: "What kind of person is one liberated in both ways? Here, a certain person dwells having touched the eight liberations with the mental body, and by wisdom, his taints are exhausted. This person is called one liberated in both ways" (as stated in the Puggalapaññatti). "Imāya ca Ānanda ubhatobhāgavimuttiyā" means, "Ānanda, because of this liberation in both ways." All the remaining words are clear. ## The Commentary on the Mahānidāna Sutta is finished.
106:
## 3. Commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth refers to the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta. In this sutta, the sequential explanation of terms is as follows: "Gijjhakūṭe" means that vultures live on the peaks of that mountain, or that its peak resembles a vulture; hence it is called Gijjhakūṭa (Vulture's Peak). At that Gijjhakūṭa mountain. "Abhiyātukāmo" means one who desires to go for the purpose of subduing. "Vajjī" refers to the Vajjian kings. "Evaṃmahiddhike" means endowed with such great royal power and majesty; by this, their state of unity is described. "Evaṃmahānubhāve" means endowed with such great majesty and influence; by this, their state of being well-trained in elephantry and so forth is described, referring to which it was said: "Indeed, these Licchavi princes are trained, indeed, these Licchavi princes are well-trained, in that they can shoot arrows one after another through a small keyhole without missing" (as mentioned in the Saṃyutta Nikāya).

"Ucchecchāmi" means I will exterminate them. "Vināsessāmi" means I will destroy them, I will make them disappear. In the term "anayavyasanaṃ," that which is not 'aya' (growth/prosperity) is 'anaya'; it is a name for the absence of prosperity. It is called 'vyasana' because it scatters or removes welfare and happiness; it is a name for the ruin of relatives and so forth. "Āpādessāmi" means I will cause them to reach [ruin].

Thus, King Ajātasattu spoke only of this war while standing, sitting, and so forth, and gave orders to his military forces, saying, "Prepare to march." Why? Near a port village by the Ganges, the distance of half a league was under the authority of King Ajātasattu, and half a league was under the authority of the Licchavi kings. The meaning is that it was a place where both authorities overlapped. In that place, valuable goods would also come down from the foot of the mountain. Hearing of this, while Ajātasattu was still planning, "I will go today, I will go tomorrow," the Licchavi kings, being united and joyful, would go earlier and take everything. King Ajātasattu, arriving later and learning of the situation, would return in anger. Those kings did the same in subsequent years as well. Then, King Ajātasattu, having developed a deep grudge, acted in that manner.

Then the King thought: "War against a group is a heavy matter; not a single blow is in vain. Indeed, if I act after consulting with a wise man, I will be faultless. And in terms of wisdom, there is no one equal to the Teacher (the Buddha). The Teacher is residing in the nearby Dhura-vihāra monastery. I shall send [someone] and...
107: ...will ask. "If there is benefit in my going, the Blessed One will remain silent; if there is no benefit, he will say, 'What is the use of the King going there?'" Thus he thought. That King sent the Brahmin Vassakāra. The Brahmin went and informed the Blessed One of this matter. Regarding that, it is said: "Atha kho rājā... pe... āpādessāmī." ## Commentary on the Conditions of Welfare for Kings. "Bhagavantaṃ bījayamāno" means the Elder Ānanda, standing in the performance of his duties, was fanning the Blessed One; although the Blessed One has no feeling of cold or heat (it was an act of service). Having heard the Brahmin's words, the Blessed One, wishing to consult with the Elder instead of the Brahmin, said: "Ānanda, what have you heard?" and so on. "Abhiṇhaṃ sannipātā" means assembling frequently, whether three times a day or at intervals. "Sannipātabahulā" means being frequent in assembly without reaching a state of weariness, such as saying, "We assembled yesterday, we assembled the day before, for what purpose do we assemble again today?" "Yāvakīvañca" means for as long as. "Vudḍhiyeva, Ānanda, Vajjīnaṃ pāṭikaṅkhā, no parihāni" means: if they do not assemble frequently, they do not hear the news coming from various directions; then they do not know, "Such a village boundary or town boundary is in disorder, or thieves have arisen in such a place." Thieves, knowing "The kings are negligent," attack villages and towns and destroy the countryside. Thus, there is decline for the kings. But if they assemble frequently, they hear various news; then they can send troops and suppress the enemies. Thieves also, thinking "The kings are vigilant, we cannot wander in groups," break up and flee. Thus, there is growth for the kings. Therefore, he said: "Ānanda, only growth is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline." In that context, "pāṭikaṅkhā" means to be desired, or it should be understood as "it will certainly happen." Regarding the words "samaggā" and so on, when the assembly drum is sounded, those who do not come, making excuses such as "Today I have work, I have a festival," are not said to assemble in concord. But those who, upon hearing the sound of the drum, come to the assembly even while eating, or while decorating themselves, or while putting on clothes—even if half-eaten, half-decorated, or in the middle of dressing—are said to assemble in concord. Having assembled, they deliberate, and having done what needs to be done, they [depart] together...
110:
'Kulitthiyo' refers to noble married women. 'Kulakumāriyo' refers to their young unmarried daughters. In the phrase 'okkassa pasayha', the terms 'okkassā' and 'pasayhā' are both names for the act of taking by force. It is also read as 'ukkassā'. In this context, 'okkassā' means dragging away, and 'pasayhā' means overwhelming and oppressing. When such acts of force are committed, the people of the country become angry, saying, 'These kings are forcibly taking the wives in our homes and our young daughters, whom we have raised by wiping away their mucus and such with our own hands, and are keeping them in their own houses.' They then enter the border regions and become bandits or associates of bandits, and destroy the countryside. However, when such acts are not committed, the people of the country, being free from anxiety, carry out their own work, and thus the royal treasury increases. In this way, the increase and decrease [of prosperity] should be understood here.

'Vajjīnaṃ vajjicetiyāni' refers to the dwelling places of yakkhas (spirits) which are called cetiyas because they are cherished and honored by the Vajjī kings in the Vajjī country. 'Abbhantarāni' refers to those located inside the city. 'Bāhirāni' refers to those located outside the city. 'Dinnapubbaṃ' means what was given in the past. 'Katapubbaṃ' means what was done in the past. 'No parihāpessanti' means they will not let them decline but will continue to offer the dhammika bali (righteous offerings) as before. For those who let the offerings to deities decline, the deities do not provide well-arranged protection. Although deities cannot cause suffering that has not yet arisen, they can increase existing ailments such as coughs and headaches; they also do not provide assistance when war is encountered. For those who do not let them decline, however, the deities provide well-arranged protection. Although they cannot produce happiness that has not yet arisen, they can heal existing ailments such as coughs and headaches; they also provide assistance on the battlefield. In this way, the increase and decrease [of prosperity] should be understood here.

In the phrase 'dhammikā rakkhāvaraṇagutti', 'rakkhā' (protection) is the prevention [of someone] from going to an undesired place. 'Gutti' (guarding) is the guarding [of things] so that desired things are not destroyed. In that protection, guarding by surrounding with an army is not what is called righteous protection, shelter, and guard for renunciants. Rather, acts such as not cutting trees in the monastery grove, not killing animals, and not catching fish in the ponds are what is called righteous protection, shelter, and guard. With the words 'anāgatā ca', [the Buddha] asks about the arising of the thoughts and intentions of those Vajjī kings.
112:
This shows that they can be conquered. The Brahmin said this after obtaining a hint from the Blessed One's discourse.

If one asks, 'Did the Blessed One not know that the Brahmin would obtain a hint from this discourse?' the answer is, 'Yes, he knew.' If he knew, why did he speak? It was out of compassion. It is said that the Blessed One had this thought: 'Even if I do not speak, he will go and conquer them all within a few days. But if I speak, it will take three years to break their unity before he can conquer them. Living for this much longer is indeed better; while living for this duration, they will perform meritorious deeds which will be their support.'

Abhinanditvā means rejoicing in the mind. Anumoditvā means expressing appreciation with words, such as 'This is indeed well-spoken by the Venerable Gotama.' Pakkāmi means he went to the King. Then the King asked, 'Teacher, what did the Blessed One say?' The Brahmin replied, 'According to the words of the Venerable Gotama, no one can conquer the Vajjian kings by war. However, they can be conquered either by persuasion or by sowing discord among them.' Then the King asked, 'If by persuasion, our elephants, horses, and so on will be destroyed. I will conquer them only by discord. What should we do?' The Brahmin replied, 'Great King, in that case, you should start a conversation about the Vajjian kings in the assembly. Then I will say, "Great King, what do you have to do with those Vajjis? Let those kings live by their own means, such as farming and trade," and then I will leave. Then you should say, "Why does this Brahmin obstruct the talk concerning the Vajjis?" In the afternoon, I will send them a gift. You should seize that gift as well, blame me, and without beating or binding me, simply shave my head bald and expel me from the city. Then I will say, "I have built the walls and moats in your city; I know the weak points, the shallow points, and the deep points, and I will soon make them straight (vulnerable)." Hearing this, you should say, "Let him go."' The King did everything accordingly.

When the Licchavis heard that the Brahmin was coming out, they said, 'He is a crafty Brahmin; do not let him cross the Ganges.' Then some said, 'It is said he was treated this way because he spoke on our behalf.' So they said, 'In that case, let him come.' When the Brahmin arrived and was seen by the Licchavis, he was asked, 'Why have you come?' and he told them the story. The Licchavis said, 'Such a heavy punishment should not have been given for such a minor offense...'
113:
"It is not appropriate," they said, and asked, "What rank do you hold in that country?" "I am a judge," he replied. "Then take that same rank here," they said. That Brahmin performed his judicial duties very well, and the princes learned arts and sciences from him.

Once he had gained their trust, one day he took a Licchavī prince aside and asked, "Do the children plow the fields?" "Yes, they do," the prince replied. "With two oxen yoked?" he asked. "Yes, with two oxen yoked," the prince replied. Saying only this much, he returned.
