Then another person asked, "What did the teacher say?" and not believing what the prince told him, thought, "He is not telling me the truth," and thus became estranged from him. On another day, the Brahmin took another Licchavī prince aside and asked, "With what curry did you eat?" and returned. When another person asked him and did not believe the answer, he too became estranged in the same way. On yet another day, the Brahmin took a Licchavī prince aside and asked, "Is it true that you are very poor?" When asked, "Who said so?" he replied, "Such-and-such a Licchavī prince said so." He took another aside and asked, "Is it true that you are a coward?" When asked, "Who said so?" he replied, "Such-and-such a Licchavī prince said so." In this way, by telling one person what another had not said, he caused discord among those kings within three years, making it so that even two of them would not travel the same road together. Then he had the assembly drum beaten. The Licchavī princes said, "Let the lords assemble, let the heroes assemble," but they did not assemble.

The Brahmin sent a message to the King, saying, "Now is the time; come quickly." Upon hearing this, the King had the war drum beaten and set out. When the people of Vesālī heard this, they beat their drums, saying, "We will not let the King cross the Ganges." Even hearing that, the princes said, "Let the hero-kings go," and so on, and did not assemble. They beat the drums again, saying, "We will not allow entry into the city; we will stay with the gates closed," but not a single person assembled. The King entered through the gates that remained open, brought everyone to ruin and destruction, and then departed.

## Commentary on the Conditions for Non-decline of Monks

Then, not long after Vassakāra Brahmin had departed, the Blessed One said, "acirapakkante" and so on. He sent monks with psychic powers to the distant monasteries and went personally to the nearby monasteries, causing them to assemble by saying, "Assemble, venerable sirs; the Blessed One wishes for you to assemble."
121:
The factor of enlightenment of rapture (pītisambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of pervading. The factor of enlightenment of tranquility (passaddhisambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of calming. The factor of enlightenment of concentration (samādhisambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of non-distraction. The factor of enlightenment of equanimity (upekkhāsambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of reflection. "They will develop" means they will increase the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness through four causes, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of states through six causes, the factor of enlightenment of energy through nine causes, the factor of enlightenment of rapture through ten causes, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility through seven causes, the factor of enlightenment of concentration through ten causes, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity through five causes. In this way, He taught the factors of enlightenment associated with the path and fruit of insight, which are a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.

In the fifth set of seven, "perception of impermanence" (aniccasaññā) is the perception that arises together with the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). The same method applies to the perception of non-self (anattasaññā) and so on. These seven are also mundane insight. According to the teaching that states, "This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation (Nibbāna)," it should be understood that here two (dispassion and cessation) are also supramundane.

In the set of six, "bodily action of loving-kindness" (mettā-kāyakamma) is bodily action that should be performed with a mind of loving-kindness. The same method applies to verbal action and mental action. Although these qualities are mentioned in terms of monks, they are also found among laypeople. For monks, fulfilling the duties of proper conduct (ābhisamācārika) with a mind of loving-kindness is called bodily action of loving-kindness. For laypeople, going to pay respects to a stupa or the Bodhi tree, going to invite the Saṅgha, going out to meet a monk seen entering the village for alms, receiving the bowl, preparing a seat, and accompanying him—these and such are called bodily action of loving-kindness.

For monks, prescribing training rules regarding conduct with a mind of loving-kindness, teaching meditation subjects, giving Dhamma discourses, and teaching the Word of the Buddha (the Tipiṭaka) are called verbal action of loving-kindness. For laypeople, saying, "Let us go to pay respects to the stupa, let us go to pay respects to the Bodhi tree, let us listen to the Dhamma, let us make offerings of lamps and flowers, let us undertake and practice the three types of good conduct, let us offer food by tickets (salākabhatta) and so on, let us offer rainy-season robes, today let us offer the four requisites to the Saṅgha, invite the Saṅgha and prepare food and so on, arrange the seats, set out drinking water, go out to meet the Saṅgha and escort them back"—such speech is...
124:
"How fortunate for me! How well-gained it is for me! My fellow practitioners partake of the alms in my bowl without even being asked." Thus, he generates joy; for him, the bowl is called "full" (Puṇṇa).

For one who thus fulfills the Sāraṇīyadhamma (virtues of courtesy), there is no envy (issā) or stinginess (macchariya). He is beloved by people and easily obtains the four requisites. Even when giving away alms from his bowl, they do not run out. At the place of distribution, he receives the most excellent items. When danger or famine arrives, the deities take care of him.

In this regard, there are these illustrative stories: Tissa Thera, residing at Senagiri, lived depending on the village of Mahāgiri. Fifty elder monks, while traveling to Nāgadīpa to pay homage to the stupas, wandered for alms in Giri village but left without receiving anything. Tissa Thera, upon entering the village, saw those elders and asked, "Venerable sirs, did you receive alms?" They replied, "We have wandered, friend." Knowing they had received nothing, he said, "Venerable sirs, please wait here for a moment until I return." They said, "Friend, we fifty people did not receive even enough to moisten our bowls." He replied, "Venerable sirs, these villagers are capable; even if they do not give alms, they know what is appropriate for the alms-round path." The elders waited. Tissa Thera entered the village. At the very first house, a great female lay devotee stood looking out for the Thera, having prepared milk-rice (khīrabhatta). Then, as soon as the Thera reached the door, she filled his bowl. Taking that food, he went to the elders and said to the Saṅghatthera (the senior-most monk), "Venerable sirs, please accept this." The Saṅghatthera looked at the faces of the other monks, thinking, "We so many people received nothing, yet this monk has returned quickly with food. How can this be?" Tissa Thera, knowing this just by their look, said, "Venerable sirs, this is alms-food obtained rightfully and justly. Please accept it without hesitation." Starting from the senior-most, he gave to all until they were satisfied, and he himself also ate until satisfied.

Then, after the meal, the elders asked, "Friend, when did you realize the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttaradhamma)?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, I have no supramundane Dhamma." They asked, "Friend, are you an attainer of jhāna?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, I do not have that either." They asked, "Friend, is this not a miracle (pāṭihāriya)?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, I have fulfilled the Sāraṇīyadhamma. From the time that Dhamma was perfected in me, even if there were a hundred thousand monks, the alms in my bowl do not run out." Hearing this, they said, "Sādhu, Sādhu, virtuous one! This is appropriate for you." This is the story regarding "alms in the bowl not running out."

This same Thera went to the place of the Giribhaṇḍa Great Offering at Cetiyapabbata and asked, "What is the most excellent item here?" They said, "Venerable sir, it is two pieces of cloth." That...
126:
The Theri, having wandered for alms at the foot of a tree the next day, approached the Thera and said, "Please partake of this alms-food." The Thera said, "It is appropriate, Theri," and remained silent. "Son, this is alms-food obtained rightfully; partake of it without hesitation," she said. "It is appropriate, Theri," he said again. The Theri took the bowl and threw it into the air. The bowl remained suspended in the air. The Thera said, "Even if it stays at a height of seven palm trees, it is still the food of a nun, Theri." He continued, "Danger does not exist at all times. When danger has subsided and I am preaching the Ariyavaṃsa (the lineage of the noble ones), if I am mentally reproached with 'O alms-gatherer, did you not spend your time eating the food of a nun?', I will not be able to remain firm. Be diligent, Theris!" and he proceeded on his way.

A tree deity was also standing there, thinking, "If the Thera partakes of the alms-food from the Theri's hand, I will not stop him. If he does not partake, I will stop him." Seeing the Thera departing, the deity descended from the tree and said, "Venerable sir, please give me the bowl." Taking the bowl, the deity led the Thera back to the foot of the tree, prepared a seat, offered alms-food, and after obtaining a promise that he would accept service after the meal, the deity supported twelve nuns and twelve monks for seven years. This is the story regarding "the deities take care of him." In that instance, the Theri was one who had fulfilled the Sāraṇīyadhamma.

In the terms "Akhaṇḍāni" etc.: Among the seven classes of offenses (āpattikkhandha), if a training rule (sikkhāpada) is broken at the beginning or at the end, that person's virtue is called "broken" (khaṇḍa), like a cloth torn at the edge. If it is broken in the middle, it is called "perforated" (chidda), like a cloth with a hole in the middle. If two or three are broken in succession, it is called "spotted" (sabala), like a cow with a different color such as black appearing on its back or belly. If it is variegated with different spots here and there, it is called "splattered" (kammāsa), like a cow with irregular spots. If it is not broken in any way, those virtues are called unbroken (akhaṇḍa), unperforated (acchidda), unspotted (asabala), and unsplattered (akammāsa). These virtues are called "liberated" (bhujissa) because they free one from the slavery of craving and make one a free person. They are called "praised by the wise" (viññūpasattha) because they are praised by the Buddha and other wise ones. They are called "untainted" (aparāmaṭṭha) because they are not touched by craving and views, and because no one can point a finger and say, "You have previously committed such an offense." They are called "conducive to concentration" (samādhisamvattanika) because they bring about access concentration (upacārasamādhi) or absorption concentration (appanāsamādhi).
127:
"They will dwell possessed of shared virtue" (sīlasāmaññagatā viharissanti) means they will dwell having virtue equal to that of the monks living in various regions. Indeed, the virtue of a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and others is the same as the virtue of other Stream-enterers living across the ocean or in the celestial realms; there is no difference in the virtue of the Path (magga-sīla). It is with reference to this that this was said.

"This view" (yāyaṃ diṭṭhi) refers to Right View associated with the Path. "Noble" (ariyā) means faultless. "Leading out" (niyyātī) means it leads out (from the suffering of the round of rebirths). "For one who acts accordingly" (takkarassa) means for one who practices in that way. "For the destruction of all suffering" (sabbadukkhakkhayāya) means for the purpose of ending all suffering. "Possessed of shared view" (diṭṭhisāmaññagatā) means they will dwell having attained a state of shared view. "Only growth" (vuddhiyeva) means for monks living in this way, only growth is to be expected, not decline.

"This very [teaching] frequently" (etadeva bahulaṃ) means that because he was nearing Parinibbāna, the Buddha, wishing to exhort the monks, repeatedly gave this very Dhamma talk. "Such is virtue" (iti sīlaṃ) means virtue of this kind, virtue of this extent. Here, the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) should be understood as virtue (sīla), one-pointedness of mind as concentration (samādhi), and insight-wisdom as wisdom (paññā). In the phrases "developed through virtue" (sīlaparibhāvito) etc., it is by being established in which virtue that they produce Path-concentration and Fruit-concentration. That concentration, when developed through that virtue, is of great fruit and great benefit. Established in which concentration they produce Path-wisdom and Fruit-wisdom, that wisdom, when developed through that concentration, is of great fruit and great benefit. Established in which wisdom they produce Path-consciousness and Fruit-consciousness, that mind, when developed through that wisdom, is rightly liberated from the taints (āsavas).

"As long as desired" (yathābhirantaṃ) means that although Buddhas have no such thing as lack of delight or anxiety, it means as long as he wished, according to his inclination. "Come" (āyāma) means "Come, let us go." There is also a variant reading "ayāma," which means "let us go." The Buddha addresses the Elder Ānanda as "Ānanda" because he was his personal attendant. Then the Elder informs the monks, "Friends, take up your bowls and robes; the Blessed One wishes to go to such and such a place."

144-145. The journey to Ambalaṭṭhikā is clear. The passage beginning with "Then the Venerable Sāriputta" (atha kho āyasmā sāriputto) has been explained in detail in the Sampasādanīya Sutta.
128:
## Explanation of the Danger of Immorality
In Pāṭaligāma, "rest house" (āvasathāgāra) refers to a house for guests. It is said that in Pāṭaligāma, friends of two kings would constantly come and drive families out of their homes to stay for a month or half a month. Those people, being constantly oppressed, built a large hall in the center of the city, saying, "Let this be a place for them to stay when they come," and they made one part a storage area for goods and another part a living area. When they heard "The Blessed One has arrived," they approached with the intention: "We should have gone to invite the Blessed One, but now the Blessed One has arrived at our dwelling place on his own; today we will have the Blessed One pronounce a blessing in the rest house." Therefore, they spoke thus. "Where the rest house was" (yena āvasathāgāraṃ) means those people, not knowing the Blessed One's mind—thinking "Buddhas have an inclination for the forest, they delight in the forest; whether they would wish to stay inside a village or not"—approached without having yet prepared the rest house. Now, having known the Blessed One's mind, they approached the rest house, thinking, "We will go ahead and prepare it." "Fully spread" (sabbasanthariṃ) means they spread it so that everything was completely covered.

"Immoral" (dussīla) means one without virtue. "Lacking in virtue" (sīlavipanna) means one whose virtue is ruined, whose restraint (saṃvara) is broken. "By reason of negligence" (pamādādhikaraṇaṃ) means due to the cause of negligence.

Although this sutta is presented in terms of laypeople, it is also applicable to monks. For a layperson, whatever craft or profession they live by—whether farming or trade—if they are negligent through acts like killing, they cannot complete those tasks in time, and then even their capital is destroyed. If they commit killing or stealing etc. during a time when such acts are prohibited, they face punishment and thus incur a great loss of wealth. A monk, too, being immoral and due to negligence, incurs loss from virtue, from the Word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana), from meditative absorption (jhāna), and from the seven noble treasures (ariya-dhana).

For a layperson, an evil reputation spreads in the midst of the four assemblies: "Such and such a person, though born in such and such a family, is immoral, of evil character, has abandoned this world and the next, and does not give even a ticket-meal (salāka-bhatta)." For a monk, too: "Such and such a person was unable to guard his virtue, or to learn the Word of the Buddha..."
129:
"He lives by medical practice and so on, and is possessed of the six types of disrespect"—thus this (ill-fame) spreads.

"Avisārada" (lack of confidence) means: for a layperson, he approaches with fear, thinking, "In a gathering of many people, someone will surely know of my deed, and then they will rebuke me," or "They will hand me over to the royal family." He sits with an unhappy face, shrugging his shoulders, looking down, and scratching the ground with his finger; he is unable to speak with confidence. For a monk as well, he approaches with fear, thinking, "Many monks are gathered; surely someone will know of my deed, and then they will prevent me from the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, remove me from the monkhood, and expel me." He is unable to speak with confidence. Even though some immoral persons wander about as if they are bold, in their hearts they are indeed dejected.

"Sammuḷho kālaṅkaroti" (one dies confused) means: while that person is lying on his deathbed, the immoral actions he has committed appear in his mind. When he opens his eyes, he sees this world; when he closes his eyes, he sees the next world. The four woeful planes appear before him. It is as if his head is being struck by a hundred spears. He dies crying out, "Stop it! Stop it!" Therefore, it is said, "He dies confused." The fifth term is quite clear.

The discourse on benefits (āniśaṃsa) should be understood as the opposite of the aforementioned (faults).

"Bahu deva rattiṃ dhammiyā kathāyā" means: with a Dhamma talk not found in other Pali texts, and with a talk of appreciation for the rest-house, like bringing down the celestial Ganges, or like squeezing a great honeycomb a league in size and giving the honey to drink, he showed (the Dhamma) for much of the night, inspiring and gladdening them before sending them away. "Abhikkantā" means (the night) that has passed, ended, and reached destruction. "Suññāgāra" means: although there was no separate secluded house, they enclosed a side of that very place with a curtain-wall and prepared a couch, thinking, "The Teacher will rest here." The Blessed One thought, "Using this place prepared by these people with the four postures will be of great benefit to them," and he lay down there in the lion's posture. Intending this, it is said, "He entered the secluded house."
136:
Tempting them with their own prosperity, he said, "For those who strive in the practice of a recluse with heedfulness, such sovereign prosperity is easily obtained," in order to generate effort in the practice of a recluse. He also spoke thus to clarify the mark of impermanence. For before long, all these people will reach destruction under the power of King Ajātasattu. Then, the monks who stood seeing their royal splendor and glory would develop the mark of impermanence, thinking, "Even such glory and prosperity are seen to reach destruction," and would reach Arahantship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Thus, he spoke to clarify the mark of impermanence.

Knowing that they were already invited by Ambapālī, why did they invite him? They invited him because of their lack of faith and also out of custom. In their minds, they thought, "That woman is a frivolous woman; even without having invited him, she might say 'I have invited him'." Moreover, inviting someone to a meal when they are about to leave after hearing the Dhamma is indeed the custom of people.

## Commentary on the Retreat at Veḷuvagāma

Veḷuvagāmaka is the village of Veḷuva near the city of Vesālī. In the terms "yathāmittaṃ" and so on, "mitta" means friends. "Sandiṭṭha" means acquaintances who have merely been met and seen here and there, not very close friends. "Sambhatta" means well-loved and firm friends. The meaning is: "Whichever monks have such friends in whichever places, let those monks enter the rainy season retreat in those places." Why did he say this? It was for their comfortable living. For those monks, the lodgings in Veḷuva village were not sufficient, and alms-food was also scarce. However, around the city of Vesālī, there are many lodgings and alms-food is easily obtained; therefore, he spoke thus. Then why did he not dismiss them saying, "Go as you please"? It was out of compassion for those monks. For the Blessed One had this thought: "I will stay for about ten months and then attain Parinibbāna. If these monks go far away, they will not be able to see me at the time of my Parinibbāna. Then they will have remorse, thinking, 'The Teacher, when about to attain Parinibbāna, did not even give us a word of reminder; if we had known, we would not have lived so far away.' If they live around Vesālī, they can come about eight times a month to hear the Dhamma and receive the advice of the Sugata." Thus, he did not dismiss them.

"Khara" means harsh. "Ābādha" means an uneven disease (affliction). "Bāḷhā" means strong (acute). "Māraṇantikā" means ending in death, or capable of leading to death. "Mindful and clearly comprehending, he endured it" means he made mindfulness well-established, and having delimited it with wisdom, he endured it. "Avihaññamāno" means by way of following the sensation...
138: "Without inner or outer" means teaching without making distinctions either by way of the Dhamma or by way of the person. One who thinks, "I will not teach this much of the Dhamma to others," is said to make the Dhamma "inner." One who thinks, "I will teach this much to others," is said to make the Dhamma "outer." One who thinks, "I will teach this person," is said to make the person "inner." One who thinks, "I will not teach this person," is said to make the person "outer." The meaning is that the teaching was given without making such distinctions. Regarding the "teacher's fist" (ācariyamuṭṭhi), such a thing exists among external teachers. In their youth, they do not tell anyone, but at the final moment, while lying on their deathbed, they tell their beloved and dear pupil. The Buddha shows that there is nothing held as a "fist" by the Tathāgata, thinking, "I will teach this in old age at the final place," or keeping it with the thought, "I will preserve it." "I alone shall lead the Bhikkhu Saṅgha," or "The Saṅgha should be dedicated to me" (mamuddesika), meaning that the dedication should exist for the sake of the benefit referred to me. This is said to one who has the thought, "Let the Bhikkhu Saṅgha be dedicated only to me and look up to me; let them not exist after my passing, or let whatever happens happen." The Blessed One does not have such a thought, because envy (issā) and avarice (macchariya) were destroyed even at the throne of enlightenment. "Sa kinti" means "Who is he?" "Āsītiko" means eighty years old. This is said to show the state of having reached the final stage of life. "Veṭhamissakena" means with repairs such as bandages, circular bindings, and so forth. "Manye" means he thinks he sustains himself with repairs like an old cart. It shows that the Tathāgata's four postures are sustained by the binding of the attainment of the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphalasamāpatti). Now, to clarify that meaning, he said, "Ānanda, at such a time," and so forth. There, "sabbanimittānaṃ" means of the signs of forms, and so forth. "Ekaccānaṃ vedanānaṃ" means of mundane feelings. "Tasmātihānanda" means, "Ānanda, because one dwells happily through this dwelling in the fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti-vihāra), you too should dwell thus for that purpose." "Attadīpā" means dwell making yourselves an island, a support, like an island in the middle of the great ocean. "Attasaraṇā" means be those who have yourselves as a resort, not another as a resort. The same method applies to the terms "dhammadīpa" and "dhammasaraṇa." "Tamatagge" is "tama agge." The middle "ta" is inserted for the sake of euphonic junction (padasandhi). The intended meaning is, "These are the very highest (tamataggā)." Thus, cutting off all connection with darkness, in the state of being exceedingly supreme...
139: "Ānanda, these shall be my monks. Whoever is desirous of training, all those monks who have the four foundations of mindfulness (catusatipatthāna) as their resort shall be the highest." Thus he concludes the teaching with the pinnacle of the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala). ## The Commentary on the Second Recitation Section is finished. ## Commentary on the Talk on the Manifestation of Signs "He entered Vesālī for alms"—when did he enter? It was when he left Ukkacela and arrived at Vesālī. It is said that after spending the rains retreat at Veḷuva village, the Blessed One set out, saying "I will go to Sāvatthī," returning by the same path he had come, and in due course reached Sāvatthī and entered Jetavana. The General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), Venerable Sāriputta, after performing the major and minor duties for the Blessed One, went to his place for the day's rest. There, after showing the duties to his pupils and when the pupils had left, he swept the place for the day's rest, spread out his leather mat, washed his feet, sat down cross-legged, and entered the fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti). Then, having emerged from the attainment at the designated time, this thought arose in him: "Do the Buddhas attain Parinibbāna first, or do the chief disciples (aggasāvaka)?" Then, knowing "The chief disciples attain Parinibbāna first," he examined his own life-force (āyusaṅkhāra). He knew, "My life-force will continue for only seven days," and thought, "Where shall I attain Parinibbāna?" Then he thought, "Venerable Rāhula attained Parinibbāna in Tāvatiṃsa; Venerable Aññāsikoṇ膽añña in the Chaddanta Lake; where shall I attain Parinibbāna?" Thinking again, he remembered his mother: "My mother, though she is the mother of seven Arahants, has no confidence in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha. Does she have the supporting condition (upanissaya) or not?" Reflecting, he saw the supporting condition for the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) and looked to see, "By whose teaching will the realization of the Dhamma occur?" He saw, "It will be by my teaching alone, not by another's. If I remain indifferent, there will be those who criticize me, saying 'Venerable Sāriputta is a refuge for other people; on the day he taught the Samacitta Sutta, a hundred thousand crores of deities reached the fruit of arahantship (yet he did not help his mother).'"
143:
The Teacher preached: "On the day the Buddha was born, the four Great Brahmas received the Great Being with a golden net." At that moment, the Brahmin lady thought, 'If my son possesses such power, how much more power must the Blessed One, my son's teacher, possess?' Immediately, the five kinds of joy (pīti) arose and permeated her entire body. The Elder thought, 'Joy and gladness have arisen in my mother; now is the time for a Dhamma talk.' He asked, "Great lay devotee, what are you thinking?" She replied, "Dear son, if my son has such virtues, what kind of virtues must his teacher have? This is what I am thinking."

"Great lay devotee, at the moment of my Teacher's birth, at his Great Renunciation, at his Enlightenment, and at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. In virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, there is no one equal to the Blessed One." He then gave a detailed Dhamma talk on the virtues of the Buddha, starting with "Itipi so Bhagavā." At the end of her beloved son's discourse, the Brahmin lady was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). She then said to her son, "Dear Upatissa, why did you do this? Why did you not give me such Deathless Dhamma for all this time?"

The Elder thought, 'I have now repaid the debt of my upbringing to my mother, the Brahmin lady Rūpasārī; this much is enough.' He said, "Go, great lay devotee," and sent her away. Then he asked, "Cunda, what time is it?" Cunda replied, "Venerable sir, it is the time of deep dawn." "Then assemble the community of monks." "Venerable sir, the Saṅgha has assembled." "Cunda, lift me up and help me sit." Cunda lifted him and helped him sit.

The Elder addressed the monks: "Friends, for forty-four years you have wandered with me. If there is any action of mine, physical or verbal, that you did not like, please forgive me, friends." The monks replied, "Venerable sir, as we have followed you like your shadow, there is nothing we did not like. Please, venerable sir, forgive us instead." Then, as the first light of dawn appeared, making the great earth resound, the Elder attained Parinibbāna into the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu). Many devas and humans paid their respects at the Elder's Parinibbāna.
144:
Venerable Cunda took the bowl, robes, and relic-water-filter of Venerable Sāriputta, went to Jetavana, and having called Venerable Ānanda, approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One received the relic-water-filter, spoke of the Elder's virtues with five hundred verses, had a relic stupa (dhātu-cetiya) built, and gave a sign to Venerable Ānanda for the journey to Rājagaha. The Elder informed the monks. The Blessed One, surrounded by a large community of monks, went to Rājagaha. While there, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna attained Parinibbāna. The Blessed One took his relics, had a stupa built, and departing from Rājagaha, traveled in stages toward the Ganges and reached the city of Ukkacela. There, on the bank of the Ganges, seated among the community of monks, he preached the sutta concerning the Parinibbāna of Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Departing from Ukkacela, he went to the city of Vesālī. Regarding this journey: "The Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robes, entered Vesālī for alms"—this is the sequential account here.

'Nisīdana' here refers to a leather mat. 'Udena-cetiya' refers to the monastery built at the site of the shrine of the yakkha Udena. The same applies to Gotamaka-cetiya and others. 'Bhāvitā' means developed. 'Bahulīkatā' means practiced frequently. 'Yānikatā' means made like a well-yoked vehicle. 'Vatthukatā' means made like a foundation in the sense of a basis. 'Anuṭṭhitā' means established. 'Paricitā' means accumulated from all sides, well-developed. 'Susamāraddhā' means well-undertaken.

Having spoken thus without limitation, and wishing to show it again with limitation, he said "Tathāgatassa kho," etc. In that passage, 'kappa' refers to the lifespan (āyu-kappa). Whatever the lifespan of humans is at that particular time, he could remain for the full duration of that lifespan. 'Kappāvasesaṃ vā' means "a little more or much more," or more than the hundred years mentioned. However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: "There is no such thing as a roar in an impossible place for the Buddhas. Just as he suppressed the painful feelings leading to death that arose at Veḷuva village for ten months, by repeatedly entering that attainment and suppressing it for ten months at a time, he could have remained for this entire Bhadda-kappa. Why then did he not remain? The so-called 'clung-to' physical body (upādinnaka-rūpa) is oppressed by things such as the breaking of teeth. The Buddhas, before reaching the state of broken teeth and so on, in the fifth portion of their lifespan, at a time when they are still dear and pleasing to the many, attain Parinibbāna. When the Buddha and the Great Disciples who followed the Buddha have attained Parinibbāna, like a single stump..."
149:
The novice (Sāmaṇera) reflected, "These goddesses are mocking me. I have not yet found my teacher. Where is my teacher, the Elder Mahāsamuddanāga?" Realizing that the Elder had created a water-chamber in the great ocean and was sitting there for his day-abiding, the novice went to that place, paid homage to the Elder, and stood there. Then the Elder said to the novice, "Dear Saṅgharakkhita, why have you entered the battlefield without training?" and asked, "Dear son, were you unable to shake the Vejayanta Palace?"

"Venerable Sir, it was because I could not find my teacher," he replied. Then the Elder said, "Dear son, if someone like you cannot shake it, who else will? Dear son, have you ever seen a lump of cow dung floating on the surface of the water? Dear son, those who bake cakes using a potsherd divide them by the edges; understand through this analogy." The novice replied, "Venerable Sir, this much is enough for the task," and after resolving that the place where the palace stood should become water, he headed towards the Vejayanta Palace.

When the goddesses saw the novice, they said, "After leaving once in shame, the novice has come again; he has come again!" Sakka, the King of Gods, said, "Do not speak thus to my son. Now he has found his teacher; in a moment, he will shake the palace." The novice then struck the pinnacle of the palace with his big toe. The palace tilted in all four directions. The goddesses cried out, "Dear son, let the palace stand still! Dear son, let the palace stand still!" The novice, having restored the palace to its original position, stood on top of the palace and uttered this inspired utterance (Udāna):

"Only today did I go forth (as a monk),
Today I have reached the destruction of the taints (āsavas),
Today I shake the palace,
Oh, how magnificent is the power of the Buddha!

Only today did I go forth... (etc.) ... Oh, how magnificent is the power of the Dhamma!

Only today did I go forth... (etc.) ... Oh, how magnificent is the power of the Saṅgha!"

Regarding the other six types of earthquakes besides these, what should be said is exactly as stated in the Mahāpadāna Sutta.

Thus, among these eight types of earthquakes, the first is due to the disturbance of the elements, the second is due to psychic power, the third and fourth are due to the power of merit (puñña-teja), the fifth is due to the power of knowledge (ñāṇa-teja), the sixth is due to the offering of applause (sādhukāra), the seventh is due to compassion, and the eighth is due to weeping. When the Great Being (Mahāsatta) descends into his mother's womb and when he is born from it, the earth shakes due to his power of merit. When he attains Buddhahood, it shakes due to the power of knowledge...
152:
Just as one might gather food, asking "What is there to eat here?" and make only a single mouthful, even so, a person of superior wisdom (ñāṇuttarika), being of purified knowledge, thinks, "What is there to attain in this slight object? This is not my burden," and having overcome those forms, enters attainment. The meaning is that as soon as the sign (nimitta) arises, he reaches absorption (appanā) in this object. By the words "I know, I see," his advertence (ābhoga) is described. And that advertence occurs only for one who has emerged from attainment, not within the attainment itself. The phrase "is one who has such a perception" means he has such a perception either through the perception of advertence (ābhoga-saññā) or the perception of jhāna (jhāna-saññā). For him, the perception of mastery (abhibhavana-saññā) exists even within the attainment, but the perception of advertence occurs only for one who has emerged from attainment.

"Unmeasured" means having a developed measure, meaning they are great. Regarding the word "overcoming (mastering)," just as a man who is a great eater, upon receiving a single serving of rice, does not see it as great, thinking, "Let there be more; what will this much do for me?", even so, a person of superior wisdom, being of purified knowledge, thinks, "What is there to attain here? This is not unmeasured; there is no burden for me in achieving one-pointedness of mind," and having overcome those objects, he enters attainment. The meaning is that as soon as the sign arises, he reaches absorption in this object.

"Perceiving no form internally" refers to one who is devoid of the perception of preliminary work (parikamma-saññā) regarding the internal forms, either because of not having acquired them or because of their non-existence.

"Alone, he sees forms externally" means that for whom both the preliminary work and the sign have arisen only externally, he is described as "perceiving no form internally, alone he sees forms externally" by virtue of the external preliminary work and absorption. The rest of the meaning here is exactly as stated in the fourth base of mastery (abhibhāyatana). Among these four, the "slight" (paritta) object comes by way of the temperament of discursive thought (vitakka-carita). The "unmeasured" (appamāṇa) object comes by way of the temperament of delusion (moha-carita). The "beautiful" (suvaṇṇa) object comes by way of the temperament of hatred (dosa-carita). The "ugly" (dubbaṇṇa) object comes by way of the temperament of lust (rāga-carita). For these individuals, these objects are suitable (sappāya). Their suitability is explained in detail in the Description of Temperaments (Carita-niddesa) in the Visuddhimagga.

In the fifth base of mastery and so on, "blue (nīlāni)" is said by way of all-inclusive grasping. "Blue-colored (nīlavaṇṇāni)" is said by way of color. "Blue in appearance (nīlanidassanāni)" is said by way of appearance; it means that the eye-openings (māna-vivara), being of unmixed color, appear as a single solid blue. "Blue in radiance (nīlanibhāsāni)" is said by way of luster; it means having a blue luster or being endowed with blue light. By this, the purity of those objects is shown.
153:
These four Abhibhāyatanas (Stages of Mastery) are spoken of by way of the power of (pure color). "Umāpuppha" means that the flax flower is smooth and soft; even when seen, it is purely blue. However, flowers like the Girikaṇṇikā (jungle jasmine) and others, when seen, contain elements of white. Therefore, only this (flax flower) is taken, not those others. "Vārāṇaseyyaka" means the (cloth) produced in the city of Vārāṇasī. In that place, even the cotton is soft, the spinners and weavers are skilled, and the water is pure and smooth. Therefore, that cloth is smooth on both sides; it appears smooth, soft, and glossy on both sides.

In the passages beginning with "yellow" and so on, the meaning should be understood in this same way. "One learning the blue kasiṇa takes the sign in something blue, whether in a flower, a cloth, or a color element," etc.—here, the method of making the kasiṇa, the preliminary work (parikamma), and the procedure for attainment (appanā) are all explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. These eight Abhibhāyatanas are also brought forth to show the state of fearlessness (of the Buddha). Having spoken of these (Abhibhāyatanas), he said: "Ānanda, for the Tathāgata who enters and emerges from such attainments, there is no fear or trepidation. Who could entertain such a thought as: 'Would the Tathāgata be afraid upon seeing Māra alone?' Ānanda, the Tathāgata, fearless and unshakeable, mindful and clearly comprehending, has relinquished the life-force (āyusaṅkhāra)."

## Explanation of the Eight Deliverances (Aṭṭhavimokkhavaṇṇanā)
The talk on the Deliverances (Vimokkha) has an evident meaning. These eight Deliverances are also brought forth to show the state of fearlessness. Having spoken of these (Deliverances), he said: "Ānanda, for the Tathāgata who enters and emerges from these attainments, there is no fear or trepidation ...pe... has relinquished (the life-force)."

Now, without giving Venerable Ānanda an opportunity, the Blessed One began another discourse in the manner beginning with "Ekamidāhaṃ". Therein, "Paṭhamābhisambuddho" means having become fully enlightened, in the very first eighth week.

"Ossaṭṭho" means the (life) that is released or determined. Having said this, he said: "Therefore, this ten-thousandfold world system shook."

## The Story of Ānanda's Request (Ānandayācanakathā)
"Alaṃ" is a word of refusal. "Bodhi" refers to the penetration of the four path-knowledges. "Saddahasi tvaṃ" means he asks whether he believes the Tathāgata regarding what was thus spoken. Therefore...
213:
...or there is none. For a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) has a pure retinue. The retinue of a Wheel-Turning Monarch is like a company of Vijjādharas (knowledge-bearers) traveling in the sky, resembling gems scattered upon a surface of sapphire (indanīla). It was the same for King Mahāsudassana. Therefore, it was said: "King Mahāsudassana followed right after the Wheel Treasure with his fourfold army."

That Wheel Treasure revolves in the region of the sky, neither too high nor too low above the treetops. It revolves in such a way that those who desire the flowers, fruits, and shoots of the trees are able to take those flowers, fruits, and shoots easily. It also revolves in such a way that those standing on the ground are able to recognize: "This is the King, this is the Viceroy, this is the General." Among the postures such as standing and so on, whichever posture one desires, one travels by that very posture. Among this multitude of the King's retinue, those devoted to arts such as painting travel while performing their respective tasks. Just as all tasks are accomplished on the ground, so too all the tasks of that King's retinue are completed in the sky. Taking the King's retinue in such a manner, that Wheel Treasure, leaving Mount Sineru on the left side, travels over the Great Ocean to the Eastern Continent (Pubbavideha), which is seven thousand leagues in extent.

In that Eastern Continent, there is a delightful piece of ground with a pure and level surface, endowed with shade and water, where provisions and requisites such as grain, milk, firewood, and grass are easily obtained, and which is capable of accommodating the assembly, being twelve leagues in diameter and thirty-six leagues in circumference. Above that piece of ground, the Wheel Treasure stands as if fixed to an axle. Then, by that sign, that great multitude descends and takes up residence while performing all their tasks such as bathing and eating as they wish. For King Mahāsudassana, everything was just the same. Therefore, it was said: "Ānanda, in whatever region the Wheel Treasure stays, there King Mahāsudassana takes up residence together with his fourfold army."

When the Wheel-Turning Monarch has thus taken up residence, those kings who are there, even upon hearing that "an external power has arrived," do not assemble their forces and prepare for battle. Indeed, immediately upon the appearance of the Wheel Treasure, there is no being who would dare to raise a weapon against that King with the thought of him being an enemy. This is the power of the Wheel Treasure.
214:
By the power of the Wheel Treasure, all the enemies of that king were completely subdued. Because that treasure of the ruler of men subdues enemies, it is called 'Arindama' (Tamer of Enemies); for that very reason, the king calls that treasure the 'Wheel' (Cakka).

Therefore, all those kings, bringing gifts appropriate to the glory and wealth of their own kingdoms, approached that Wheel-turning King. Bowing their heads, they worshipped his feet with the consecration of the radiance of the jewels in their crests, and through words such as 'Come, O Great King,' they submitted themselves to his service, asking, 'What shall we do?' They did the same for King Mahāsudassana. With reference to this, it was said: 'Ananda, in the eastern direction... O Great King, may you provide instruction.'

In that passage, 'Svāgataṃ' means a good arrival. For when some people arrive, others grieve, and when they leave, others rejoice. When some arrive, others rejoice, and when they leave, others grieve. You are such a person that your arrival brings joy and your departure brings grief. Therefore, your arrival is said to be a good arrival (su-āgamana).

When addressed thus, the Wheel-turning King does not say, 'Provide me with such an amount of annual tax,' nor does he seize the wealth of one king to give to another. Instead, investigating matters such as killing (pāṇātipāta) with wisdom appropriate to his status as a King of Dhamma, he preaches the Dhamma with a lovely and melodious voice, saying: 'Look, dear ones, the act of killing, when practiced, developed, and frequently performed, leads to hell,' and so on, giving advice such as 'One should not kill,' and so forth. King Mahāsudassana did the same. Therefore, it was said: 'King Mahāsudassana spoke thus: "One should not kill... and enjoy your wealth as you have done before."' 

If it is asked, 'Do all kings accept this advice of the King?', even the advice of the Buddha is not accepted by all beings; how then would all accept the advice of the King? Therefore, only the wise who understand cause and effect accept it. However, all become followers. Therefore, it was said: 'Ananda, those who...' and so on.

Then, after giving advice to the inhabitants of the eastern continent in this manner and having finished his morning meal, the Wheel Treasure, by the power of the Wheel-turning King, rose into the sky and descended into the Eastern Ocean. As the Wheel Treasure descended into the Eastern Ocean, the waters of the great ocean receded for about a league (yojana), like a king of nagas contracting its hood upon smelling the scent of Agada medicine, with the waves becoming still, and stood within the ocean like a wall of beryl (veḷuriya). At that very moment, as if wishing to see the glory born of the king's merit, beneath the waters of the great ocean...
215:
...various jewels scattered across the ocean floor came from here and there and filled that place. Then, the king's retinue, seeing the floor of the great ocean filled with various jewels, took as much as they desired in the folds of their garments (ucchanga) and so on. When the retinue had taken the jewels as they pleased, the Wheel Treasure turned back. As it turned back, the retinue went in front, the king in the middle, and the Wheel Treasure at the end. The waters of the ocean followed continuously, striking the edge of the wheel's rim (nemimaṇḍala), as if enticed by the glory of the Wheel Treasure or as if unable to bear separation from it. In this way, the Wheel-turning King, having conquered Pubbavideha bounded by the Eastern Ocean, and desiring to conquer Jambudīpa bounded by the Southern Ocean, proceeded toward the Southern Ocean along the path shown by the Wheel Treasure. King Mahāsudassana went in the same way. Therefore, it was said: 'Then, Ananda, the Wheel Treasure, having descended into the Eastern Ocean and emerged, turned toward the southern direction.'

The manner of its turning, the arrangement of the army, the arrival of rival kings, the giving of instruction to them, the descent into the Southern Ocean, the receding of the ocean waters, and the taking of jewels—all these should be understood in the same way as previously described.

Having conquered Jambudīpa, which is ten thousand yojanas in extent, and emerging from the Southern Ocean, he went in the same manner as previously described to conquer the Western Continent (Aparagoyāna), which is seven thousand yojanas in extent. Having conquered that continent bounded by the ocean, he emerged from the Western Ocean and went in the same way to conquer the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), which is eight thousand yojanas in extent. Having conquered that continent bounded by the ocean, he emerged from the Northern Ocean.

By this much, the Wheel-turning King attained sovereignty over the earth bounded by the four oceans. Having thus achieved victory, in order to display the glory of his royal success, he rose into the sky with his retinue and looked upon the four great continents, each surrounded by five hundred small islands, which appeared like four great Jātassara lakes adorned with well-bloomed groves of Paduma, Kumuda, and Puṇḍarīka lilies. Along the path shown by the Wheel Treasure...
216:
Following the path indicated by the Wheel Treasure, he returned to his royal capital in due course. Then, that Wheel Treasure stood at the palace gate as if beautifying the interior of the palace.

When the Wheel Treasure was thus established, there was no need for any activity involving torches or lamps within the royal palace. The radiance of the Wheel Treasure alone dispelled the darkness of the night. However, for those who desired darkness, there was indeed darkness. For King Mahāsudassana, all this happened in the same way. Therefore, it was said: "Having plunged into the southern ocean... p... such a Wheel Treasure appeared."

## Explanation of the Elephant Treasure

When the Wheel Treasure had thus appeared, the ministers of the Universal Monarch prepared a level and clean area of ground at the usual place for the auspicious state elephant. They had it smeared with fragrant perfumes such as red sandalwood, scattered with various beautiful and fragrant flowers below, and decorated above with a canopy adorned with delightful garlands of flowers interspersed with golden stars, making it like a celestial mansion. Then they requested, "O King, please contemplate the arrival of such an Elephant Treasure."

That Universal Monarch, having given great gifts and undertaken the precepts in the manner previously described, sat reflecting on the perfection of that merit. Then, urged by the power of his merit, a noble elephant—desiring to enjoy that special honor—arrived from either the Chaddanta or Uposatha lineage and stood in that place. It had a pure white body adorned with feet, neck, and mouth as red as the rising sun; it was firmly established on seven points, with well-proportioned limbs and a body as pleasing as a blooming red lotus. Possessing psychic power and able to travel through the air like a yogi, it was like a silver mountain with edges tinged with red arsenic powder. If it came from the Chaddanta lineage, the youngest elephant would come. If it came from the Uposatha lineage, the eldest would come. In the Pāḷi text, however, it only appears as "Uposatha, the king of elephants." A king of elephants is not for the use of just anyone; therefore, the commentaries state that the youngest from the Chaddanta lineage comes. That noble elephant arrives while the Universal Monarchs, who have fulfilled their duties, are contemplating in the manner described. For King Mahāsudassana, however, it came to the usual place for the auspicious state elephant of its own accord, displaced the ordinary elephant there, and stood in its place. Therefore, it was said: "Furthermore, Ānanda... p... the king of elephants."
217:
Upon seeing the Elephant Treasure that had thus appeared, the elephant keepers and others, being greatly delighted, went quickly and informed the King. The King arrived in great haste and, seeing the Elephant Treasure with a clear and trusting mind, thought, "Friends, the elephant vehicle is indeed excellent, if only it would submit to training," and extended his hand. Then, like a calf born of a domestic cow and raised in that very house, the elephant approached the King, showing its tameness by drooping its ears. The King desired to ride the elephant. Then his attendants, knowing his intention, brought the Elephant Treasure near, having decorated it with golden banners, golden ornaments, and covered it with a golden net. The King, without making the elephant kneel, ascended by a ladder made of the seven kinds of jewels, his mind inclined toward traveling through the sky. Simultaneously with the King's thought, that king of elephants leaped into the sky, which had the color of indanīla emeralds, like a king of swans. Then, in the same manner as the procession of the Wheel Treasure, the entire royal retinue followed. Thus, the King, together with his retinue, traversed the entire earth and returned to the capital within the time of the morning meal. In this way, the Elephant Treasure of a Universal Monarch possesses great psychic power. For King Mahāsudassana, such an Elephant Treasure also appeared. Therefore, it is said: "The King, having seen... appeared."

## Explanation of the Horse Treasure

When the Elephant Treasure had thus appeared, the ministers of the Universal Monarch made the usual place for the auspicious state horse clean and level, decorated it, and encouraged the King to contemplate its arrival in the same manner as before. The King, having performed acts of giving and honor and having undertaken the precepts as before, sat comfortably on the upper floor of the palace, reflecting on the perfection of his merit. Then, urged by the power of his merit, a king of horses named Valāhaka arrived from the noble Sindhava breed and stood in that place. It had the glorious appearance of a mass of white clouds in the autumn season entwined with streaks of lightning; it had red feet and a red muzzle, with a body as pure, smooth, and compact as a mass of moonlight. Because it had a black head like a crow's neck or an indanīla emerald, it was called 'Kāḷasīsa'. Because it had fine, rounded, and straight hair like white Muñja grass, as if it had been perfectly groomed, it was called 'Muñjakesa', and it was capable of traveling through the sky. For King Mahāsudassana, this horse arrived of its own accord, just like the Elephant Treasure. All the rest is to be understood as described for the Elephant Treasure.
218:
It should be understood in the same manner as described for the Elephant Treasure. Referring to such a Horse Treasure, the Blessed One said, "Puna ca paraṃ" and so forth.

## Description of the Gem Treasure
To the Wheel-turning Monarch who possesses such a manifest Horse Treasure, the Gem Treasure comes from Mount Vepulla. It is four cubits in length and has a circumference equal to the hub of a chariot wheel. It is adorned at both ends with two golden lotuses and clusters of extremely pure pearls emerging from the edges of the pericarp. Surrounded by eighty-four thousand jewels, it diffuses the splendor of the full moon surrounded by a host of stars. When that Gem Treasure is placed in a pearl net and hoisted into the air to a height of sixty cubits by a succession of bamboo poles, its radiance spreads throughout the surrounding area for a distance of one yojana during the night.

By that radiance, the entire area becomes illuminated as if it were the time of dawn. Then, farmers engage in plowing, merchants open their shops, and various artisans perform their respective tasks, thinking, "It is daytime." For King Mahāsudassana as well, all this happened in the same way. Therefore, it was said: "Furthermore, Ānanda... the Gem Treasure appeared."

## Description of the Woman Treasure
To the Wheel-turning Monarch for whom the Gem Treasure has thus appeared, the Woman Treasure appears, who is the cause of special sensual pleasure. They bring the noble queen for him from the Madda royal family, or she comes of her own accord from the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) due to the power of merit. The rest of her accomplishments are mentioned in the Pāḷi text itself in this manner: "Furthermore, Ānanda, the Woman Treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana; she was beautiful, lovely to behold..." and so forth.

In that text, she is called "abhirūpā" (beautiful) because she possesses an extraordinary appearance due to the perfection of her physical form. She is called "dassanīyā" (lovely to behold) because she delights the eyes just by being seen; thus, she is worth looking at even if one has to abandon other duties. She is called "pāsādikā" (pleasing) because she gladdens the mind with joy just by being seen. "Paramāya" means supreme, as she brings about such pleasure. "Vaṇṇapokkharatāya" means being endowed with beauty of complexion. "Samannāgatā" means possessed of. Alternatively, she is called "abhirūpā" because she is neither too tall nor too short. She is called "dassanīyā" because she is neither too thin nor too stout.
219:
That queen is pleasing because she is neither too dark nor too fair. She is endowed with supreme beauty of complexion because she surpasses human appearance without reaching divine appearance. The radiance of human complexion does not emanate outward, but the radiance of deities emanates even to a very great distance.

The bodily radiance of that queen of the Wheel-turning Monarch illuminates an area of twelve cubits. Among the terms such as "nātidīghā" (not too tall), the first pair describes her perfection of height, the second pair describes her perfection of girth, and the third pair describes her perfection of complexion. Alternatively, these six terms describe the absence of physical defects, while the phrase "atikkantā mānusi-vaṇṇaṃ" (surpassing human appearance) describes her physical perfection. "Tūlapicuno vā kappāsapicuno vā" means she is as soft as silk-cotton or seed-cotton that has been placed in clarified butter and beaten a hundred times. "Sīte" means she is warm during the king's cold season. "Uṇhe" means she is cool during the king's hot season. "Candanagandho" means the scent of yellow sandalwood, which is always well-ground, fresh, and mixed with the four types of perfumes, wafts from her body. "Uppalagandho vāyati" means that when she laughs or speaks, the extremely fragrant scent of a blue lotus, as if just blossomed at that moment, wafts from her mouth.

To show the conduct appropriate to the physical perfection of that queen, who is thus endowed with the perfection of appearance, touch, and scent, the passage beginning with "Taṃ kho pana" is stated. In that text, she is called "pubbuṭṭhāyinī" because upon seeing the king, she rises before any other business, like one being burned by fire. She is called "pacchānipātinī" because she lies down or sits only after performing duties such as fanning the king when he is seated. She is called "kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī" because she asks with her voice, "Lord, what shall I do?" and makes it known to the king. She is called "manāpacārinī" because she acts only in ways that please the king. She is called "piyavādinī" because she speaks only words that the king likes.

Now, to show that the conduct of that queen arises only from purity of heart and not from deceit, the passage beginning with "Taṃ kho pana" is stated. In that text, "no aticarī" means she does not transgress in conduct; it means that apart from the king, she does not desire another man even in her mind.

Among those qualities, those mentioned at the beginning such as "abhirūpā" and those at the end such as "pubbuṭṭhāyinī" are natural qualities. However, qualities such as "atikkantā mānusi-vaṇṇaṃ" should be understood as having arisen due to the power of past deeds, starting from the appearance of the Wheel Treasure, depending on the merit of the Wheel-turning Monarch.
220:
Qualities such as great beauty and so forth also became complete in every aspect from the moment the Wheel-Treasure appeared. Therefore, it is said: "Such a Woman-Treasure appeared."

## Explanation of the Householder-Treasure

After the Woman-Treasure had appeared in this way, the Householder-Treasure appeared so that the various tasks involving the wealth of the Wheel-Turning Monarch could be carried out with ease. This Householder-Treasure is naturally very wealthy, born into a rich family. He is a merchant-householder who increases the King's accumulation of wealth. Due to the power of the Wheel-Treasure and as a result of his own past kamma, a divine eye (dibbacakkhu) appears to this householder. With that eye, he can see treasures and pots of gold hidden within the earth up to a distance of one league (yojana). When the householder sees those treasures, he becomes joyful and, going to the King, invites him to use the wealth, thus fulfilling all tasks requiring riches. He did the same for King Mahāsudassana. Therefore, it is said: "Ananda... furthermore... such a Householder-Treasure appeared."

## Explanation of the Counselor-Treasure

After the Householder-Treasure had appeared in this way, the Counselor-Treasure (Parināyakaratana), the eldest son capable of managing all the affairs of the Wheel-Turning Monarch, appeared. He is indeed the King's eldest son. By nature, he is wise, learned, sharp-witted, and capable of clearly explaining meanings he knows to others. Relying on the power of the King's merit and through the power of his own kamma, the knowledge of others' minds (paracittañāṇa) arises in this eldest son. With that knowledge, he knows the thoughts of the King's retinue within twelve leagues and can distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful to the King. Seeing his own power, that eldest son, with a joyful heart, invites the King by offering guidance in all state affairs. He did the same for King Mahāsudassana. Therefore, it is said: "Furthermore... the Counselor-Treasure appeared." In that text, "thapetabbaṃ thapetunti" means to appoint those who should be appointed to various positions.

## Explanation of the Possession of the Four Psychic Powers

"Samavepākiniyā" means having the quality of digesting food evenly (samavipācaniyā). "Gahaṇiyā" refers to the heat element born of kamma (kammaja-tejo-dhātu). Among them, for one person, food is digested as soon as it is eaten; for another...
221:
...or else, it remains right there [in the stomach] like a bundle of rice. Both these types of persons are not endowed with the digestive fire that digests evenly. But for whom the desire to eat arises again when it is time for a meal, only this person is known as one endowed with the digestive fire called samavepākinī.

## Explanation of the Dhammapāsāda Lotus Ponds

"He created" means that he did not create them by having a drum beaten in the city and gathering a crowd of people. Rather, as soon as the King's thought arose, eighty-four thousand lotus ponds appeared, breaking through the surface of the earth. This was said in reference to those ponds.

"With two railings" means that with one railing, they were enclosed only at the edge of the bricks, and with the other railing, they were enclosed at the boundary of the pond's perimeter.

"This thought occurred"—why did it occur? It is said that one day, the Great Man, observing the great multitude of people going about after bathing and drinking, thought, "These people are going about as if they were madmen. If only these people had flowers to wear, it would be good." After that, this thought arose in that King.

In that passage, "blooming in all seasons" means that flowers usually bloom only in one particular season. But I will act in such a way that "they will bloom in all seasons," so he thought.

"He caused to be planted" means that he did not have various colored lotus seeds and so forth brought from various places to be planted. Rather, everything was accomplished as soon as the King's thought arose. The world, however, thought that they were planted by the King. Therefore, it is said, "He caused to be planted." From that time on, the great multitude of people went about wearing various kinds of water-born and land-born flowers, as if they were celebrating a festival.

Then the King, wishing to make the people even more endowed with happiness, planned the arrangement for the happiness of the people, saying, "Suppose I... at the banks of these lotus ponds," and so forth, and he did everything. In that passage, "they bathed them" means that one person rubbed the body, another prepared the bathing powders, another fetched water for the person bathing at the bank, and another received and gave the clothes.

"He established"—how did he establish? He had suitable ornaments made for both women and men, and placed only women there for the purpose of attending and serving, while placing everything else for the purpose of distribution as gifts; thus King Mahāsudassana gave gifts. He had a drum beaten, saying, "Enjoy these gifts." The great multitude of people, having come to the banks of the lotus ponds, bathed, changed their clothes, anointed themselves with various perfumes, and adorned themselves with exquisite flowers...
222:
Going to the place of almsgiving, among the many kinds of rice gruel, rice, solid food, and the eight kinds of drinks, whatever a person desired, they ate and drank that. Having worn delicate linen cloths of various colors from the Khoma region and enjoyed the prosperity, those who already possessed such things left them behind and went away. Those who did not possess them took them and went away. Even with elephants, horses, and vehicles, after riding and wandering for a while, those who had no need for them left them behind, while those who had need took them and went away. After sleeping on noble beds and enjoying the prosperity, those who had no need left them behind, while those who had need took them and went away. Even after enjoying prosperity with women, those who had no need left them behind, while those who had need took them and went away. Even after adorning themselves with the seven kinds of jeweled ornaments and enjoying the prosperity, those who had no need left them behind, while those who had need took them and went away. That almsgiving was also given repeatedly and persistently. The inhabitants of Jambudīpa had no other business; they wandered about merely enjoying the King's almsgiving.

Then the brahmins and householders thought: "Although this King is giving such an alms, he does not order anything to be brought, such as rice or milk. Even if the King does not order it, it is not proper for us to remain silent." Having thought thus, they collected much wealth and offered it to the King. Therefore, it was said, "Then, Ānanda, the brahmins and householders," and so on. Why did they think collectively in this way? Because some might bring a little from their house, and some might bring much. When those items were being gathered, a sound of dispute might arise: "Did you bring something good only from your house and not from mine? Did you bring much only from your house and not from mine?" To prevent such disputes from arising, they thought collectively in this way.

"Come, friend" means "Come, dear friend." "The palace named Dhamma"—he gave the order by assigning the name to the palace. Vissakamma the young deva asked again, "O King, how large do you want the palace to be?" When told, "Let it be one yojana in length and half a yojana in width, and let it be made entirely of jewels," he agreed, saying, "So be it, your words are excellent." Having made King Mahāsudassana, the King of Dhamma, accept it, he created it. In that context, "Ānanda, this is good for you" means "Ānanda, this is good for the King," which is the meaning of his acceptance. "By remaining silent" means...
223:
"There will be an opportunity for me to practice the Dhamma of a recluse," he desired, and thus accepted (endured) it by remaining silent. "Sāramaya" means made of the heartwood of sandalwood (candana).

In the phrase "dvīhi vedikāhi" (with two railings), one railing was at the top of the pinnacle of that palace, and the other was above the lower boundary.

"Duddikkho ahosi" means it was difficult to look at. It means it was hard to see because it was so full of radiance. "Musati" means it steals away (the eyes), makes them flutter, and does not allow them to stay still and gaze steadily. "Viddhe" means pierced through, or distant because the clouds have cleared away. "Deve" means in the sky.

"Māpesi kho" (he created) does not mean he ordered, "I will create a pond here, destroy your houses." Rather, by the mere arising of his thought, the earth split open and such a pond appeared. "Te sabbakāmehi" means he satisfied them with all desired objects—the recluses with the requisites of recluses, and the brahmins with the requisites of brahmins.

## The Commentary on the First Recitation (Paṭhamabhāṇavāra) is finished.

## Commentary on the Attainment of Jhana (Jhānasampatti)

"Mahiddhiko" means being endowed with great psychic power, characterized by the appearance of eighty-four thousand ponds by the mere arising of a thought. "Mahānubhāvo" means being endowed with great majesty because of the greatness of those desired benefits to be experienced. "Seyyathidaṃ" is an indeclinable (nipāta). Its meaning is "Which are those three?" "Dānassa" refers to the giving away of abundant offerings. "Damassa"—although in the Āḷavaka Sutta "dama" is said to be wisdom, in this sutta it refers to the act of observing the Uposatha performed by restraining oneself. "Saṃyamassa" refers to virtue (sīla).

## Commentary on the Bodhisatta's Previous Practice (Pubbayoga)

At this point, the previous practice (pubbayoga) of that King should be understood. It is heard that in the past, the King was born into a householder's family. At that time, during the dispensation of the living Buddha Kassapa, an elder monk lived in the forest. The Bodhisatta...
224:
That person (the Bodhisatta), who had entered the forest for his own business, saw the Elder, approached and paid homage to him. Observing the Elder's dwelling place and walking path, he asked, "Venerable Sir, does the Noble One reside here?" Upon hearing the reply, "Yes, lay devotee," he thought, "It is proper to build a leaf-hut for the Noble One here." Abandoning his own work, he cut timber and bamboo, built and roofed a leaf-hut, plastered the walls with fine clay, fitted a door, and made a wooden floor. Then, wondering, "Will the Noble One use it or not?", he sat down in a suitable place. The Elder returned from the village, entered the leaf-hut, and sat on the wooden floor. The lay devotee also came, paid homage, and sitting nearby, asked, "Venerable Sir, is the leaf-hut comfortable for residing?" "Lay devotee, it is comfortable and suitable for a renunciant," the Elder replied. When asked, "Venerable Sir, will you reside in this dwelling?", the Elder replied, "Yes, lay devotee." Knowing by his manner of acceptance that he would reside there, the devotee made the Elder promise, "Please come regularly to the door of my house," and then said, "Venerable Sir, please grant me one boon." The Elder replied, "Lay devotee, renunciants have transcended boons." The devotee then said, "Venerable Sir, please grant me a boon that is both allowable and blameless." The Elder said, "Speak, lay devotee." "Venerable Sir, in a place of permanent residence, people desire the Noble One's presence on both auspicious and inauspicious occasions; they tend to get angry with a monk who does not come. Therefore, even if you go to another place of invitation, please finish your meal only after entering my house," he requested. The Elder accepted.

That person spread a reed mat in the leaf-hut and arranged a couch and a stool; he provided a backrest, placed a foot-washing vessel, dug a pond, made a walking path, and scattered sand. Seeing that deer came and rubbed against the walls, causing clods of earth to fall, he enclosed the area with a thorn fence. Seeing that deer entered the pond and made the water muddy, he lined the inside with stones and enclosed the outside with a thorn fence, and planted rows of palm trees along the inner edge of the fence. Seeing that deer disturbed the smooth ground of the great walking path, he enclosed the walking path with a fence and planted rows of palm trees along the inner edge of the fence. Having thus completed the monastery grounds, he donated to the Elder the three robes, alms-food, medicine, a vessel for drinking and utility water, a needle-case, a small razor, a nail-cutter, a needle, a walking staff, sandals, a water-pitcher, an umbrella, a lamp-stand, an ear-pick, a water-filter, a dhamakaraṇa (water-strainer), an alms-bowl, a cup, and all other requisites used by monks. There was no requisite that the Bodhisatta had not previously donated to the Elder. That person, observing the precepts and performing the Uposatha...
225:
He served the Elder for the rest of his life. The Elder, residing right there, attained Arahatship and passed into Parinibbāna.

The Bodhisatta, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, was reborn in the celestial realm. Passing away from that celestial realm and coming to the human world, he was reborn in the royal city of Kusāvatī and became King Mahāsudassana.

"Thus, merit performed towards a noble recipient of offerings, such as the Sasana, even if not very great, yields grand results; therefore, a wise person should perform such merit."

Mahāviyūha refers to a great gabled palace made of silver. Desiring to live in that palace, he went there. "Sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) are only this much; you must withdraw from sensual thoughts by this measure. Beyond this is not your ground; this is called the House of Jhana; this is not a dwelling place for you,"—in this way, he restrained the three kinds of thoughts right at the palace door.

In the first Jhana and so forth, there is no separate task of performing the preparatory work (parikamma) for the Kasina. If he desires the blue Kasina, he looks at a blue gem; if he desires the yellow Kasina, he looks at gold; if he desires the red Kasina, he looks at a red gem; if he desires the white Kasina, he looks at silver. Thus, wherever he looks, the Kasina itself becomes manifest.

Everything that should be said regarding "accompanied by loving-kindness" (mettāsahagatena) and so forth has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, in the Pali text, only the four Jhanas and the four Immeasurables (appamaññā) are mentioned. However, the Great Man (Mahāpurisa), having produced all eight attainments (samāpatti) and the five supernormal powers (abhiññā), entering the attainments in fourteen ways such as in forward and backward order, subsists on the bliss of the attainments, just as a large bee entering a honeycomb subsists on the taste of honey.

## Description of the Eighty-Four Thousand Cities and So Forth

'Kusāvatīrā jadhānippamukhāni' means that the royal city of Kusāvatī is the chief of those cities, the most excellent of all cities. 'Bhattābhihāro' refers to the food that is brought forward.
226:
Why did he think, "For a hundred years, for a hundred years"? It was because he was weary of the sound of those elephants. Indeed, it is said, "Sound is a thorn to one who has entered meditative attainment." Therefore, the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) was weary of the sound. If he was weary of the sound, why did he not say, "Do not come"? He did not say so because he thought, "Now the King no longer looks after us," and those eighty-four thousand elephants would lose their regular food; he did not want that lack of food to happen to them.

## Explanation of Queen Subhaddā's Approach
"This thought occurred" — when did this occur? It occurred on the day of the King's passing. On that day, it is said that the deities thought, "Let not the King pass away without a protector; let him pass away surrounded by many harem women, daughters, and sons." Then, having influenced the Queen, they caused such a thought to arise in her mind. "Yellow-colored garments" — it is said that those garments were naturally pleasing to the King's mind; therefore, she said, "Put on those garments." "Queen, stay right here" — this means, "Queen, this meditation chamber (jhānāgāra) is not a place for living together with you; it is the place where I experience the bliss of jhāna; do not enter here."

"This thought occurred" — in the world, beings shine exceedingly bright at the time of death. Therefore, seeing the King's exceptionally clear sense faculties (indriya), such a thought arose. Then, not wishing for the King's death, thinking, "Let not the King pass away," she intended to speak of his complete virtues and make him remain alive, and thus she said, "O King, these possessions..." and so forth. In that passage, "Arouse desire" means "arouse affection, find delight." "Regard for life" means "have regard, attachment, and craving (taṇhā) for life."

"Queen, you [spoke] to me thus" — this refers to when the Queen, thinking of the King as a monk, said, "O King, we women do not know the customary language (upacāra-kathā) of monks; how should we speak, Great King?" The King then said, "Queen, address me in this way," and so forth. "Is censured" means censured by Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples, and other wise and learned persons. For what reason? Indeed, dying with attachment is the cause for being reborn in one's own house as a yakkha, a dog, a goat, an ox, a buffalo, a mouse, a cock, a louse, a fly, or a mosquito, and so on.
227:
Then, Ānanda, Queen Subhaddā wiped away her tears — this means the Queen went to a suitable place, wept and lamented, and then, having wiped away her tears, spoke these words.

## Explanation of the Rebirth in the Brahma World

"Or to a householder" — why is this said? Because those householders and sons of householders, like Soṇa the merchant's son and others, possess great wealth. It is said that a single meal for Soṇa the merchant's son was worth two hundred thousand. Thus, for those who eat such a meal, there occurs for a moment a state of being intoxicated by food, fainting from food, and exhaustion from food.

"At which time I lived" — this means the city where I lived; that was only one city. In the remaining cities, sons, daughters, and others, as well as servants, lived. The same principle applies to the palaces and gabled houses. Among the couches and so forth, he used only one couch; the remaining couches were for the use of his sons and others. Among the women, only one attended him; the others were merely attendants. By the word "I wear," it means I wear only one pair of garments; the remaining garments were for the one million six hundred and eighty thousand men who moved about as attendants. "I eat" — this shows that, at the most, I eat only about one nāḷi measure of rice; the remaining food was for the eight hundred and forty thousand men who moved about as attendants. Indeed, one pot of cooked rice is sufficient for ten people.

Those eighty-four thousand cities, eighty-four thousand palaces, and eighty-four thousand gabled houses arose as the result (nissanda) of the gift of a single leaf-roofed hut (paṇṇasālā). The eighty-four thousand couches arose as the result of the gift of a bed (mañcaka) given for the purpose of lying down. The eighty-four thousand elephants, horses, and chariots arose as the result of the gift of a stool (pīṭha) given for the purpose of sitting. The eighty-four thousand gems arose as the result of the gift of a single lamp. The eighty-four thousand lotus ponds arose as the result of the gift of a single lotus pond. The eighty-four thousand women, sons, and householders arose as the result of the gift of utility vessels, alms-bowls, cups, water-strainers (dhamakaraṇa), filters, needles, awls, razors, nail-clippers, keys, ear-picks, foot-scrubbers, sandals, umbrellas, and walking sticks. The eighty-four thousand milch cows arose as the result of the gift of the taste of milk. The eighty-four thousand crores of garments arose as the result of the gift of inner and outer robes.
228:
They came into existence through such consequences. It should be understood that the eighty-four thousand pots of cooked rice arose as a result of offering the five kinds of food.
