Thus, the Blessed One, having explained the prosperity of King Mahāsudassana in detail from the beginning, and wishing to show all that prosperity as being like children playing with sandcastles, said "Look, Ānanda," and so forth, while lying on the couch of his Parinibbāna. In that context, "they have changed (vipariṇatā)" means they have reached a state where they cannot be designated, like a lamp that has gone out after abandoning its natural state. "Ānanda, formations are thus impermanent" means they are called impermanent because they do not exist after having come into being in this way.

With this sequence of teaching, the Blessed One lived like a man who, having tied a ladder to a Campaka tree a hundred cubits high, climbed up, picked a Campaka flower, and then descended while untying the ladder. Similarly, he climbed the ladder of King Mahāsudassana’s prosperity, which was many hundreds of millions of years high, took hold of the characteristic of impermanence standing at the peak of that prosperity, and descended as if untying the ladder. Because he showed prosperity at the beginning and impermanence at the end, in ancient times, King Vasabha, while listening to the elders who were reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya chanting this sutta at the Ambalaṭṭhika near the eastern side of the Lohapāsāda, thought: "Friends, what has my grandfather (the Buddha) said here? He only speaks of prosperity in the place where he himself ate and drank." But when the Buddha said, "Ānanda, formations are thus impermanent," the King said, "Friends, having seen this matter, the One with Five Eyes (the Buddha) spoke thus." He then folded his left arm, struck his thigh with his right hand, and joyfully gave a cry of "Sādhu, Sādhu!"

"Thus they are not lasting (addhuvā)" means they are devoid of a permanent nature, like water bubbles and the like. "Thus they are unsatisfying (anassāsikā)" means they are devoid of satisfaction, like water drunk in a dream or like applied sandalwood paste.

"One should lay down the body (sarīraṃ nikkhipeyya)" means one should cast off the body. Now, however, he says, "Ānanda, for the Tathāgata, since defilements have been abandoned, there is no more laying down or tending to another body." After saying this, he addressed the Elder again: "The power of a Universal Monarch disappears on the seventh day after the King has gone forth. But for Mahāsudassana, on the seventh day after his death, the seven-gemmed walls, the seven-gemmed palm trees, the eighty-four thousand lotus ponds, the Dhamma Palace, the Dhamma Pond, and the Wheel Treasure—all these disappeared." Regarding treasures like the elephant and others, it is the natural law that they die together with the Universal Monarch when their lifespan ends.
229: If their lifespan still remains, the Elephant Treasure goes to the Uposatha elephant clan, the Horse Treasure goes to the Valāhaka horse clan, and the Gem Treasure goes back to Mount Vepulla. The power of the Queen Treasure disappears. The eyes of the Householder Treasure become ordinary. The ability of the Counselor Treasure vanishes. "The Blessed One said this" means the Blessed One spoke everything, both what is included in the Pali text and what is not. The remaining words are clear in meaning. ## The Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Sutta is finished.
230:
## 5. Commentary on the Janavasabha Sutta
## Commentary on the Declaration regarding the People of Nātika and so forth
273-275. This sutta beginning with "Thus have I heard" is the Janavasabha Sutta. In that sutta, the explanation of obscure terms is as follows: "Parito parito janapadesu" means in the surrounding districts. "Paricārake" refers to those who serve the Triple Gem: the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. "Upapattīsu" means in the occurrences or fulfillments of path-knowledge, destiny (gati), and merit. "Kāsikosalesu" means in the Kāsī and Kosala regions, in the Kāsī kingdom and the Kosala kingdom. This method should be understood everywhere. However, in these six kingdoms—Aṅga, Magadha, Yonaka, Kamboja, Assaka, and Avanti—he did not declare those who served the Triple Gem. In fact, among these sixteen great districts (Mahājanapadas), he only declared them in the first ten. "Nātikiyā" refers to the inhabitants of Nātika village.

"Tena" means by that state of being a Non-returner (Anāgāmī) and so forth. "Sutvā" means having heard the Buddha's answer to the questions, which he declared by distinguishing with his Omniscient Knowledge, they reached a conclusion regarding the states of Non-returner and so forth, and were delighted by that state of being a Non-returner and so forth. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, the word "tena" is explained as "te Nātikiyā" (those people of Nātika). In this sense, the letter "na" is merely a particle (nipāta).

## Commentary on the Discourse of Venerable Ānanda
"One who is in the state of praising the Blessed One" means passing away while praising thus: "Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the Saṅgha! Oh, the Dhamma is well-expounded!" "Many people would be inspired" means "Our mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, or friend used to eat and sleep together with us; we did pleasant things for them; they are said to be a Non-returner, a Once-returner, or a Stream-enterer. Oh, how good! Oh, how wonderful!" In this way, many people would gain faith.

"Gati" refers to the occurrence of path-knowledge. "Abhisamparāya" refers to the future life (upapatti-bhava) which occurs by the power of path-knowledge. "He saw" means how many people did he see? He saw two million four hundred thousand (2.4 million) people.
231:
Upasantapadisso means having a peaceful appearance (having a peaceful vision). Bhātiriva means shining excessively, being exceedingly beautiful. Indriyānaṃ means the faculties, with the mind-faculty as the sixth. In saying, "Ānanda, I saw," he said that he saw not 10, 20, 100, or 1000, but exactly two million four hundred thousand (2,400,000) people.

## Description of Janavasabha the Yakkha

Seeing that "so many people have been liberated from suffering depending on me," strong joy (somanassa) arose. The mind became clear. Due to the clarity of the mind, the heart-blood produced by the mind became clear. Due to the clarity of the heart-blood, the faculties with the mind-faculty as the sixth became clear. After saying all this, he said, "Then, Ānanda..." and so forth. In those words, because that deva, having heard the Blessed One's Dhamma talk, became the leader of one hundred and ten thousand (110,000) people and became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), he was given the name "Janavasabha."

"Seven times from here" means seven times after passing away from this deva world. "Seven times from there" means seven times after passing away from that human world. "Fourteen rounds of saṃsāra" means all fourteen sequences of the aggregates. "Knows having lived" means knowing having lived by way of rebirth. "In the place where I lived before" means having lived before this current existence, both as a companion of King Vessavaṇa in the deva world and as a king in the human world. Because of having lived like this before, and because of having performed much merit in the Triple Gem as a Sotāpanna now, although he is capable of being reborn in higher deva worlds by the power of that merit, he was reborn right here in this realm (Cātumahārājika) due to strong attachment (nikanti) to the place where he lived for a long time.

By the words "My hope (āsa) still remains," he shows that he did not spend time heedlessly or sleeping, thinking "I am a Sotāpanna." He undertook insight (vipassanā) to attain the path of Once-returner (Sakadāgāmi). "I will penetrate [the truth] this very day" shows that he lives with such effort (ussāha). "From which day" refers to the day he became a Sotāpanna upon first seeing [the Buddha] in the Laṭṭhivana Grove. "Venerable Sir, from that day I know I will no longer fall into the lower realms for a long time" means starting from that day, for a long time consisting of the fourteen previous existences, he will no longer fall into the lower realms; he knows the nature of not falling (avinipātadhammatā) attained through the path of Stream-entry in the Laṭṭhivana Grove.
232:
"Anacchariya" means being repeatedly wonderful. When reflecting again and again, it is wonderful that I, while traveling on some business, saw the Blessed One on the way. It is also wonderful that I heard the words spoken by the Great King Vessavaṇa to his own retinue, just as if I had seen them in the presence of the Blessed One. The "two reasons" are the fact of seeing [the Blessed One] on the way and the desire to report the words heard in the presence of Great King Vessavaṇa.

## Explanation of the Assembly of Gods

"They assemble"—why do they assemble? Those gods assemble for four reasons: to support the monks entering the rains-retreat (vassa), to support the monks performing the pavāraṇā ceremony, to listen to the Dhamma, and to enjoy the celestial sports near the Pāricchattaka tree. Among these four, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, when it is said "Tomorrow the rains-retreat must begin," the gods of the two [lower] heaven worlds assemble in the Sudhammā assembly hall and deliberate: "In such-and-such a monastery, one monk is entering the rains-retreat; in such-and-such a monastery, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, or a thousand monks are entering the rains-retreat. Provide good protection for the venerable ones in those various places." In this way, they provide support for the monks entering the rains-retreat. At that time, they assembled for this very reason. "This is in their place" means this is the place for those Four Great Kings. Only after those Great Kings have sat down does it become our place. "For the sake of which benefit" means for the benefit of supporting the monks entering the rains-retreat. "Reflecting on that benefit, deliberating on that benefit" means reflecting on the benefit of protecting the community of monks living in the forest, and deliberating with the Four Great Kings: "Provide protection for the community of monks who have completed the rains-retreat in such-and-such places." "They have spoken words" means the thirty-three deities have spoken, and the Great Kings are those to whom the words were spoken. Likewise, the thirty-three deities give advice, and the others [the Great Kings] are those to whom the advice was given. In both phrases, "taṃ" is merely a particle. "They have not yet gone" means they have not yet arrived. "Extensive" means great in significance. "The power of the gods" means the radiance of the clothes, ornaments, mansions, and bodies of all the deities, which spreads for twelve leagues. However, the bodily radiance of gods with great merit spreads for a hundred leagues. Surpassing that power of the gods. "Precursor" means just as the dawn is the precursor of the rising sun, this natural appearance is the precursor of the arrival of the Great Brahma. "Inaccessible" means the Tāvatiṃsa gods cannot see the natural appearance of Brahma. "In the range of the eye" means in the sensitivity of the eye (cakkhu-pasāda) or in the appearance of the object; the natural appearance of that Brahma cannot be perceived by the clear sight of the gods' eyes. Indeed, lower gods can only see higher gods if the latter create a coarse physical form. "Obtaining joy" means attaining happiness.
233:
Just as the dawn is the precursor and the first sign when the sun is about to rise, even so, this appearance indicates that it is the first sign when the Great Brahma is about to arrive.

## Commentary on the Story of Sanankumāra

Anabhisambhavanīyo means unattainable (invisible). The meaning is that the Tāvatiṃsa gods cannot see the natural form of that Brahma. Cakkhupathasmiṃ means in the sensitivity of the eye or in the range of vision. The meaning is that his natural form does not come into the range of the gods' vision; it does not become an object of their senses. Indeed, deities in lower realms can only see the gross forms created by deities of higher realms. Vedapaṭilābhaṃ means obtaining joy and delight. Adhunābhisitto rajjena means recently consecrated in kingship. This meaning of obtaining joy by a newly consecrated king should be illustrated by the story of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya.

That King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya, after defeating thirty-two Tamil kings and being consecrated in Anurādhapura, was so overwhelmed with joy that he could not sleep for a whole month. Therefore, he informed the Saṅgha of monks, saying, "Venerable sirs, I cannot sleep." The Saṅgha said, "Great King, if that is so, undertake the Uposatha today." Thus, the king undertook the Uposatha. The Saṅgha sent eight monks who were experts in the Abhidhamma, saying, "Recite the Cittayamaka." They went and said, "Great King, please lie down," and began the recitation. While listening to the recitation, the king fell asleep. The elders left, saying, "Do not wake the king." The king woke up at sunrise the next day and, not seeing the elders, asked, "Where are the venerable ones?" When told, "They left after knowing you had fallen asleep," the king said, "Friends, there is no medicine unknown to the sons of my grandfather (the Buddha); they even know the medicine for sleep."

Pañcasikho means being like the Gandhabba Pañcasikha, who has five top-knots. It is said that all the deities love the form of the Gandhabba youth Pañcasikha. Therefore, Brahma also manifested himself by creating such a form. Pallaṅkena nisīdi means he sat down cross-legged.

Vissaṭṭho means having a voice well-released from defects, not oppressed by bile or phlegm. Viññeyyo means having a voice that makes the meaning understood. Mañjū means having a voice that is sweet and soft. Savanīyo means having a voice that is worthy of being heard and pleasant to the ear.
234:
Bindu means having a compact or unified tone. Avisārī means being well-purified and not scattered. Gambhīro means originating from a deep place starting from the root of the navel, not produced merely by the impact of the tongue, teeth, lips, and palate. Indeed, a sound produced merely by the impact of the tongue, teeth, lips, and palate is unpleasant and cannot be heard from afar. Ninnādī means being resonant like the sound of a great thundercloud or a mudiṅga drum. Furthermore, it should be understood here that each subsequent word clarifies the meaning of the preceding one.

Yathāparisaṃ means making it known to the entire assembly, however large it may be. That Brahma's voice resonates only within the assembly and does not diffuse outside. The words beginning with "Ye hi keci" are spoken to show the practice for the welfare of many people. The phrase "Saraṇaṃ gatā" does not refer to those who have taken refuge casually, but rather to those who have established their refuge without doubt. Gandhabbakāyaṃ paripūrenti means they fill the host of Gandhabba deities. Thus, it is said that from the time our Teacher appeared in the world, the six deva realms and so on have been continuously filled with assemblies, like a tube packed with flour or like a forest of reeds or canes.

## Commentary on the Development of the Bases of Power

Yāvasupaññattā cime tena bhagavatā means these have been very well-prescribed and well-spoken by that Blessed One, my Teacher. In these bases of power (iddhipāda), it should be understood that it is called "iddhi" in the sense of accomplishment, and "pāda" in the sense of foundation. Iddhipahutāya means for the sake of being capable in supernormal powers. Iddhivasavitāya means for the sake of having mastery over supernormal powers, or it means having mastery through repeated practice. Iddhivikubbanatāya means for the sake of being able to display various transformations through supernormal power.

In the phrases such as "chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ," concentration caused by desire or dominated by desire is called "desire-concentration" (chandasamādhi). This is a designation for the concentration obtained by making the wholesome desire to act the predominant factor. Volitional formations that are primary are called "exertion-formations" (padhānasaṅkhāra). This is a designation for the energy of Right Effort (sammappadhāna) which accomplishes the four functions. Samannāgataṃ means being endowed with desire-concentration and exertion-formations. Iddhipāda refers to the remaining group of mental factors and consciousness which, in the sense of foundation, are the basis for the desire, concentration, and exertion-formations associated with the direct-knowledge mind, which are called "iddhi" either in the sense of accomplishment or because by means of this, beings become accomplished, prosperous, and exalted. For it is said: "The base of power is the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness of one who is so [attained]" (Vibhaṅga 434).
235:
In this way, the meaning should be understood for the remaining [bases of power, such as the base of power consisting of energy]. Just as concentration obtained by making desire the predominant factor is called concentration of desire (chanda-samādhi), so too, concentration obtained by making energy, mind, or investigation the predominant factor is called concentration of investigation (vīmaṃsā-samādhi), and so on. Alternatively, access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) is called the base (pāda), and the first jhāna is called the power (iddhi). The first jhāna together with its access is the base, and the second jhāna is the power. Thus, the meaning in this context of the bases of power (iddhipāda) should be understood as the base in the preceding stage and the power in the subsequent stage. The detailed explanation of the bases of power has been stated in the Visuddhimagga and the Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā.

Some teachers say, "The power (iddhi) is accomplished (in the ultimate sense), but the base of power (iddhipāda) is not." To refute the view of those teachers, the section called Uttara-cūḷika-vāra in the Abhidhamma is brought forward: "There are four bases of power: the base of power consisting of desire, the base of power consisting of energy, the base of power consisting of mind, and the base of power consisting of investigation. Therein, what is the base of power consisting of desire? Here, a monk, at a time when he develops supramundane jhāna which is leading out, leading to the diminution [of rebirth], for the abandoning of wrong views, for the attainment of the first stage (Sotāpatti-magga), secluded from sensual pleasures, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult practice and slow realization. At that time, whatever desire, state of desiring, wish to act, or wholesome desire for the Dhamma there is—this is called the base of power consisting of desire. The remaining states are states associated with the base of power consisting of desire" (as found in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi). These bases of power are mentioned here only in terms of the supramundane. Among those four, the Elder Raṭṭhapāla produced the supramundane state by making desire the leader. The Elder Soṇa did so by making energy the leader, the Elder Sambhūta by making mind the leader, and the Venerable Mogharāja by making investigation the leader.

Among those four, there is this analogy: Suppose there are four sons of ministers who, desiring a high position, live in dependence on a king. One of them, having a desire for service and knowing the king's intention and preference, serves him day and night, pleases the king, and attains a high position. Like that minister's son, one who produces the supramundane state with desire as the leader should be understood.

Another minister's son thinks, "Who can serve every single day? When a task arises, I will please the king through my effort." When a border region rebels, he is sent by the king, and by crushing the enemy through effort, he attains a high position. Like that minister's son, one who produces the supramundane state with energy as the leader should be understood.
236:
Another minister's son thinks, "Serving every day or shielding spears and arrows with one's chest is just a burden. I will please the king through the power of counsel." Because he was practiced in the art of knowing the battlefield (khattavijjā), he pleased the king through strategic counsel and attained a high position. Like that minister's son, one who produces the supramundane state with mind as the leader (such as the Elder Sambhūta) should be understood.

Yet another minister's son thinks, "What is the use of such service and so on? Kings usually give high positions to those of noble birth. If he gives to such a person, he will give to me too." Relying solely on his noble birth (jātisampatti), he attained a high position. Like that minister's son, one who produces the supramundane state by relying on extremely pure wisdom, with wisdom as the leader (such as the Elder Mogharāja), should be understood.

Anekavihita means having many varieties. Iddhividha means the categories of psychic power.

## Explanation of the Threefold Attainment of Opportunity

"For the attainment of happiness" means for the attainment of the happiness of jhāna, the happiness of the path, and the happiness of the fruit. "Mixed" (saṃsaṭṭha) means having an associated mind. "Noble Dhamma" (ariya-dhamma) means the Dhamma taught by the Noble Buddha. "Hears" (suṇāti) means hearing what is taught either in the presence of the Blessed One or by monks, nuns, and so on. "Attends wisely" (yoniso manasikāra) means attending by way of method, by way of the path, by way of cause, as "impermanent" and so on, in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma. It is said: "Wise attention means attention to the method, attention to the path; the turning of the mind, the repeated turning, the application, the attention to the mind as impermanent in what is impermanent, as suffering in what is suffering, as non-self in what is non-self, as foul in what is foul, or in accordance with the [Four Noble] Truths." When such wise attention is mentioned, it means one begins the work. "Unmixed" (asaṃsaṭṭha) means dwelling without being mixed with either the objects of sensuality or the defilements of sensuality. "Happiness arises" means the arising of the happiness of the first jhāna. "Joy greater than happiness" means that for one who has emerged from the meditative attainment, successive joy arises due to the condition of the happiness of jhāna. Pamuda refers to weak rapture that is merely the nature of gladness. Pāmojja refers to stronger rapture and joy. "The first attainment of opportunity" is so called because the first jhāna stands having removed the five hindrances and having taken its own opportunity.
237:
"Are coarse" (Oḷārikā) means here, let bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhāra) and verbal formations (vacīsaṅkhāra) be coarse first; how are mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra) coarse? They are coarse because they have not yet been abandoned. Indeed, bodily formations are abandoned by the fourth jhāna (catutthajjhāna), verbal formations by the second jhāna (dutiyajjhāna), and mental formations by the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). Thus, even when bodily and verbal formations are abandoned, those mental formations still remain; therefore, in comparison to what has been abandoned, they are called coarse because they are not yet abandoned. "Happiness" (sukha) refers to the happiness of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) associated with the fourth jhāna that arises for one emerging from the attainment of cessation. "Joy that is greater than happiness" refers to the successive joyful feeling (somanassavedanā) for one who has emerged from the attainment of fruition. "Attainment of the second opportunity" (dutiyo okāsādhigamo) means the fourth jhāna stands having taken its own opportunity by setting aside pleasure and pain; therefore, it is called "attainment of the second opportunity." In this context, if the fourth jhāna is taken, the second and third jhānas are already included; therefore, they are not mentioned separately.

## In the words beginning with "This is wholesome" (Idaṃ kusalaṃ)

Wholesome (kusala) refers to the ten courses of wholesome action (kusalakammapatha). Unwholesome (akusala) refers to the ten courses of unwholesome action (akusalakammapatha). The dyad of blameworthy things (sāvajjaduka) and so forth should also be understood by the power of those wholesome and unwholesome things. All those wholesome and unwholesome things have corresponding states with darkness (unwholesome) and brightness (wholesome); therefore, they are called states with corresponding darkness and brightness. Nibbāna alone is a state without a counterpart (unrivaled). "Ignorance is abandoned" means the ignorance (avijjā) that covers the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa) is abandoned. "Knowledge arises" means the knowledge (vijjā) associated with the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga) arises. "Happiness" refers to both the happiness of the path of Arahantship and the happiness of fruition (phala). "Joy that is greater than happiness" refers to the repeated joyful feeling (somanassavedanā) for one who has emerged from the attainment of fruition. "Attainment of the third opportunity" means the path of Arahantship stands having taken its own opportunity by setting aside all defilements; therefore, it is called "attainment of the third opportunity." As for the remaining paths, if that path of Arahantship is taken, they are already included within; therefore, they are not mentioned separately.

These three attainments of opportunity are explained in detail by way of the thirty-eight objects of meditation. How? Having defined all objects by way of access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā) according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga, the first jhāna in twenty-four places is called the "attainment of the first opportunity." The second and third jhānas in thirteen places, and the fourth jhāna and the attainment of cessation in fifteen places, are called the "attainment of the second opportunity." The ten access jhānas (upacārajjhāna), which are the proximate cause of the path, belong to the attainment of the third opportunity. Alternatively, among the three trainings (sikkhā), the training in higher virtue (adhisīlasikkhā) belongs to the attainment of the first opportunity, the training in higher mind (adhicittasikkhā) to the second, and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññāsikkhā) to the third; thus it is also stated by way of the trainings. Also in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, from the minor section on virtue (cūḷasīla) up to the first jhāna is called the attainment of the first opportunity. From the second jhāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana)...
238:
...from the second jhāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) is called the attainment of the second opportunity (okāsādhigama). From insight (vipassanā) up to the fruition of Arahantship (arahatta) is called the attainment of the third opportunity; thus it is also stated by way of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. Among the three Baskets (Piṭaka), the Vinaya Piṭaka belongs to the first attainment of opportunity, the Suttanta Piṭaka to the second, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka to the third; thus it is also stated by way of the Piṭakas.

In ancient times, it is said that the Great Elders would recite this very Janavasabha Sutta on the day of entering the rains-retreat (vassūpanāyikā). For what reason did they recite it? They recited it with the intention: "We shall be able to explain by distinguishing the three Baskets." Indeed, for one who speaks by well-combining with the three Baskets, it cannot be said that it is poorly spoken. This sutta, being spoken only by incorporating the three Baskets, should be understood as well-expounded.

## Description of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Catusatipaṭṭhānavaṇṇanā)

"For the attainment of the wholesome" (kusalassādhigamāya) means for the sake of attaining the path-wholesome (maggakusala) and the fruit-wholesome (phalakusala). Both of these are indeed wholesome (kusala) in the sense of being faultless (anavajja) or in the sense of being secure (khema). In that teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, "is rightly concentrated" (sammāsamādhiyati) means having a well-placed mind, a one-pointed mind, in that internal body. "He produces the knowledge and vision in the external body of another" (bahiddhā parakāye ñāṇadassanaṃ abhinibbatteti) means he directs knowledge from his own body towards the body of another. This method applies everywhere. And in all places, by the word "mindful" (satimā), it means the mindfulness that grasps the body and so forth. By the word "world" (loko), the body and so forth that are grasped are themselves the world. These four foundations of mindfulness should be understood as being spoken as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.

## Description of the Seven Requisites of Concentration (Sattasamādhiparikkhāravaṇṇanā)

In the phrase "requisites of concentration" (samādhiparikkhārā), there are three kinds of requisites (parikkhāra). In the passage "The chariot has virtue as its equipment (sīlaparikkhāro), jhāna as its axle, and energy as its wheels," the term parikkhāra means ornament or decoration. In the passage "It is well-protected by the seven city-requisites (nagaraparikkhārehi)," the term parikkhāra means surroundings or retinue (parivāra). In the passage "The requisite for life as support for the sick (medicine)," the term parikkhāra means equipment or necessity (sambhāra). But here, by way of the requisite as retinue, it is called "seven requisites of concentration." "Encircled" (parikkhata) means surrounded. "This is called the noble right concentration" means this noble right concentration is called right concentration as it is surrounded by seven factors, like a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) surrounded by seven jewels. "With its support" (saupaniso) means it is said to be with a basis or with a retinue. "For one of right view" (sammādiṭṭhissa) means for the person established in right view, "right intention arises" (sammāsaṅkappo pahoti). This method applies to all terms.
239:
This Right Concentration, surrounded by (the seven factors), is called "Noble Right Concentration." "Sa-upanisa" means it exists together with its basis or together with its attendants. "Sammādiṭṭhissa" means for a person established in Right View. "Sammāsaṅkappo pahoti" means Right Intention arises. This method should be understood for all terms. This meaning should be understood both by way of the Path and by way of the Fruit. How? For one established in the Right View associated with the Path, Path-Right Intention arises... [and so on] ...for one established in Path-Knowledge, Path-Liberation (liberation from defilements by the Path of Arahatship) arises. Similarly, for one established in the Right View of the Fruit, Fruit-Right Intention arises... [and so on] ...for one established in the Knowledge associated with the Fruit, Fruit-Liberation (liberation from defilements associated with the Fruit) arises.

The terms beginning with "Svākkhāto" have already been explained in the Visuddhimagga. "Apārutā" means they are opened. "Amatassa" means of Nibbāna. "Dvārā" means the Noble Paths which are the ways of entry. "Aveccappasādena" means with unwavering confidence. "Dhamma-vinītā" means they have emerged by means of the Noble Path which leads out from the round of rebirths.

In this context, the phrase "itarā pajā" refers to Non-returners (Anāgāmīs). It means that there are also Non-returners. "Puññabhāgā" means they are produced by a portion of merit. "Ottappaṃ" means possessing moral dread. By the word "ottappaṃ," it is shown: "I am unable to count because of the fear of false speech, lest I might occasionally speak a falsehood; it is not that I lack the power to count."

By the words "What do you think, Lord?", he is merely questioning King Vessavaṇa. It is not that King Vessavaṇa holds the view that such a Teacher never existed before or will not exist in the future. Indeed, there is no difference in the realization of the Dhamma among all Buddhas.

"Sayamparisāyaṃ" means in his own assembly. "Tayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ" refers to this entire holy life of the Three Trainings. The remaining words are clear. These words were placed here by the Elder Recensors of the Dhamma.

## The Commentary on the Janavasabha Sutta is Finished.
240:
## 6. Commentary on the Mahāgovinda Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Mahāgovinda Sutta. In this Mahāgovinda Sutta, the explanation of the obscure terms is as follows. "Pañcasikho" refers to one who has five crests or five locks of hair hanging down at the back.

It is said that when this celestial youth Pañcasikha was performing meritorious deeds in the human world, during his time as a boy with five top-knots, he was the chief of cowherds. Taking other boys with him, he wandered about performing such meritorious deeds as building rest-houses at the four-way junctions outside the village, digging ponds, constructing bridges, leveling uneven roads, and removing trees that might strike the axles of carts. He passed away while still a youth. That existence of his was desirable, pleasant, and delightful. After passing away, he was reborn in the Cātumahārājika heaven with a lifespan of nine million years. The physical form of that celestial youth Pañcasikha was three gāvutas in height and resembled a mass of gold.

That celestial youth, having adorned himself with ornaments amounting to a thousand cartloads (one vāha), and anointing himself with perfumes amounting to nine kumbhas, wearing divine red garments and wearing an ear-ornament (crest-flower) made of red gold, wanders about in the form of a boy with five top-knots, with five locks of hair hanging on his back. Therefore, they know him only as "Pañcasikha."

"Abhikkantāya rattiyā" means at midnight when the first watch of the night has passed and ended. "Abhikkantavaṇṇo" means having a complexion that is exceedingly desirable, pleasant, and delightful. Although he was naturally of a pleasing appearance, because he came fully adorned, he was of surpassing beauty. "Kevalakappaṃ" means entirely, from all around. Here, the word "kevala" expresses the sense of "without remainder," as in the phrase "kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ." The word "kappa" expresses the sense of "all around," as in the Pali "kevalakappaṃ jetavanaṃ" and so on. "Obhāsetvā" means having suffused with his own radiance, making it shine with a single light like the moon or the sun.

## Explanation of the Assembly of Devas

"Sudhammāyaṃ sabhāyaṃ" means in the celestial assembly hall named Sudhammā, which arose as a result of the merit of a woman named Sudhammā who donated a pinnacle made of wood one cubit in length. It is said that the floor of that Sudhammā assembly hall is made of crystal, and the pillars are made of rubies...
241:
The pillars are made of gold. The lotus-shaped pots (capitals) placed on the pillars and the inner cross-beams are made of silver. The figures of beasts are made of coral. The rafters, the roof-ridges, and the eaves-trims are made of the seven kinds of gems. The inner roof is made of indranīla (sapphire) bricks. The outer roof is made of gold. The pinnacle is made of silver. It is three hundred yojanas in length and width. It is nine hundred yojanas in circumference. It is five hundred yojanas in height. In such an assembly hall named Sudhammā, (the devas assemble).

In the passages beginning with Dhataraṭṭho, the meaning should be understood as follows: The Great King Dhataraṭṭha, the king of the Gandhabbas, surrounded by one hundred thousand crores of Gandhabba devas, causing them to hold one hundred thousand crores of golden planks and golden spears, sits in the eastern direction facing west, placing the devas from the two (lower) deva realms in front of him.

The Great King Virūḷhaka, the king of the Kumbhaṇḍas, surrounded by one hundred thousand crores of Kumbhaṇḍa devas, causing them to hold one hundred thousand crores of silver planks and golden spears, sits in the southern direction facing north, placing the devas from the two deva realms in front of him.

The Great King Virūpakkha, the king of the Nāgas, surrounded by one hundred thousand crores of Nāgas, causing them to hold one hundred thousand crores of large ruby planks and golden spears, sits in the western direction facing east, placing the devas from the two deva realms in front of him.

The Great King Vessavaṇa, the king of the Yakkhas, surrounded by one hundred thousand crores of Yakkhas, causing them to hold one hundred thousand crores of large coral planks and golden spears, sits in the northern direction facing south, placing the devas from the two deva realms in front of him—thus it should be understood.

Regarding the statement, "Thereafter, our seat is located," it means that behind those four Great Kings, there is an opportunity for us to sit. Beyond that place, we do not get to enter or to see. The reason for the assembly here is only of the four kinds previously mentioned. Among those four, the support for those entering the rains retreat (vassūpanāyika-saṅgaha) has been explained in detail. Just as they assemble and consult on the day of entering the rains retreat, likewise on the day of Mahāpavāraṇā, the full moon day of Assayuja, they assemble and consult, saying, "Where shall we go today, and in whose presence shall we perform the Pavāraṇā?" Among those hosts of devas, Sakka, the king of devas, mostly performs the Pavāraṇā at the great monastery named Piyangu-dīpa. The remaining devas...
242:
The devas, taking celestial flowers such as the Pāricchattaka and celestial sandalwood powder, go only to places that delight their hearts and perform the Pavāraṇā. Thus, they assemble for the sake of mutual support through Pavāraṇā.

In the deva realm, however, there is a creeper named Āsāvatī. Thinking that this creeper will bloom, the devas go to attend to it for a thousand years by human reckoning. When the Pāricchattaka tree blooms, they go to attend to it for a whole year. Those devas are joyful from the time the pale leaves of that Pāricchattaka tree appear. As it is said:

"Monks, at the time when the Pāricchattaka Kovīḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas has pale leaves, at that time, monks, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are joyful, thinking, 'Now the Pāricchattaka Kovīḷāra has pale leaves; before long, the leaves will fall.' Monks, at the time when the Pāricchattaka Kovīḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas has fallen leaves, it becomes full of buds, it becomes full of net-like young leaves, it becomes full of large buds, it becomes full of flower-stalks. Monks, at that time, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are joyful, thinking, 'Now the Pāricchattaka Kovīḷāra has produced flower-stalks; before long, it will be in full bloom.'

Monks, the radiance of the Pāricchattaka Kovīḷāra tree in full bloom spreads for fifty yojanas all around; its fragrance travels one hundred yojanas downwind. Such is the power of the Pāricchattaka Kovīḷāra tree," (the Buddha said).

When the Pāricchattaka tree blooms, there is no need for climbing (to pluck flowers), nor for taking a hook to bend the branches, nor for making flower baskets to carry the flowers. The 'cutting wind' arises and plucks the flowers from their stalks; the 'receiving wind' catches the falling flowers; the 'bringing wind' brings them into the Sudhammā celestial assembly hall; the 'sweeping wind' removes the old flowers; the 'spreading wind' spreads the petals, calyxes, and stamens while making them appear as if they are dancing. In the center, there is a Dhamma-throne. Above it, there is a jeweled throne one yojana in size, over which a white parasol of three yojanas is held. Immediately next to that jeweled throne is Sakka's...
243:
The seat of the King of Devas is spread. Following that, the seats for the thirty-three deities are spread, and after that, the seats for other powerful deities. For the undistinguished deities, however, the flower pericarp itself serves as their seat.

The deities enter the celestial assembly and take their seats. At that time, pollen dust rises from the flowers, strikes the flower pericarp above, and as it falls, it makes the three-gāvuta-sized bodies of the deities appear as if they were smoothly adorned with lac-dye. This play of the deities comes to an end only after four months. In this way, they assemble to enjoy the play with the Pāricchattaka flowers.

Eight days every month, the great preaching of the Dhamma is proclaimed in the celestial realm. In the Sudhammā celestial assembly hall there, either the Great Brahmā Sanankumāra, or Sakka the King of Devas, or a monk who is a Dhamma preacher, or another deity who is a Dhamma preacher, delivers a discourse on the Dhamma. On the eighth day of the lunar fortnight, the ministers of the Four Great Kings; on the fourteenth day, their sons; and on the fifteenth day, the Four Great Kings themselves go out, taking golden plates and natural vermilion, and wander through the villages, market towns, and royal capitals.

Those celestial kings write on the golden plates with natural vermilion: "Such a woman or such a man has gone to the Buddha for refuge, has gone to the Dhamma for refuge, has gone to the Saṅgha for refuge. They observe the five precepts. They keep the Uposatha eight days a month. They fulfill the duty of attending to their mother. They fulfill the duty of attending to their father. In such a place, an offering was made with a hundred handfuls of lotuses or with a pot of flowers. A thousand lamps were lit as an offering. They caused the hearing of the Dhamma at irregular times. They caused the construction of the parasol-railing, the surrounding-railing, the enclosure-railing, the lion throne, and the lion staircase. They fulfill the three types of right conduct. They undertake and practice the ten wholesome paths of action." Having written this, they bring it and place it in the hands of the celestial youth Pañcasikha. Pañcasikha places it in the hands of the celestial youth Mātali. Mātali, the charioteer, places it in the hands of Sakka, the King of Devas.

When those who perform meritorious deeds are few, the golden plate record is small. Upon seeing that small golden plate, the deities become displeased, saying, "Alas, sirs, the great multitude of people live in negligence; the four woeful states will be filled, and the six celestial realms will be empty." But if the golden plate record is large, upon seeing that large golden plate, the deities say, "Alas, sirs, the great multitude of people live without negligence; the four woeful states will be empty..."
244:
"...will be empty, the six celestial realms will be filled. We shall have the opportunity to celebrate the constellation festival, honoring the new deities of great merit who have arrived after performing meritorious deeds in the Buddha's Dispensation." Thus, they become joyful. Taking that golden plate record, Sakka, the King of Devas, reads it aloud. When he speaks in his normal voice, the sound reaches twelve yojanas. When he speaks with a loud voice, it stands covering the entire celestial city of ten thousand yojanas. In this way, they assemble for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. In this Sutta, however, it should be understood that they have assembled for the purpose of favoring with Pavāraṇā.

"Tathāgataṃ namassantā" means paying homage to the Tathāgata through nine reasons. "Dhammassa ca sudhammataṃ" refers to the excellence of the Dhamma, characterized by being well-expounded (svākkhātata) and so forth, and the good practice of the Saṅgha, characterized by practicing uprightly (ujuppaṭipannatā) and so forth.

## Explanation of the Eight True Qualities
"Yathābucca" means according to what is true, according to nature. "Vaṇṇe" means qualities or virtues. "Payirudāhāsī" means spoke or preached. Regarding "Bahujana-hitāya paṭipanno" (practiced for the welfare of the many), how did he practice? Even while aspiring for Buddhahood by combining the eight factors at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, he is said to have practiced for the welfare of the many.

While fulfilling these ten perfections—the perfection of generosity (dāna), the perfection of virtue (sīla), the perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma), the perfection of wisdom (paññā), the perfection of energy (viriya), the perfection of patience (khanti), the perfection of truthfulness (sacca), the perfection of determination (adhiṭṭhāna), the perfection of loving-kindness (mettā), and the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā)—for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, he was indeed practicing for the welfare of the many.

When he was the ascetic Khantivādī, when he was Prince Cūḷadhammapāla, when he was the elephant king Chaddanta, when he was the dragon kings Bhūridatta, Campeyya, and Saṅkhapāla, and when he was the monkey king Mahākapi—while performing such difficult tasks, he was indeed practicing for the welfare of the many. While existing in the life of King Vessantara, giving the seven great hundredfold gifts, causing the earth to tremble in seven places, and reaching the pinnacle of the perfections, he was indeed practicing for the welfare of the many. While staying for the full lifespan in the Tusita heaven in the existence immediately following that of Vessantara, he was indeed practicing for the welfare of the many.

There, having seen the five prognostic signs and being entreated by the deities and Brahmās of the ten thousand world-systems, he made the five great observations and gave his word to favor the deities and Brahmās...
245:
Even while passing away from the Tusita heaven and taking conception in his mother's womb, he practiced for the welfare of many.

Having dwelt in his mother's womb for ten months, even while being born from his mother's womb in the Lumbinī grove; having lived as a householder for twenty-nine years, even while departing in the Great Renunciation and becoming a monk on the banks of the Anomā River; having exerted himself in meditation for six years, wearying his body, and even while ascending the Bodhi throne and penetrating Omniscience; even while spending the seven weeks (Satta-sattāha) at the site of enlightenment (Bodhimanda); even while arriving at Isipatana and turning the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma; even while performing the Twin Miracle; even while descending from the heaven of the thirty-three (Devorohaṇa); even while remaining as a Buddha for forty-five years; even while relinquishing the life-force; even while attaining Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder of the mental aggregates and materiality between the twin Sal trees—he practiced for the welfare of many. It should be understood that as long as his relics, even as small as mustard seeds, remain, he is one who has practiced for the welfare of many. The remaining terms are merely synonyms for this 'bahujanahitāya' (for the welfare of many). Among those terms, each subsequent term explains the meaning of the preceding one.

'We do not see (anyone other than the Buddha) in the past, nor do we see (anyone) now'—in this statement, it means that in the past, we do not see any person other than the Buddha; in the future, we do not see any; and as for the present, because there is no other Teacher, we do not see anyone other than that Blessed One. In the Commentary (Atthakathā) also, it is said: 'The Buddhas of the past and future are just like our Teacher; what is Sakka saying?' and then, 'At present, there is no other Teacher who practices for the welfare of many except our Teacher; therefore, he says "I do not see."' Just as in this case, this meaning should be understood in the subsequent passages as well. Terms such as 'Svākkhāta' and 'Kusala' have the meanings already mentioned.

In the phrase 'The water of the Ganges with the water of the Yamunā,' at the confluence of the Ganges and Yamunā rivers, the water merges and becomes one in color, smell, and taste; in the middle, it is identical like a piece of gold, not distinct as when mixed with the water of the great ocean. The path of practice for pure Nibbāna is also pure. Indeed, it is impossible to see Nibbāna in old age after having practiced medicine and the like in one's youth and frequented improper places. The path leading to Nibbāna should be pure, like the sky. Just as the sky is unattached and pure, and just as the moon and sun move through the sky to whatever place they desire, so too is the practice of a monk going towards Nibbāna, whether in a family or a group...
246:
...unattached, unbound, and like the sky. That practice, being of such a nature, was prescribed, spoken, and taught by the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said: 'Nibbāna and the practice are in harmony.'

'Paṭipannānaṃ' refers to those established in the practice. 'Vusitavataṃ' refers to those who have completed the practice of the Noble Path. 'Laddhasahāyo' means a companion (sahāya) because of traveling together in various matters. The phrase 'Adutiyo asahāyo appaṭisamo' (peerless, without companion, incomparable) is spoken in the sense of being without equal. 'Apanujja' means that even while dwelling among those trainees (sekha) and Arahants in the attainment of fruition, he dwells mentally secluded, repeatedly devoted to solitary delight.

'Abhinipphanno kho pana tassa bhagavato lābho' means that great gain arose for the Blessed One. From when did it arise? It arose from the time he subdued King Bimbisāra, having attained supreme enlightenment, passed the seven weeks, turned the Wheel of Dhamma at Isipatana, gradually tamed devas and humans, ordained the three matted-hair ascetics (Jaṭilas), and gone to Rājagaha. Referring to the great gain and honor that arose from the time of subduing King Bimbisāra, it is said: 'At that time, the Blessed One was honored, revered, respected, worshipped, and esteemed, and he was a recipient of the four requisites: robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal offerings.' The gain, honor, and respect, arising from the overflowing merit accumulated over four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons, came overwhelming him like a great flood.

It is heard that at one time in the cities of Rājagaha, Sāvatthī, Sāketa, Kosambī, and Bārāṇasī, sequential alms-giving (paṭipāṭibhatta) for the Blessed One arose. Among those people, one person wrote a notice and hung it at the monastery gate, saying, 'I will give an offering by spending a hundred pieces of wealth.' Another wrote two hundred, another five hundred, a thousand, two thousand, five thousand, ten thousand, twenty thousand, fifty thousand, a hundred thousand, two hundred thousand, and so on, hanging their notices at the monastery gate to give offerings. Even when he was wandering through the countryside, the great multitude followed him, filling carts with goods to get the opportunity to give an offering. As the Blessed One said: 'At that time, the people of the countryside, having loaded many carts with salt, oil, rice, and food, followed closely behind the Blessed One. "In whatever place..."'
247:
People followed the Buddha with carts full of provisions, hoping for an opportunity to offer alms to the Exalted One as he traveled. The Buddha said, "Wherever we find a turn, there we shall perform the offering of alms-food." In this manner, many stories in other Khandhakas and the Vinaya should be understood.

In the Asadisa-dāna (Incomparable Alms-giving), however, the Buddha's gain and honor reached the pinnacle. Once, after the Buddha had wandered through the countryside and arrived at Jetavana, the King invited him and offered alms. On the second day, the citizens offered alms. Then the King offered an alms-giving superior to that of the citizens, and the citizens offered an alms-giving superior to that of the King. After many days had passed in this way, the King thought, "These citizens perform a more excellent alms-giving day by day. It would be a cause for reproach if I, the lord of the earth, were defeated by the citizens in giving."

Then Queen Mallikā suggested a plan to the King. The King had a pavilion built in the palace courtyard using Sālakalyāṇī wooden planks, covered it with blue lotuses, and prepared five hundred seats. He placed five hundred elephants behind the seats, and each elephant held a white umbrella over a monk. Between every two seats, a princess adorned with all ornaments ground the four kinds of scents. She placed the ground scents into a scent-casket in the middle. Another princess stirred the scents with a handful of blue lotuses. Thus, each monk was attended by three princesses. Another adorned woman held a palm-leaf fan and fanned them. Another held a dhammakaraṇa (water filter) and filtered water. Another brought water from the bowl.

There were four priceless items for the Buddha: a foot-rest, a bowl-stand, a backrest, and a gem attached to the base of the umbrella. Even the gift for the saṅghanavaka (the most junior monk) was worth a hundred thousand. In that alms-giving, Aṅgulimāla Thera was the saṅghanavaka. An elephant brought near his seat could not approach the Thera, and they reported this to the King. The King asked, "Is there no other elephant?" They replied, "There is a fierce elephant, but it is impossible to bring him." The Buddha asked, "Great King, who is the saṅghanavaka monk?" "It is Aṅgulimāla Thera, Bhante," he replied. "Great King, if that is so, adorn that fierce elephant and bring him," the Buddha said. When they adorned and brought the elephant, the elephant, due to the Thera's power, did not even dare to breathe through its nose and became still. Thus, alms were given continuously for seven days. On the seventh day, the King paid homage to the Buddha and said, "Bhante, please preach the Dhamma to me."
248:
In the assembly of King Pasenadi of Kosala, there were two ministers named Kāḷa and Juṇha. Kāḷa thought, "The wealth of the royal family is being destroyed. What will these many monks do? After eating, they will just go to the monastery and sleep. If a royal servant received this wealth, what task could he not accomplish? Alas, the King's property is being wasted." Juṇha, however, thought, "How great is this kingship! Who else could perform such an alms-giving? How can one be called a king if, even while established in kingship, he cannot give such a gift?"

The Buddha, observing the disposition of the assembly and knowing the thoughts of these two ministers, reflected: "If I preach the Dhamma today according to Juṇha’s wish, Kāḷa’s head will split into seven pieces. I have fulfilled the Perfections out of compassion for all beings. Juṇha will realize the Path and Fruit on another day when I preach, but now I will show consideration for Kāḷa." Thus, he spoke only this four-line verse to the King:

"The miserly do not go to the world of the devas,
Fools, indeed, do not praise giving;
But the wise man, rejoicing in giving,
Becomes happy hereafter because of that very joy."

The King became displeased and thought, "I have given a great alms-offering, yet the Teacher preached only a little Dhamma to me. I suppose I was unable to win the heart of the Ten-Powered One." After eating his morning meal, he went to the monastery, paid homage to the Buddha, and asked, "Bhante, I have given a great alms-offering, but the appreciation (anumodanā) given to me was not great. Bhante, what fault is there in me?" The Buddha replied, "Great King, there is no fault in you. However, because the assembly was not pure, I did not preach the Dhamma (in detail)." When asked why the assembly was not pure, the Teacher revealed the thoughts of the two ministers.

The King asked Kāḷa, "Dear Kāḷa, is it true that you thought thus?" "It is true, Great King," he replied. The King said, "While I am giving my own property, where does it hurt you? I do not wish to see you anymore. Banish him from my country!" Then he summoned Juṇha and asked, "Dear Juṇha, is it true that you thought thus?" "It is true, Great King," he replied. The King said, "May it be according to your heart's desire," and seated five hundred monks in that very pavilion on the prepared seats, surrounded by those same princesses. Taking wealth from the royal treasury, he commanded, "Perform an alms-giving equal to the one I gave for seven days."

After Juṇha had given the alms as the King commanded, on the seventh day, he requested, "Bhante, please preach the Dhamma to me." The Buddha, combining the appreciation for both alms-givings, delivered a great Dhamma discourse like two great rivers overflowing with currents of water. At the end of the discourse, Juṇha became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). The King, being greatly inspired, offered the Aṭṭhīsītibāhiravatthu (eighty-fold external gifts) to the Buddha. Thus, it should be known how gain and honor arose for the Buddha. In the word "siloko," it means the praise of virtues. That praise of virtues, starting from the time the Buddha preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta...
249:
"Give a gift similar to the one I have given for seven days," he said. The minister Juṇha gave the gift just as the King had said. Having given the gift, on the seventh day, he requested, "Venerable Sir, please preach the Dhamma to me."

The Blessed One, performing the appreciation (anumodanā) for both gifts together, preached a great Dhamma discourse, like two great rivers simultaneously overflowing with currents of water. At the end of the discourse, the minister Juṇha became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). The King, being filled with faith, offered the gift called Aṭṭhīsītibāhiravatthu to the Blessed One. Thus, it should be known that gain (lābha) arose for the Blessed One.

"Abhinipphanno siloko" refers to the praise of His virtues. That fame also arose for the Blessed One from the time He set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion. To speak at length, from the time He set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, kings also spoke of the Blessed One's virtues. Brahmins, householders, Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, Gandhabba deities, devas, and even Brahmās spoke of His virtues, beginning with "Itipi so Bhagavā..." and so on. Other heretics also gave a thousand coins to a man of the Vararoja clan and sent him, saying, "Speak ill of the recluse Gotama." He took the thousand coins and looked at the Ten-Powered One from the soles of His feet to the tips of His hair, but seeing not even a fault the size of a louse's egg, he thought: "The mouth of one who speaks ill of this faultless body—endowed with the various thirty-two marks of a Great Man, adorned with the eighty minor marks, surrounded by a fathom-wide aura, and possessing the splendor of the Nandana Grove beautiful with celestial flowers, like the sky bright with the stars and the Parijatta tree in full bloom—would twist, and his head would split into seven pieces. There is no way to speak ill; I shall only speak of His virtues." Thus, he spoke only of His virtues in over a thousand verses from the soles of His feet to the tips of His hair. At the time of the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya), however, this praise reached its summit. In this way, fame (siloko) arose.

"Yāva maññe khattiyā" means that Khattiyas, Brahmins, Vessas, Suddas, Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, Yakkhas, Asuras, Devas, and Brahmās all live with a nature of loving-kindness, being joyful and delighted. "Vigatamado kho pana" means that the Blessed One does not consume food with intoxication or heedlessness, thinking "This many people live loving me"; rather, the Blessed One consumes food being free from intoxication.
250:
"Yathāvādī" means that as the Blessed One speaks with His voice, so is His bodily action. As He acts with His body, so is His verbal action. The body does not exceed the speech, nor does the speech exceed the body; the speech conforms to the body, and the body conforms to the speech. For example:

'On the left side, he is like a pig; on the right side, like a goat.
By voice, he is like a calf; by horns, like an old ox.'

This Pig-Ogre (Sūkarayakkha), seeing pigs, shows his left side which resembles a pig and catches and eats them. Seeing goats, he shows his right side which resembles a goat and catches and eats them. Seeing calves, he makes a sound like a calf and catches and eats them. Seeing oxen, he creates horns like their horns, and when they approach from afar thinking "It looks like an ox," he catches and eats them.

Another example is in the Dhammikavāyasa Jātaka, where a crow questioned by birds said, 'I eat only the wind. Because I eat only wind, I stand on one leg, opening my mouth, fearing that insects might die. Therefore, you too—

'May you be well; practice the Dhamma. O kinsmen, practice the Dhamma.
One who practices the Dhamma sleeps happily in this world and the next.'

Thus, he inspired confidence and trust in the birds. Then, thinking 'This bird is truly good, a most righteous bird; standing on one leg, he speaks "Dhamma, Dhamma"', the birds who had come to trust him were eaten. Therefore, their speech did not conform to their bodies, and their bodies did not conform to their speech. It is not so with the Blessed One. The Blessed One's speech conforms to His body, and His body conforms to His speech; this is what is shown.

Because the Blessed One has crossed over doubt, He is 'Tiṇṇavicikiccho'. Because He is free from wavering thoughts such as "How is this? How is that?", He is 'Vigatakathaṃkatho'. Just as ordinary people wonder: "This is a tree; what is a tree? This is a village, this is a district, this is a country; what is a country? Why is this tree's trunk straight and this one's crooked? Why are some thorns straight and some crooked? Why do some flowers have a good scent and some a bad scent? The fruit..."
251:
Some people have doubts, wondering, "Why are some thorns curved? Why are some flowers fragrant? Why are some flowers foul-smelling? Why are some fruits sweet? Why are some fruits not sweet?" The Teacher is not like that. Indeed, the Teacher is one who has abandoned all doubtful vacillation, knowing, "Because of the abundance of such and such elements, this thing is thus." Just as those who have attained the first jhāna and so forth might have doubt regarding the second jhāna and so forth, and just as Paccekabuddhas have doubt in terms of conventional usage because they lack the definitive realization of omniscience, it is not so for the Buddha. He shows that the Blessed One has abandoned all doubtful vacillation in all things.

"Pariyositasankappo" means that some people reach the fulfillment of their intentions and the completion of their desires through mere virtue, some through mere insight, some through the first jhāna... some through the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, some through the mere state of a stream-enterer... some through the mere state of an arahant, some through the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, and some through the knowledge of private enlightenment. But my Teacher is not like that. He shows that my Teacher has reached the fulfillment of his intentions through omniscience (Sabbaññutañāṇa).

In the phrase "Ajjhāsayaṃ Ādibrahmacariyaṃ," the words are in the nominative case with the sense of the instrumental. It means that through the Noble Path (Ariyamagga)—which is the supreme aspiration, the excellent support, the original holy life, and the ancient holy life—he has crossed over doubt, is free from vacillation, and has reached the fulfillment of his intentions. Because of the statement, "In things unheard of before, he himself realized the truths; through that realization of the truths, he attained omniscience and mastery over the powers," it should be understood that the Blessed One's fulfillment of intentions was accomplished through the Noble Path alone.

"Yathariva Bhagavā" means that just like the Blessed One, they speak wishing, "Oh, if only four Victors (Jinas) would wander through the four directions on the surface of this Jambudīpa and teach the Dhamma!" Other deities, desiring them to wander together in the three circles, said, "Three Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas." Still others, thinking, "It is difficult for four or three Buddhas to arise after fulfilling the ten perfections. However, if one were to reside permanently and teach the Dhamma, and another were to wander and teach, then this Jambudīpa would be beautiful and many would attain welfare and happiness," said, "Friends, that would be good."

In the phrase "Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ," both "ṭhāna" and "avakāsa" are synonyms for "cause" (kāraṇa). Because the effect stands depending on that cause, it is called "ṭhāna." Because the effect cannot exist elsewhere without that cause, it is like a location and is called "avakāsa." The word "yaṃ" is in the nominative case with the sense of the instrumental. The meaning is that there is no cause for two Buddhas to arise simultaneously in a single world system.
252:
"There is no cause by which two Buddhas could arise together in a single world system."

Furthermore, in this context: "As far as the sun and moon revolve, shining and illuminating the quarters, so far does the world extend a thousandfold; therein your power is exercised." In this verse, a single world system (cakkavāḷa) is one world element (lokadhātu). In the passage "A thousandfold world element shook," a thousand world systems are one world element. In the passage "If he wished, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could make his voice heard throughout the three-thousandfold great-thousandfold world element, and pervade it with his radiance," the three-thousandfold great-thousandfold world element is one world element. In the passage "And this ten-thousandfold world element," ten thousand world systems are one world element. Referring to that ten-thousandfold world system, it is said "in a single world system."

This extent of world systems is called the birth-field (jātikhetta). Even within those ten thousand world systems, Buddhas do not arise anywhere except in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa) of Jambudīpa in this particular world system. Outside the birth-field, the place where Buddhas arise is not known at all. "Yenatthena" means by the sense of including the invitation (pavāraṇā).

## Commentary on the Story of Sanankumāra
"By appearance and by fame" means by the retinue of ornaments and by the glory of merit. In the phrase "Sādhu Mahābrahme," the word "sādhu" is an exclamation of appreciation. "Sankhāya modāma" means we rejoice having known.

## Commentary on the Story of Govinda the Brahmin
One cannot limit it by saying, "That Blessed One was a person of great wisdom only for this much time." Rather, that Blessed One was a person of great wisdom for a very long time. He asks, "What do you think?" Then, wishing to answer the question himself, he says, "Friends, it is not wonderful that now, having fulfilled the perfections and broken the peak of the three Māras, the Blessed One is of great wisdom with the unique knowledge (asādhāraṇañāṇa) of realization. Where is the wonder in this? Rather, friends, I will tell you of the state of being of great wisdom even in the time when he was possessed of passion, etc., abiding in partial knowledge (padesañāṇa) before his omniscience had matured." Thus, wishing to bring forth the matter hidden by past lives, he spoke the words beginning with "Bhūtapubbaṃ ahosi."

"Purohita" refers to the chaplain who advises on all matters. "Govinda" refers to one who has been consecrated with the consecration of being placed in the position of Govinda. Specifically, his original name was different. From the time of his consecration, he came to be called Govinda.
253:
That Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections, having crushed the heads of the three Māras at the foot of the Bodhi tree, and having penetrated the unique knowledge (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), became one of great wisdom; what is there to wonder at in this? O deities, indeed, I shall tell you of the state of great wisdom even during the time when he was still possessed of lust, etc., while established in partial knowledge (padesa-ñāṇa) before his omniscience had matured. Thus, wishing to show the reason hidden by previous existences, he spoke the words beginning with 'Bhūtapubbaṃ' (Once upon a time).

A purohita is a chaplain who advises on all matters. Govinda is one consecrated with the consecration of the Govinda office. Although his original name was different by nature, from the time of his consecration, he came to be known as 'Govinda'. Jotipāla is so named because he is radiant (jotana) and because he protects from harm (pālana). It is said that on the day of Jotipāla's birth, all weapons in the city glowed. The King, seeing his own auspicious weapon glowing at dawn, stood in fear. The Brahmin Govinda went to the King's presence early in the morning and asked if he had slept well. The King said, 'Teacher, how could I have slept well?' and told him the reason. 'Do not fear, Great King; a son has been born to me. By his power, the weapons throughout the whole city are glowing,' he replied. The King thought, 'Will this boy be my enemy?' and became even more afraid. When asked, 'What are you thinking, Great King?', he told him the reason. Then Govinda reassured him, 'Do not fear, Great King; this boy will not wrong you. Indeed, in the whole of Jambudīpa, there will be no one equal to him in wisdom. By my son's words, the doubts of the people will be cut away, and he will advise you in all matters.' The King was pleased and said, 'Let this be the milk-money for the boy,' giving a thousand pieces of wealth, and added, 'Show the boy to me when he is grown.' When the boy gradually reached maturity, they named him 'Jotipāla' because of his radiance and his ability to protect from harm. Therefore, it is said, 'He is called Jotipāla because of his radiance and protection.'

'Sammā vossajjitvā' means having relinquished well. This is the very reading. 'Alamatthadasataro': one who is capable and discerning of various matters is 'alamatthadasa'; because he excels those who can discern such matters, he is 'alamatthadasatara'. 'Jotipālassa eva māṇavassa anusāsaniyā' shows that even the father, the Brahmin Govinda, would consult the youth Jotipāla before giving advice.
254:
'Bhava-m-atthu bhavantaṃ Jotipālaṃ' means may there be prosperity, the attainment of special distinction, and all auspicious blessings for the venerable Jotipāla. 'Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ' (words of rejoicing) means concluding the polite conversation that dispels grief related to death by such means as, 'Great King, do not worry; this death is a constant law for all beings.' 'May the venerable Jotipāla not reject us by [refusing] to advise' means when asked to 'advise,' do not refuse by saying 'I cannot advise.' 'Abhisambhosi' means he arranged and accomplished it. People said this: seeing that the youth Jotipāla was even wiser than his father, advising on all matters and accomplishing all tasks, they were pleased at heart and said, 'Friends, this Brahmin's father was Govinda, but this one is indeed Mahāgovinda.'

## Explanation of the Division of the Kingdom
'To where those six khattiyas were' refers to those six khattiyas called 'friends,' who were said to be the younger brothers of King Reṇu, born of the same father. Therefore, Mahāgovinda, thinking, 'This King Reṇu, having been consecrated, may or may not divide the kingdom among these princes; it would be well if I were to send them to Reṇu beforehand to obtain a promise,' approached those six khattiyas. 'Rājakattāro' refers to the ministers who appoint kings.

'Intoxicating sensual pleasures' refers to the strands of sensual pleasure that cause intoxication and negligence. As time passes, this King Reṇu might not even be able to remember [his promise]; therefore, it means, 'Come, sirs, please come.'

'Sirs, I remember' refers to the fact that at that time, it was an era when people spoke the truth. Therefore, instead of saying something false like 'When did I say that? Who saw it? Who heard it?', he said, 'Sirs, I remember.' 'Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ' refers to the polite conversation of this nature: 'Great King, why do you grieve for your father who has gone to the world of devas? This death is the constant nature of all beings; conditioned things are such.' 'Sabbāni sakaṭamukhāni paṭṭhapesi' means he established all six kingdoms to be like the front of a cart. Each king's territory was three hundred yojanas. At the entrance to King Reṇu's territory, it was ten gāvutas wide. In the middle, however, King Reṇu's territory was like a canopy.
255:
(The Brahmin Mahāgovinda) arranged and established the six kingdoms in a shape resembling the front of a cart. The kingdom of each king measured three hundred yojanas; the area of access to King Reṇu's kingdom was ten gāvutas, and in the center, King Reṇu's kingdom was like a canopy. Why did he arrange it thus? It was so that the kings, when coming to see each other from time to time, could come and go through their own territories without harassing the kingdoms of others. Indeed, when a king enters another's kingdom and says, "Give me rice, give me oxen," the people complain, saying, "These kings do not travel through their own domains but are harassing us." However, when a king travels through his own domain, the people do not consider it harassment, thinking, "This king ought to receive such and such from us." Having considered this benefit, the Brahmin Mahāgovinda arranged it in this way, thinking, "May the kings, being in harmony and rejoicing, rule their kingdoms for a long time."

"Dantapura of the Kaliṅgas, Potana of the Assakas,
Māhissati of the Avantis, and Roruka of the Sovīras.
Mithilā of the Videhas, Campā built among the Aṅgas,
And Bārāṇasī of the Kāsīs—these were built by Govinda."

These seven cities were built by the Brahmin Mahāgovinda himself for the benefit of those kings.

"Sattabhū, Brahmadatta, Vessabhū together with Bharata,
Reṇu, and the two Dhataraṭṭhas—these were the seven burden-bearers at that time."

These are the names of those seven kings. Among them, one was named Sattabhū, one was named Brahmadatta, one was named Vessabhū, one together with that Vessabhū was named Bharata, one was named Reṇu, and two were named Dhataraṭṭha. Thus, these seven were the great kings who bore the burden of the realm on the surface of Jambudīpa.

## The Explanation of the First Recital Section is finished.
256:
## Commentary on the Spreading of the Sound of Fame

Regarding the word 'upasaṅkamiṃsu' (they approached): They approached thinking, "This prosperity of our sovereignty has not arisen through the power of anyone else, but was accomplished through the power of Mahāgovinda. Mahāgovinda has united us seven kings and established us upon the surface of Jambudīpa; it is not easy to repay the gratitude of one who has been a benefactor from the start. Let this Mahāgovinda himself advise us seven people; let us appoint him to the positions of both General (senāpati) and Chaplain (purohita). By doing so, we shall attain prosperity."

Mahāgovinda also thought, "I have united these kings. If these kings were to have other generals and chaplains, they would listen to the words of their own generals and chaplains and become divided among themselves. Therefore, I shall accept the positions of general and chaplain for them." Having thought thus, he consented, saying, "Very well, your majesties."

Regarding 'satta ca brāhmaṇamahāsāle' (and seven great wealthy Brahmins): He thought, "I may or may not be present in all places. In places where I am not present, these men shall perform the necessary duties." Thus, he appointed seven assistant chaplains (anupurohita). It is in reference to them that it is said, "satta ca brāhmaṇamahāsāle."

They are called 'nahātaka' (cleansed) because they bathe twice a day, in the evening and in the morning. Alternatively, they are called 'nahātaka' because, having bathed at the conclusion of their religious vows, they do not eat or drink with other Brahmins from that time onwards.

'Abbhuggacchi' means it spread upwards particularly. At that time, it is said that people in every place where they sat would say, "It is not possible to advise the whole of Jambudīpa in this way without consulting with Brahmā." 

Regarding 'na kho panāhaṃ' (but I do not): It is said that the Great Being (the Bodhisatta) thought, "This false reputation has arisen for me. The arising of a reputation is not difficult, but maintaining a reputation that has arisen is indeed difficult. This reputation has arisen while I was acting without thinking or consulting (with Brahmā); if I act after thinking and consulting, it will spread even more widely." While seeking a means to see Brahmā, he saw that (the Karuṇā-brahmavihāra) and reflected on the meaning beginning with "sutaṃ kho pana metaṃ" (I have heard this).
257:
For the reason he approached King Reṇu, he did so after informing the King in this way: "When I am staying in solitude, I do not wish for anyone to see me or speak to me during these four months of the rainy season." He approached him for the purpose of cutting off distractions, thinking, "Being free from distractions, I shall dwell in comfort." This same method should be understood in all instances of addressing.

"Sādisiyo" means those of similar appearance and similar caste.

"Navaṃ sandhāgāraṃ kāretvā" means having caused to be built a splendid rest-house (pavilion) surrounded by reeds on the outside, suitable for dwelling throughout the four months of the rainy season, and complete with places for the night, places for the day, and a cloister-walk. "Karuṇaṃ jhānaṃ jhāyī" means he developed and practiced the third and fourth jhānas having compassion as the object. In this context, by taking compassion as the starting point, the remaining three Brahma-vihāras are also included. "Ukkaṇṭhanā paritassanā" means that for one established in the ground of jhāna, there is no dissatisfaction (weariness) caused by lack of delight, nor is there trembling (anxiety) caused by fear; rather, it means there was a longing for the Brahma's arrival and a desire for his coming.

## Description of the Conversation with Brahma

"Bhayaṃ" means only the fear arising from mental agitation. "Ajānantā" means not knowing. "How shall we know you?" means "How are we to know you—where does this person live, what is his name, what is his clan?"—in what manner should we recognize you?

"They know me as Kumāra (the Youth) or as a boy." (One who) dwells in the sublime world, very ancient, and of old. He shows, "I am that ancient youth, the Brahma named Sanaṅkumāra." "O Govinda the wise, know thus; recognize me in this way."

"A seat, water, foot-oil, and sweet vegetables (we offer) to the Brahma;
We ask the noble guest about the hospitality-offering,
May the venerable one accept our hospitality-offering."

In this context, "agghaṃ" refers to that which should be offered to a guest. For that very reason, this place has been prepared; please sit here. This water is pure; please drink this drinking water and wash your feet. This foot-oil is oil prepared for the benefit of the feet; please anoint your feet with this oil. This is sweet vegetable (or nourishment).

In the practice of a Bodhisatta, the holy life is not like the holy life of others; that Bodhisatta does not practice hoarding by thinking, "This thing will be for tomorrow, this thing will be for the third day."
258:
