He performs what is called hoarding (sannidhi). "Madhusāka" refers to cooked vegetables that are boiled in water without adding honey, salt, or spices. Referring to those cooked vegetables, he said, "Please enjoy these vegetables," with the intention of saying, "We ask the Brahma about the hospitality-offerings," and so on. All these hospitality-offerings do not exist among Brahmas. We ask the Brahma about those hospitality-offerings. The meaning is: "May the venerable Brahma perform the hospitality for us who ask in this way; may the venerable Brahma accept this hospitality-offering of ours."

If it is asked, "Does this Mahāgovinda the Brahmin not know that the Brahma will not consume even one of these?" The answer is: It is not that he does not know; he knows. Even though he knows, he asks based on the importance of the duty (vatta) that a great guest who has arrived in one's presence should be invited.

Then the Brahma, reflecting, "Does this wise man ask knowing that I do not consume (these), or does he ask out of pride?" realized, "He asks based on the importance of duty." Thinking, "Now it is proper for me to accept," he said, "Govinda, we accept your hospitality-offering as you have said." "O Govinda the wise, whatever you say, such as 'This seat is prepared, please sit here,' according to those words, we are as if seated on your seat, as if we have drunk the water, let my feet be as if washed, let them be as if anointed with oil, and let the water-boiled vegetables be as if consumed. From the time I have consented to the things given by you, whatever you say is already accepted by me." Therefore, he said, "Govinda, we accept your hospitality-offering as you have said." After thus accepting the hospitality-offering, wishing to give the opportunity to ask questions, he said, "For the sake of benefit in the present life," and so on.

"Kankhī akankhiṃ paravediyesu" means: "Being one who has doubts, I ask the venerable Brahma who is free from doubt regarding the problems that have been prepared by others and made known to others."

"Hitvā mamattaṃ" means having abandoned the craving for requisites such as "This property is mine, this is mine." "Manujesu" means among beings; the meaning is that any human being among creatures abandons the attachment of "mine." "Ekodibhūto" means being alone, standing alone, and sitting alone. According to the word-definition (vacanattha), because one arises or proceeds alone, one is called "ekodi"; being of such a nature, one is called "ekodibhūto." "Karuṇedhimutto" means one who is intent on the jhāna of compassion, meaning one who has produced that jhāna. "Nirāmagandho" means one who is free from the foul smell of defilements. "Ettha ṭhito" means one who is established in these qualities.
259:
"Sikkhamāno" refers to one who practices those qualities of the Brahmavihāras. This is just a brief explanation here. The detailed explanation was already given above by the Brahmin Mahāgovinda and the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra.

In that detailed explanation, "ete avidvā" means "I do not know, I do not know those foul smells (āmagandha)." "Idha brūhi dhīrā" means "O wise one, tell me those foul smells here in this human world." "Kenāvaṭā vā pajā kurutū" means "By what kind of obstruction of defilements is a being obstructed so that they rot and emit a foul odor?" "Āpāyikā" means going to the states of misery (apāya). "Nivutabrahmalokā" means that for such a being, the Brahma world is obstructed and closed. It is a question asking by which defilement the path leading to the Brahma world is obstructed, covered, and hidden for beings.

Anger (kodha) characterized by being incensed; falsehood (musāvāda) characterized by deceiving others; fraud (nikati) characterized by showing something similar to deceive; betrayal (dubbha) characterized by betraying friends; extreme stinginess (kadariyatā) characterized by rigid miserliness; overbearing pride (atimāno) characterized by thinking too highly of oneself; envy (usūyā) characterized by disparaging others' success; desire (icchā) characterized by longing; selfishness (vivicchā) characterized by various forms of stinginess; oppressing others (paraheṭhanā) characterized by harming others; greed (lobha) characterized by attachment to any object; hatred (dosa) characterized by malice; intoxication (mada) characterized by pride; and delusion (moha) characterized by bewilderment. A being associated with these fourteen defilements is not free from foul smells; rather, they are like a rotting corpse emitting a putrid odor. Such a being is one who goes to the states of misery and whose path to the Brahma world is covered. When teaching this Mahāgovinda Sutta, it should be explained by comparing it with the Āmagandha Sutta. The Āmagandha Sutta should also be explained by comparing it with this Mahāgovinda Sutta.

"Te na sunimmadayā" means those foul smells cannot be easily suppressed or easily abandoned. It means they are difficult to give up and difficult to conquer. "Yassa dāni bhavaṃ govindo kālaṃ maññati" means "Whatever time the venerable Govinda considers right for renunciation, let that renunciation take place." If you renounce in this way, my coming to you will be a good coming, and the Dhamma talk given will be well-spoken. "O wise one, you are the most excellent man in the whole of Jambudīpa, and you are in your youth, the first stage of life. Your renunciation, abandoning such great wealth and splendor, is exceedingly noble, like a scent-elephant (gandhahatthī) breaking its iron chains and departing. This renunciation is indeed the tradition of the Bodhisattas." Saying this and encouraging the Great Being in his renunciation, Sanaṅkumāra Brahmā returned to the Brahma world. The Great Being also thought, "It is not proper for me to renounce directly after leaving this house of meditation. I am the one who advises the royal family on their welfare, so I will first inform the King. If the King also wishes to renounce, that would be excellent. If he does not, I will hand over the office of chaplain and then renounce." Then, the meaning is conveyed by the words, "Atha kho bho mahāgovindo... porohacce cherameti." In those words, "tvaṃ pajāna hi rājā" means "By your kingship, you yourself..."
260:
"Being the most excellent man in the whole of Jambudīpa and being in your youth, the first stage of life, your renunciation, abandoning such great wealth and splendor, is exceedingly noble, like a scent-elephant breaking its iron shackles and departing. This is indeed the tradition of the Bodhisattas." Having thus strengthened the Great Being's resolve for renunciation, Sanaṅkumāra Brahmā returned to the Brahma world.

## Description of Addressing King Reṇu

The Great Being also thought, "It is not proper for me to renounce directly after leaving this (house of meditation). I am the one who advises the royal family on their welfare, so I will first inform the King. If the King also follows and renounces, that would be excellent. If he does not, I will hand over the office of chaplain and then renounce." Thinking thus, he approached the King. This matter is stated with the words, "Atha kho bho mahāgovindo... nāhaṃ porohacce rame," and so on.

In that Pali, "tvaṃ pajānassu rajjena" means "You yourself should know (manage) your kingship." "Nāhaṃ porohicce rame" means "I no longer delight in being a chaplain; I am weary of it. Look for another teacher who can advise you. I no longer delight in the position of chaplain."

Then the King thought, "The wealth in the house of the Brahmin who has been in seclusion for four months has surely decreased." Wishing to invite him with wealth, he said, "If you have any lack of sensual pleasures, I will fulfill them for you." Then again, he thought, "Could this person have been harmed by someone while living alone?" and said—

"Whoever harms you, I shall prevent him; I am the commander-in-chief of the land. You are like a father to me, and I am like a son. O Govinda, do not forsake us."

The meaning of that verse is: Whoever harms you, I will stop him. You just point out, "It is this person," and I will know what needs to be done in this matter. "Bhūmisenāpati ahaṃ" means, in another way, "I am the lord of the earth; as such, I will hand over this kingship to you alone." "Tuvaṃ pitā ahaṃ putto" means "You will stand in the position of a father, and I will stand in the position of a son." Therefore, you, Govinda, should set aside my wishes and act according to your own will; let it be as you desire. As for me, I will follow your will, and while consuming the alms-food given by you, I will serve you, perhaps holding a sword and shield, or I will drive the chariot for you. Or there is the reading "mā no govinda, pajahī."
261:
The Pali text. The meaning of that Pali is: "You stand in the position of a father; I shall stand in the position of a son. O Lord Govinda, do not forsake us, do not abandon us." Then, the Great Being (Mahāpurisa), wishing to show that the thought the King had conceived did not exist in him, said:

"I lack nothing in terms of sensual pleasures,
There is nothing that oppresses me;
Having heard the word of a non-human (Brahma),
Therefore, I no longer delight in the home."

In that Pali, "na matthi" means it does not exist for me. "Gahe" means in the house. Then the King asked that Brahmin Govinda thus:

"What is the appearance of the non-human (Brahma)?
What benefit did he speak to you?
Hearing which word do you wish to utterly abandon us,
The home, and all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa?"

In that verse, "jahāsi no gahe amhe ca kevalī" means that the King, who looked after the Brahmin's houses filled with wealth as if they were his own, says: "Hearing what word do you abandon our home, us, and all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa without exception?"

Then, the Great Being, wishing to tell King Reṇu, spoke the words beginning with "upavutthassa me pubbe." In that Pali, "upavutthassa" refers to one who has dwelt in solitude for four months. "Yiṭṭhakāmassa me sato" means for me who desires to perform a sacrifice. "Aggi pajjalito āsi, kusapattaparitthato" means that the fire was prepared to be kindled, surrounded by kusa grass, and having added ghee, curd, honey, and so on; it means for me who stood thinking, "I shall give gifts to the multitude," after kindling the fire in this way.

"Sananatana" refers to Sanaṅkumāra Brahma. Thereafter, the King, having a desire to renounce the world himself, spoke the words beginning with "saddahāmi." In that Pali, "kathaṃ vattetha aññathā" means how will you practice in another way? "Te taṃ anuvattissāma" means we also shall follow and practice only as you do; it means we shall follow and renounce. There is also a variant reading "anuvajissāma," which means we shall follow along. "Akāco" means without flaw, not coarse. "Govindassānusāsane" means we shall practice by placing only Lord Govinda as our teacher under the instruction of Lord Govinda.
262:
## Explanation of the Invitation to the Six Nobles

"Approached where those six nobles were" means he approached King Reṇu, encouraging him and instilling even firmer effort by saying, "Noble King, it is excellent. While there are beings who seize kingship even by killing parents, brothers, sisters, and so on, a great king who wishes to renounce such great royal glory performs a noble deed." "Thus they planned in unison" means they planned together, thinking that according to the King's way of thinking, the Brahmin's wealth and possessions might at some time diminish. "We shall entice and win him over with wealth" means to entice or to treat with hospitality. "Let that much wealth be brought" means let it be brought or taken; it is said to mean, "Take as much as you desire." "Only by the power of the young lords" means that it is because of the young lords, and only because it was given by you, that such abundant property has arisen.

"If we shall renounce sensual pleasures" means if we shall abandon both the objects of sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and the defilements of sensuality (kilesa-kāma). Sensual pleasures in which worldlings are attached; worldlings are stuck and clinging to those sensual pleasures. If this is so, "Exert your energy, be firm by undertaking unremitting effort. Be endowed with the power of patience"—thus he inspires effort in the kings.

"This path is the straight path" means this path of the Karuṇā-jhāna (compassion absorption) is called the straight path. "This path is the unsurpassed path" means this alone is the unsurpassed, noble path leading to rebirth in the Brahma world. "The True Dhamma protected by the virtuous" means this is the Dhamma protected by the virtuous ones, namely the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples. Thus, by praising the virtues of the Karuṇā-jhāna, he makes them firm so that those kings do not retreat.

"O friends, who indeed can know life?" means, O friends, that which is called life (jīvita) is like a water bubble, like a dewdrop on the tip of a blade of grass, having the nature of perishing in an instant; who can know the destination of that life, or at what moment it will break? "The hereafter must be gone to" means one must certainly go to the next world; regarding that matter of going, a wise man of good family should contemplate and know with wisdom. "Mantā" refers to wisdom (paññā); it means one should contemplate, understand, investigate, and know with that wisdom. Alternatively, the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. "Mantāyaṃ boddhabbaṃ" means it should be understood by wisdom, it should be known by knowledge. What should be understood? The fact that life is difficult to know, and...
263:
One should know the certainty of going to the afterlife. Having known this, one should cut off all obstacles (that hinder merit), perform meritorious deeds, and lead the holy life (brahmacariya). Why? Because for a being who is born, there is no such thing as not dying. Therefore, one should perform merit and lead the holy life.

## Instructions to the Great Brahmin Householders and Others
Sir, what is called monkhood has few followers and few gains. Truly, from the time of becoming a monk, people speak of even a king who has renounced his kingdom and become a monk by harassing him and making him a lowly, helpless person. Gains are also very few; even after wandering through an entire village, it is difficult to obtain even enough food to swallow. This state of being a Brahmin, however, has great majesty because of many followers, and great gains because of being endowed with offerings and honor. You, sir, are currently the supreme chaplain (purohita) in the entire Jambudīpa; in all places, you receive the best seat, the best water, the best food, the best scent, and the best flowers.

"Like a king among kings" means, "Sirs, I am now like a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) among ordinary kings." "Like a Brahmā among Brahmās" means being like a Great Brahmā among ordinary Brahmās. "Like a deity among householders" means being like Sakka, the king of devas, among the remaining householders.

## Description of the Instructions to the Wives
"Forty wives are similar" means there are forty wives of similar appearance and similar caste. Besides them, that Brahmin also has many dancing women who stay through the three stages of life.

## Description of Mahāgovinda's Renunciation
"Wanders on a journey" means wandering through villages and market towns in succession; wherever he goes, there is an uproar like the arrival of a Buddha. When people hear that "the wise Mahāgovinda is coming," they have pavilions built in advance, decorate the roads, go out to meet him, and bring him in. Great gain and honor arise, overwhelming like a great flood. "To the chaplain of seven kings" means because he was the chaplain to seven kings. Thus, just as people now say "Namo Buddhassa" (Homage to the Buddha) when some suffering or distress arises, at that time they said, "Homage to the Brahmin Mahāgovinda, homage to the chaplain of seven kings."
264: By the method starting with ‘mettasahagatena’ (accompanied by loving-kindness), only the Divine Abodes (Brahma-vihāras) appear in the Pali text. In fact, the Bodhisatta, being a Great Man (Mahāpurisa), attained all eight meditative attainments and five higher powers. ‘He taught the path for the disciples to attain companionship with the Brahma world’ means he taught the Jhanic path which is the cause for being reborn with Brahmas in the Brahma world.‘Entirely’ (sabbena sabbaṃ) refers to those who attained the eight attainments and five higher powers. ‘Those who did not entirely understand the teaching’ refers to those who did not know even one of the eight attainments, nor were they able to attain them. ‘Amoghā’ (not in vain) means they are not empty because they have results (vipāka). ‘Avanjhā’ means they are not barren. ‘They produce the lowest of all’ means they produce the bodies of Gandhabba deities, who are lower than all other deities. ‘Saphala’ (fruitful) means they are beneficial by leading to rebirth in the remaining celestial worlds. ‘Sa-udrayā’ (with increase) means they have the benefit of growth by leading to rebirth in the Brahma world.‘I remember’ (sarāmahaṃ) means ‘Pañcasikha... I remember.’ By this word ‘sarāmahaṃ’, this Mahāgovinda Sutta should be regarded as ‘Buddhabhāsita’ (spoken by the Buddha). ‘Not for disenchantment’ (na nibbidāya) means it does not lead to disenchantment with the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa). ‘Not for dispassion’ (na virāgāya) means it does not lead to the fading of lust for the round. ‘Not for cessation’ (na nirodhāya) means it does not lead to the cessation of the round. ‘Not for tranquility’ (na upasamāya) means it does not lead to the calming of the round. ‘Not for higher knowledge’ (na abhiññāya) means it does not lead to knowing the round with higher knowledge. ‘Not for enlightenment’ (na sambodhāya) means it does not lead to awakening from the round by being free from the sleep of defilements. ‘Not for Nibbāna’ (na nibbānāya) means it does not lead to the deathless Nibbāna.‘For absolute disenchantment’ (ekantanibbidāya) means it leads specifically to disenchantment with the round of rebirths. Here, by the word ‘nibbidāya’, insight (vipassanā) is meant. By the word ‘virāgāya’, the Path (magga) is meant. By the words ‘nirodhāya’ and ‘upasamāya’, Nibbāna is meant. By the words ‘abhiññāya’ and ‘sambodhāya’, the Path is meant. By the word ‘nibbānāya’, Nibbāna itself is meant. Thus, the explanation of the definitions (vavatthāna-kathā) should be understood as: insight in one place, the Path in three places, and Nibbāna in three places. In a figurative sense (pariyāyena), all these terms are synonyms for the Path and also synonyms for Nibbāna. Regarding what should be said about Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) and so on, take note as already stated in the Explanation of the Truths (Sacca-vaṇṇanā) in the Visuddhimagga.‘Those who did not entirely’ means those who do not know how to fulfill all four Noble Paths, but attain only three, two, or one. ‘Of all these sons of good family’ means of the sons of good family who practiced the holy life of the Path. ‘Not in vain... fruitful, with increase’—thus He concluded the teaching by placing the Fruit of Arahantship at the summit.
265:
“Having paid homage to the Blessed One and performed circumambulation” means accepting the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One with the mind, delighting in it, praising it with words, and rejoicing. Placing the great joined palms (añjali) on the head, and entering into the midst of the six-colored rays of the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala) as if diving into clear lac-dye, he paid homage in the four directions. Having performed the clockwise circumambulation three times, repeatedly praising the Blessed One, he disappeared from before the Teacher and went to his own deva world.

## The Commentary on the Mahāgovinda Sutta is finished.
266:
## 7. Commentary on the Mahāsamaya Sutta
## Commentary on the Introduction
'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so forth is the Mahāsamaya Sutta. In this sutta, this is the explanation of the terms not yet explained. 'Sakkesu' means in the Sakyan country. According to the origin story told in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, based on the exclamation of the father, King Okkāka, 'Sakyā vata bho kumārā' (Indeed, the princes are capable), a certain region which is the residence of the princes who obtained the name 'Sakka' is called 'Sakka' by way of conventional usage (ruḷhī). It means in that Sakyan country. 'Mahāvane' means in the great forest which grew naturally, was not planted by anyone, and is continuous with the Himālaya mountains. 'Sabbheheva arahantehi' means together with all the Arahants who attained Arahantship on the very day this Mahāsamaya Sutta was preached.

In this sutta, this is the sequential account: It is said that the Sakyans and Koliyans built a single dam across the river named Rohiṇī between the cities of Kapilavatthu and Koliya and cultivated crops. Then, in the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, when the crops began to wither, the laborers from both cities gathered. Then the laborers of Koliya city said: 'If this water is divided and taken by both sides, it will not be enough for you, nor for us. However, our crops can reach maturity with just one watering. Give this water to us.' The laborers of Kapilavatthu city said: 'After you have filled your granaries, we would not be able to wander at your doorsteps with baskets and sacks in hand, carrying red gold, rubies, and dark coins (kahāpaṇa). Our crops can also reach maturity with just one watering. Give this water to us.'

'We will not give it,' 'We also will not give it.' Thus, as the quarrel escalated, one man stood up and struck another. That person also struck another, and thus by striking one another, they insulted the royal lineages and increased the quarrelsome anger. The Koliyan laborers said: 'You Kapilavatthu residents boast, relying on those who, like dogs and foxes, cohabited with their own sisters. What can their elephants, horses, and armed forces do to us?' The Sakyan laborers also said: 'You now boast, relying on the children of lepers who, being helpless and destitute, lived in Kollo trees like animals. Their elephants, horses, and armed forces...'
267:
"...what can they do to us?" Those laborers went and reported to the ministers in charge of the work. The ministers, in turn, reported to the royal families. Thereupon, the Sakyans, thinking, "We shall show our strength and power to those who live with their sisters," set out prepared for war. The Koliyans also, thinking, "We shall show our strength and power to those who live in Kola trees," set out prepared for war.

The Blessed One, having arisen from the attainment of Great Compassion at dawn and surveying the world, saw these two sides of kings setting out prepared for war. Having seen them, he reflected, "If I go, will this quarrel be settled or not?" Upon reflection, he decided, "I will go there and teach three Jātakas—the Phandana Jātaka, the Dubbiyamakkaṭa Jātaka, and the Laṭukika Jātaka—to settle the quarrel. Then, to demonstrate unity, I will teach two Jātakas—the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka and the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka—and then the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. Upon hearing the teaching, the kings of both cities will each offer two hundred and fifty princes. I will ordain those princes, and then a great assembly will take place." Therefore, while those kings were setting out for war, without informing anyone, he took his bowl and robes and went alone. He sat cross-legged in the air between the two armies, emitting rays of six colors.

As soon as the kings of Kapilavatthu saw the Blessed One, they thought, "The Blessed One, our supreme kinsman and teacher, has arrived. Has he seen the cause of our quarrel?" Then they thought, "It is not proper for us to strike the bodies of others with weapons while the Blessed One has arrived. Let the Koliyan kings kill us or oppress us if they wish." Thus, they discarded their weapons and sat down, paying homage to the Blessed One. The Koliyan kings also thought in the same way, discarded their weapons, and sat down, paying homage to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One, though he already knew, asked, "Great Kings, why have you come?" They replied, "Venerable Sir, we have not come to play at the water-crossing, nor to play in the river, nor to play on the mountain, nor to view the hills. Indeed, we have come to this place having prepared for battle." "Great Kings, on account of what are you quarreling?" "Venerable Sir, on account of water." "Great Kings, how much is water worth?" "Venerable Sir, water is of little value." "Great Kings, how much is the earth worth?" "Venerable Sir, the earth is invaluable." "Great Kings, how much are Khattiyas worth?" "Venerable Sir, Khattiyas are invaluable." "Great Kings, why do you destroy invaluable Khattiyas on account of water which is of so little value?" Having said this, he remarked, "There is no such thing as delightful happiness in quarreling. Great Kings, because of quarreling, a tree deity once bore a grudge in an improper situation against a black lion..."
268:
Saying, “It has reached even unto this whole aeon,” the Blessed One told the Phandana Jātaka. After that, saying, “Great King, one should not believe and follow the words of others. Indeed, by believing the words of others, because of the words of a single small rabbit, all the four-footed animals in the Himavanta forest, which is three thousand leagues in extent, once leaped into the great ocean. Therefore, one should not believe and follow the words of others,” he told the Pathavīundriya Jātaka. After that, saying, “Great King, sometimes even the weak see the flaw and opportunity of the strong, and sometimes the strong see the flaw of the weak. Indeed, even a female quail once killed a noble elephant,” he told the Laṭukika Jātaka. Having thus told these three Jātakas for the purpose of quelling the quarrel, he told two more Jātakas for the purpose of illustrating unity. How? Saying, “Great King, no enemy can see an opening against those who are united,” he told the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka. After that, saying, “Great King, no enemy could see an opening against those who were united. But when they quarreled with one another, the fowler’s son deprived them of life and carried them away. There is no pleasure in quarreling,” he told the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka. Having thus told these five Jātakas, he told the Attadaṇḍa Sutta at the conclusion.

The kings, being filled with devotion, said, “If the Teacher had not come, we would have slaughtered one another with our own hands and caused a river of blood to flow. We would not see our sons and brothers at the doors of our houses, and there would be no one to carry news back and forth for us. It is only because of the Teacher that we have received our lives. If the Teacher had remained in the household life, the sovereignty of the four great islands with their two thousand surrounding small islands would have been in his hands. He would have had more than a thousand sons, and he would have traveled only with a royal retinue. However, he renounced such prosperity, went forth, and attained Omniscience. Let him now also travel with a royal retinue.” Thus, the kings living in both cities offered two hundred and fifty princes each. The Blessed One ordained those princes and went to the Mahāvana forest. Because they had been ordained out of respect for the Buddha and not of their own will, dissatisfaction (anabhirati) arose in them. Their former wives also sent messages, saying, “Noble sons, be weary (of the monkhood); the household life is not stable,” and so forth. Those monks became even more dissatisfied.

Reflecting on this, the Blessed One knew their state of dissatisfaction and thought, “These monks are dissatisfied even while living together with a Buddha like me. Now, I shall tell them of the virtues of Lake Kuṇāla, and by taking them there, I will dispel their dissatisfaction.” He then spoke of the virtues of Lake Kuṇāla. The monks then felt a desire to see that lake. When the Blessed One asked, “Monks, do you wish to see Lake Kuṇāla?” they replied, “Venerable Sir, we wish to see it.” He said, “Monks, if that is so, come, let us go.”
269:
Thinking, "I will dispel their dissatisfaction," the Blessed One spoke of the beauty of Lake Kuṇāla. Those monks wished to see that lake. "Monks, do you wish to see Lake Kuṇāla?" he asked. "Yes, Blessed One, we wish to see it," they replied. "If so, come, let us go," he said. "Blessed One, how shall we go to the place where those with psychic powers go?" they asked. "Simply have the desire to go; I will take you by my own power," he said. "Very well, Blessed One," they replied. Then the Blessed One, taking the five hundred monks, flew into the sky and, landing at Lake Kuṇāla, said to those monks, "Monks, whatever fish in this Lake Kuṇāla you do not know by name, ask their names."

Those monks asked, and the Blessed One answered everything they asked. He had them ask and then explained not only the names of the fish, but also the names of the trees in that forest, and the birds and four-legged animals at the foot of the mountain. Then, the Kuṇāla bird king arrived, sitting on a stick held in the beaks of two birds, surrounded by a flock of birds from the front, the back, and both sides. Seeing that bird king, the monks said, "Blessed One, this must be the king of these birds, and these must be his attendants." "Monks, it is just as you think; this bird king is also of my lineage, my own ancestry," he said. "Blessed One, now we have first seen these birds. However, we wish to hear the discourse where the Blessed One said, 'This bird king is also of my lineage, my own ancestry,'" they requested. "Monks, do you wish to hear it?" he asked. "Yes, Blessed One, we wish to hear it," they replied. "In that case, listen," he said, and then, adorning it with three hundred verses, he told the Kuṇāla Jātaka, dispelling their dissatisfaction. At the conclusion of the teaching, all the monks were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry, and through the Path, psychic powers also came to them. The Blessed One thought, "Let this much benefit be for these monks for now," and flying into the sky, he went to the Mahāvana forest. While those monks had gone there by the power of the Blessed One, upon returning, they descended into the Mahāvana forest surrounding the Blessed One by their own power.

The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat and, calling those monks, said, "Come, monks, sit down. I shall teach you the meditation subjects for the abandoning of the defilements that are to be abandoned by the three higher paths." The monks thought, "The Blessed One, knowing our dissatisfaction, took us to Lake Kuṇāla and dispelled it. To us who reached the Fruit of Stream-entry there, he now gives the meditation subjects for the three higher paths here. It is not proper for us to waste time thinking, 'We are Stream-enterers'; we should strive to be like superior persons." Those monks paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One, stood up, shook out their sitting mats, and went to sit individually in mountain caves and at the roots of trees.
270:
The Blessed One thought: "These monks have meditation subjects that are naturally not abandoned. For a monk who has obtained the proper means, there is no such thing as exhaustion. As they go along, they will develop insight, reach the fruition of Arahantship, and thinking, 'We shall report the special qualities we have individually attained,' they will come to me. When they arrive, the deities from the ten thousand world-systems will gather in a single world-system; there will be a Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya). It is proper for me to sit in a secluded place." Then, having had a Buddha-seat prepared in a secluded spot, he sat down.

The Elder who had first taken his meditation subject and departed reached the fruition of Arahantship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Then another, and another, until all five hundred blossomed with the fruition of Arahantship, like lotuses blooming in a lotus pond. The monk who first reached Arahantship thought, "I will report this to the Blessed One," and having released his cross-legged posture and shaken out his sitting cloth, he stood up and approached the presence of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala). In this same manner, all five hundred monks came in succession, as if entering a refectory.

The monk who arrived first paid homage, spread his sitting cloth, and sat in a suitable place. Wishing to report the special quality he had attained, he looked back at the path he had come, wondering, "Is there anyone else besides me, or not?" and he saw another monk, and then another. Thus, although all those monks had arrived and were sitting in suitable places, this monk did not speak out of deference to that monk, and that monk did not speak out of deference to this monk. It is said that Arahants have two characteristics: the thought arises, "Oh, may the world with its devas quickly realize the special quality I have attained!" However, like a man who has found a jar of treasure, they do not wish to inform others of their attainment.

At that moment, as the assembly of Noble Ones descended and stayed there, the full moon rose and entered the path of the wind. It was free from the five defilements—clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu—from around the eastern Yugandhara mountain. It appeared like a great silver mirror-disk held up in the east to show the delightful beauty of the world adorned by the appearance of a Buddha, or like a glorious silver wheel being turned by its rim. At such a moment, second, and instant, the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Great Wood (Mahāvana), together with a large community of monks, about five hundred monks, all of whom were Arahants.

Among them, the Blessed One was born in the lineage of Mahāsammata, and those five hundred monks were also born in the clan of Mahāsammata. The Blessed One was born in the womb of a queen of the Khattiya caste, and those monks were also [born in the womb of Khattiyas]. The Blessed One was one who went forth from the Khattiya caste, and those monks were also ones who went forth from the Khattiya caste. The Blessed One went forth having abandoned the white parasol and renounced the sovereignty of a Wheel-Turning Monarch that was within his reach; those monks also went forth having abandoned the white parasol and renounced the sovereignties that were within their reach...
271:
Those monks were also born in the womb of a queen of the Khattiya caste. Just as the Blessed One was one who went forth from the Khattiya caste, those monks were also ones who went forth from the Khattiya caste. Just as the Blessed One went forth having abandoned the white parasol and renounced the sovereignty of a Wheel-Turning Monarch that was within his reach, those monks also went forth having abandoned the white parasol and renounced the sovereignties that were within their reach. Thus, the Blessed One, in a pure place and at a pure time of night, being pure himself, had a pure retinue. Being free from lust (vītarāga) himself, he had a retinue free from lust. Being free from hatred (vītadossa) himself, he had a retinue free from hatred. Being free from delusion (vītamoha) himself, he had a retinue free from delusion. Being free from craving (nittaṇha) himself, he had a retinue free from craving. Being free from defilements (nikkilesa) himself, he had a retinue free from defilements. Being peaceful (santa) himself, he had a peaceful retinue. Being disciplined (danta) himself, he had a disciplined retinue. Being liberated (mutta) himself, he had a retinue liberated from defilements, and thus he shone exceedingly. This speech is called "the ground of praise" (vaṇṇabhūmi); as much as one is able to speak of his virtues, so much should be spoken. Thus, referring to these monks, it is said: "together with about five hundred monks, all of whom were Arahants."

"Mostly" (yebhuyyena) means that many devas and Brahmas gathered; only a few, such as the non-percipient (asañña) Brahmas, the formless (arūpa) Brahmas, and those devas absorbed in meditative attainments, did not gather. The order of the gathering of those devas was as follows: the devas in the vicinity of the Great Wood (Mahāvana) stirred, saying, "Friends, come! Seeing the Buddha is of great benefit; hearing the Dhamma is of great benefit; seeing the Community of Monks is of great benefit. Come, let us go!" Making a great sound, they came, paid homage to the Blessed One and to the Arahants who had reached the fruition of Arahantship at that moment, and stood at a respectful distance. In this manner, hearing the sounds of various devas, [others came] from distances of a quarter-league, half-league, three-quarters of a league, and a league. Devas gathered from the Himalayas (Himavanta), which is three thousand leagues wide; from the sixty-three thousand cities [mentioned] three times; from the nine million nine hundred thousand market towns; from the nine hundred and sixty million seaports; from the fifty-six places of jewels such as the island of Sīhaḷa; thus from the whole of Jambudīpa, the Eastern Continent, the Western Continent, the Northern Continent, and the two thousand small islands; from the entire world-system; and from the second and third world-systems, up to the ten thousand world-systems. Here, "ten world-elements" (dasa-lokadhātu) refers to the ten thousand world-systems. Therefore, it is said: "Devas from the ten world-elements mostly gathered."

The entire world-system, filled with the devas who had gathered in this way, was packed as tightly as needles in a needle-case, all the way up to the Brahma world. The height of that Brahma world should be understood thus: if a great stone, as large as a seven-storied gabled house of the Brazen Palace (Lohapāsāda), were dropped from the Brahma world...
272:
(A stone) reaches the earth only after four months. In such a vast space, the deities and Brahmas were so densely packed that there was no gap for flowers or smoke thrown from below to rise upwards, nor for mustard seeds thrown from above to descend. Just as the seating area of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) is not crowded and high-ranking kings who arrive find a place, yet it becomes extremely crowded further away, so too the area where the Blessed One sat was not crowded, and the high-ranking deities and Great Brahmas who arrived found their places. Indeed, in the immediate vicinity of the Blessed One, as mentioned in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, even in a space the size of the tip of a hair, deities stood by creating subtle forms in groups of ten, twenty, or even thirty. At the very end of all, the deities stood in groups of sixty each.

"Suddhāvāsakāyikānaṃ" refers to those living in the Pure Abodes. The Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) are the five Brahma realms which are the dwellings of the pure Non-returners (Anāgāmīs) and those who have destroyed the taints (Khīṇāsavas/Arahants). Why did this thought occur to them? It is said that those Brahmas, having entered into meditative attainments (samāpatti) and emerged at the determined time, looked upon the Brahma realms and saw them empty, like a dining hall after dinner. Then, reflecting, "Where have the Brahmas gone?", they realized there was a Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya) and thought: "This assembly is magnificent; we have been left behind. It is difficult for those left behind to find a place. Therefore, when we go, let us not go empty-handed, but let us each compose a verse (gāthā) before going. By that verse, we shall make our arrival known at the Great Assembly and also speak in praise of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala)." Thus, because they reflected upon emerging from their meditative attainment, this thought arose.

In the Pali text, "They appeared before the Blessed One," it is spoken as if they descended directly in front of the Blessed One, but the meaning should not be understood in that way. Those Brahmas, while still standing in the Brahma world, composed the verses; then one descended at the edge of the eastern world-system (Cakkavāḷa), one at the edge of the southern world-system, one at the edge of the western world-system, and one at the edge of the northern world-system. Then, the Brahma who descended at the edge of the eastern world-system, having entered the blue kasiṇa (nīlakasiṇa) and emitted blue rays, made his arrival known as if covering the deities of the ten thousand world-systems with a jeweled net, and then...
273:
No one is able to obstruct the path of approach to the Buddha (Buddhavīthi). Therefore, that Brahma came only along the path of approach to the Buddha, which is habitually used by deities and Brahmas, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood at a respectful distance. Standing at a respectful distance, he recited the verse he had composed.

The Brahma who descended at the edge of the southern world-system also entered the yellow kasiṇa (pītakasiṇa) and emitted golden rays, making his arrival known as if clothing the deities of the ten thousand world-systems with a golden cloth, and stood in the same manner. The Brahma who descended at the edge of the western world-system also entered the red kasiṇa (lohitakasiṇa) and emitted red rays, making his arrival known as if wrapping the deities of the ten thousand world-systems with a noble red blanket, and stood in the same manner. The Brahma who descended at the edge of the northern world-system also entered the white kasiṇa (odātakasiṇa) and emitted white rays, making his arrival known as if clothing the deities of the ten thousand world-systems with a cloth the color of jasmine (sumanā), and stood in the same manner.

In the Pali text, however, it is said: "They appeared before the Blessed One. Then those deities paid homage to the Blessed One and stood at a respectful distance," thus describing their appearance in front and their standing after paying homage as if occurring at the same moment. Although their appearance in front and standing at a respectful distance occurred in the sequence described above, they are shown together (in the Pali). As for the recitation of the verses, they are spoken separately in the Pali.

Among those verses, "Mahāsamaya" means a great gathering. "Pavana" refers to a forest grove. By both words, he said that today in this forest grove, there is a great gathering, a great assembly. Then, to show those who have come to that assembly, he said, "The hosts of deities (devakāyā) have assembled." There, "devakāyā" means groups of deities. Seeing the hosts of deities thus assembled, [he thought,] "We too have come to this Dhamma-assembly (dhamma-samaya)." For what reason? "To see the unconquered Sangha (aparājita-saṅgha)," meaning they have come to see this unconquered Sangha, which cannot be defeated by anyone and which has today crushed the three Māras and won the battle. That Brahma, having recited this verse and paid homage to the Blessed One, stood at the edge of the eastern world-system.

Then the second Brahma, having arrived in the same manner as already described, spoke. In that verse, "tatra bhikkhavo" means the monks at that place of assembly. "Samādahaṃsu" means they composed [their minds] with concentration (samādhi). "They made their own minds straight" means they removed all crookedness, craftiness, and deviousness from their minds and made them straight. Like a charioteer [holding] the reins...
274:
"Gahētvā" means just as a charioteer, holding the whip in his hand while the Sindhu horses run evenly, holds all the reins without urging or restraining them; likewise, all these five hundred wise monks, endowed with six-factored equanimity and guarded sense doors, protect their faculties. "O Blessed One, we have come here to see those monks," it means. That second Brahma also went and stood in his own place.

Then the third Brahma also came and spoke in the same manner as mentioned before. In that verse, "chettvā khīlaṃ" means having cut the stakes of lust, hatred, and delusion. "Palighaṃ" means the bar of lust, hatred, and delusion itself. "Indakhīlaṃ" also refers to the threshold pillar of lust, hatred, and delusion. "Ūhacca anējā" means that these monks, being motionless due to the absence of the agitation of craving, have uprooted the threshold pillar. Those monks wander without obstruction in the four directions. "Suddhā" means being free from the defilements. "Vimalā" means being stainless, and this word is a synonym for "suddhā." "Cakkhumatā" means because they were disciplined by the Blessed One who is endowed with the five eyes. Those monks are well-tamed in the eye-door, ear-door, nose-door, tongue-door, body-door, and mind-door. "Susunāgā" refers to the Arahants who are like young noble elephants. "O Blessed One, we have come to see the Arahants who are like young noble elephants, tamed by such an unsurpassed meditation master," he addressed. That Brahma also went and stood in his own place.

Then the fourth Brahma also came and spoke in the same manner as mentioned before. In that verse, "gatāsē" means they have gone for refuge with a mind free from doubt. That Brahma also went and stood in his own place.

## Description of the Assembly of Devas

Then the Blessed One, looking out, saw the assembly of devas from the surface of the earth to the edge of the universe and up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm, and thought: "This assembly of devas is vast. The monks, however, do not know that the assembly of devas is so great. Indeed, I shall inform them." Having thought thus, the passage beginning with "Then the Blessed One addressed the monks..." should be understood in detail. In that text, "ētaparamā" means this is the maximum extent for these devas. Since there are no other Buddhas at this time, the third turn (vāra) "Monks, even now..." was not spoken. Why did he say, "Monks, I shall inform you"? It was to gladden the hearts of the devas. It is said that the devas thought: "The Blessed One will mention the names and clans of only the great and powerful devas in such a large assembly; how could he mention the names and clans of the lesser ones?" At that time, the Blessed One, knowing the thoughts of the devas, as if putting a hand into the mouth to knead the heart, or as if catching a thief with the stolen goods...
275:
Then the Blessed One, reflecting "What are these devas thinking?", knew the thoughts of those devas—as if putting a hand into the mouth to knead the heart, or as if catching a thief with the stolen goods—and thought: "I shall proclaim the names and clans of all the devas, both of lesser and greater power, who have come from the ten thousand world systems."

Buddhas are indeed great; they are superior beings among all creatures. Whatever object there is in the world including the devas—seen, heard, sensed (through nose, tongue, and body), known, reached, sought, or pondered by the mind—there is no such object that does not appear before the range of their knowledge. Whether it be a visual object among the various colors like blue as analyzed in the Abhidhamma, or a sound object among various sounds like the sound of a drum, there is nothing that does not appear in the knowledge of those Buddhas. Thus it was said:

"Monks, whatever in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmas, among the progeny with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, known, reached, sought, or pondered by the mind—all that I know, all that I see, all that I have fully realized with higher knowledge."

In this way, the Blessed One, whose knowledge is unobstructed in all objects, divided all those devas into two groups: those capable of realization (bhabba) and those incapable (abhabba). Beings described as being endowed with the "obstruction of kamma" (kammāvaraṇa) and so on are called "incapable." Even if they live in the same monastery, the Buddhas do not look upon them. On the other hand, those who are "capable," even if they live far away, the Buddhas go to them and favor them with their presence. Therefore, in that assembly of devas as well, he set aside the incapable devas and took hold of the capable ones.

Having taken hold of them, he divided them into six groups according to their temperaments (carita): "This many devas are of lustful temperament, this many are of hateful temperament, this many are of deluded temperament." Then, while considering the appropriate Dhamma teaching for them, he determined the discourse: "I shall preach the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta to the devas of lustful temperament, the Kalahavivāda Sutta to those of hateful temperament, the Mahābyūha Sutta to those of deluded temperament, the Cūḷabyūha Sutta to those of speculative temperament, the Tuvaṭṭaka practice to those of faithful temperament, and the Purābheda Sutta to those of intellectual temperament."

Again, he reflected on that assembly: "Should I preach by my own inclination, or by the inclination of others, or by an occasion that has arisen, or by way of questioning?" Then, knowing "They will understand if I preach by way of questioning," he considered: "Is there anyone capable of understanding the inclination of the devas and asking questions according to their temperaments?" He saw that not even one among those five hundred monks was capable. Then he reflected on the eighty Great Disciples and the two Chief Disciples, and saw that they too were not capable. He then reflected: "If there were Paccekabuddhas, would they be capable?"
276: Seeing that "they too are unable," He thought, "If it were a Paccekabuddha, would he be able?" Knowing that "even a Paccekabuddha would not be able," He considered, "Would someone among Sakka, Suyāma, and others be able?" If any of them were able, He would have them ask and He Himself would answer; however, not a single one of them was able. Then the thought occurred to the Blessed One: "Only a Buddha like me would be able. Is there any other Buddha like me anywhere?" Spreading His infinite Omniscient Knowledge throughout the infinite world systems and looking, He did not see another Buddha. This is not surprising; that He does not see anyone equal to Himself now is consistent with what was said in the commentary to the Brahmajāla Sutta regarding the day of His birth—not seeing anyone equal to Himself, He uttered the irreversible Lion's Roar: "I am the foremost in the world." Thus, not seeing anyone else equal to Himself, He thought: "If I ask and I myself answer, these deities will not be able to penetrate the meaning. But if another Buddha asks and I answer, it will be a marvel, and the deities will be able to penetrate the meaning. Therefore, I shall create a Nimmitabuddha." Having entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for direct knowledge, and emerging from it, He performed the preliminary work with sense-sphere consciousness, resolving: "Let the holding of the bowl and robes, the looking ahead and looking aside, and the bending and stretching of this Nimmitabuddha be exactly like mine." Then, with fine-material-sphere consciousness, He determined the creation of the Nimmitabuddha, appearing like the moon's orb emerging after breaking through the range of the eastern Mount Yugandhara. Seeing that Nimmitabuddha, the host of deities said, "Friends, has another moon arisen?" Then, as it drew closer and did not resemble the moon, they said, "It is not the moon; the sun has arisen." Again, as it drew closer, they said, "It is not the sun; it is a celestial mansion." Again, as it drew closer, they said, "It is not a celestial mansion; it is a son of the devas." Again, as it drew closer, they said, "It is not a son of the devas; it is a Great Brahmā." Again, as it drew closer, they said, "It is not a Great Brahmā; friends, another Buddha has arrived." In that assembly, the worldling deities thought, "When there was only one Buddha, there was such a gathering of deities; how much greater will it be with two Buddhas?" The Noble deities, however, thought, "There cannot be two Buddhas in a single world system; surely the Blessed One has created another Nimmitabuddha equal to Himself." Then, while the host of deities was watching, the Nimmitabuddha arrived and, without bowing to the Blessed One, sat on the created seat exactly equal to Him in front. The Blessed One possessed the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and the Nimmitabuddha also possessed only those thirty-two marks.
277: From the Blessed One's body, the six-colored rays emitted, and from the body of the created Nimmitabuddha, the six-colored rays also emitted. The rays emitting from the Blessed One's body touched the body of the Nimmitabuddha, and the rays emitting from the Nimmitabuddha's body touched the body of the Blessed One. Those rays ascended from the bodies of both Buddhas, reached the Akaniṭṭha realm, and stayed there. From there, they returned, descended upon the heads of the deities, and remained at the rim of the universe. The entire interior of the universe shone like a shrine-house adorned with golden rafters. Deities from ten thousand world systems gathered in a single universe and stood within the interior of the rays of the two Buddhas. While still sitting, the Nimmitabuddha, praising the abandonment of defilements at the Blessed One's Bodhi-throne, spoke this verse: "I ask the Sage of vast wisdom, Who has crossed over, reached the far shore, attained Nibbāna, and is firm of mind; Having gone forth from the home life and discarded sensual pleasures, How should a monk live rightly in the world?" (Sn 361) The Blessed One, thinking, "I will announce the names and clans of the deities who have arrived to gladden their hearts," said, "Monks, I shall announce..." and so forth. In that verse, "silokamanukassāmīti" means "I shall bring forth (proclaim) a collection of words defined by syllables and feet." "Yattha bhummā tadassitāti" means "In whatever places there are earth-bound deities residing in dependence on those places." With the words beginning with "ye sitā girigabbharanti," He proclaimed the virtues of those monks. It means "monks who live in dependence on mountain caves." "Pahitattā" means "having a mind sent towards Nibbāna." "Samāhitā" means "having an undistracted mind." "Puthū" means "many monks." "Sīhāva sallīnā" means "dwelling alone like lion-kings, they have attained the state of being solitary." "Lomahansābhisambhuno" means "they remain having overcome the bristling of hair; it means they are without fear." "Odātamanasā suddhā" means "being pure with a bright mind." "Vippasannāmanāvilā" means "exceptionally clear and without turbidity." "Bhiyyopañcasate ñatvā" means "knowing the monks who were more than five hundred along with the Blessed One." "Vane kāpilavatthave" means "in the forest grove near the city of Kapilavatthu." "Tato āmantayī satthā" means "at that time, the Teacher addressed and spoke to them."
278:
"Sāvake sāsane rate" refers to those who are called "disciples" (sāvaka) because they have arisen at the end of hearing his Dhamma teaching, and "delighting in the teaching" (sāsane rata) because they delight in the teaching of the threefold training (sikkhattaya). He spoke all these words as if spoken by another, because he said, "I shall recite the verses."

"Monks, the hosts of devas have arrived; recognize them, monks" means he spoke for the purpose of directing their minds toward the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa), so that they might recognize those devas with the divine eye. Having heard that instruction of the Blessed One, those monks exerted effort at that very moment to attain that divine eye.

Just by making such an effort, knowledge became manifest to those monks. What kind of knowledge? The divine eye that can see non-human beings (amanussa) arose. That divine eye was not produced by them through preliminary preparation (parikamma) at that moment. Indeed, it was accomplished through the Noble Path (ariya-magga) itself. However, they only performed the mere directing of the mind toward that knowledge in order to see the non-human beings. The Teacher, referring to this very divine eye accomplished through the Noble Path, said: "You have the knowledge; bring it forth and recognize those devas with it," thus saying, "Recognize them, monks."

"Some saw a hundred" means among those monks, some saw a hundred non-human beings. "A thousand, and then seventy thousand" means some saw a thousand, and some saw seventy thousand devas.

"Some saw a hundred thousand" means some monks saw a hundred thousand devas. "Some saw without limit" means they saw a vast number; it means they saw without being limited by the count of hundreds or thousands. Why? Because all the quarters were pervaded and filled with devas.

"Having known all that" means having known all that was seen by each of those monks. "The One with Vision, having discerned" means the Teacher, endowed with the five eyes, having discerned clearly as if seeing lines on the palm of the hand. "Then he addressed" means he spoke the previously mentioned verse for the purpose of proclaiming their names and clans. The connection here is: "I shall proclaim to you which devas there are; recognize them, see them, and look at them." "Girāhi" means with words. "Anupubbaso" means in due order.

"Those seven thousand yakkhas are terrestrial devas of Kapilavatthu" means that here, the seven thousand terrestrial devas who arose depending on Kapilavatthu are indeed of the yakkha kind.
279:
(The Blessed One) spoke. "Iddhimanto" means those endowed with divine power. "Jutimanto" means those endowed with majesty. "Vaṇṇavanto" means those endowed with beauty of body. "Yasassino" means those endowed with followers. "Modamānā abhikāmuṃ" means they came with joyful hearts. "Bhikkhūnaṃ samitiṃ vanaṃ" means they came to this Mahāvana forest, to the presence of the monks, to see the monks. Or, "samitiṃ" means an assembly, thus it also means they came to see the assembly of monks.

"Six thousand from Hemavata, yakkhas of various colors" means the six thousand yakkhas who arose on Mount Hemavata; and all of them have various colors such as blue and so on.

"Three thousand from Sātāgira" means the three thousand yakkhas who arose on Mount Sātāgiri. "Thus these sixteen thousand" means all these aforementioned devas are sixteen thousand. "Five hundred from Vessāmitta" means the five hundred devas who arose on Mount Vessāmitta.

"Kumbhīra of Rājagaha" means the yakkha named Kumbhīra who arose in the city of Rājagaha. "The abode of Vepulla" means his place of residence is Mount Vepulla. "More than a hundred thousand yakkhas attend on him" means more than a hundred thousand yakkhas attend on that deva king. "Kumbhīra of Rājagaha, he too came to the forest assembly" means that Kumbhīra, the deva king, also came to this forest with his followers to see the assembly of monks.

"The king Dhataraṭṭha rules the eastern quarter" means he governs the eastern direction. "Lord of the Gandhabbas" means he is the chief of the Gandhabbas in all four quarters. All those Gandhabbas act according to the will of that King Dhataraṭṭha. "The Great King of great fame" means this Great King has a large following.

"He has many sons, named Inda, of great strength" means that King Dhataraṭṭha has many sons of great strength; all of them bear the name of Sakka, the king of devas. "Virūḷha rules that quarter" means King Virūḷhaka governs that (southern) quarter.
280:
"Puttāpi tassā" means that this Great King Virūḷhaka also has sons similar to those [of King Dhataraṭṭha]. In the Pali text, however, they write "Mahabbalā". In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), the reading is "Mahābalā" in all instances.

"King Dhataraṭṭha in the eastern direction, Virūḷhaka in the south, Virūpakkha in the west, and Kuvera in the northern direction. These four Great Kings stood shining all around the four directions in the Great Forest near the city of Kapilavatthu."

These verses are taught by way of encompassing all the Great Kings of the Four Quarters.

The meaning of this passage is as follows: In the ten thousand world-systems, there are Great Kings named Dhataraṭṭha. All of them, accompanied by more than a hundred billion Gandhabbas, arrived and stood filling the entire interior of the world-system, starting from the Great Forest of Kapilavatthu in the eastern direction. Similarly, Virūḷhaka and others stood in the southern direction and so forth. Therefore, it is said, "They stood shining all around the four directions." This means that these Great Kings, having come from various world-systems, stood in the four directions like great masses of fire on mountain tops, shining brilliantly. Since these Great Kings came specifically with reference to the Great Forest of Kapilavatthu, even though they stood filling the entire world-system, it is said, "in the Great Forest of Kapilavatthu."

"Tesaṃ māyāvino dāsā, āguṃ vañcanikā saṭhā" means that these Great Kings have servants who are deceitful, characterized by concealing the wrongs they have committed, and who are of crooked conduct. These servants are called "vañcanika" because they deceive people both in their presence and behind their backs, and "saṭha" because they are endowed with extreme craftiness. The meaning is that these servants also arrived. "Māyā Kuṭeṇḍu Viṭeṇḍu, Viṭucca Viṭuṭo sahā" means that all these servants are indeed deceivers. By name, one is called Kuṭeṇḍu and one is called Viṭeṇḍu. In the Pali text, however, they write "Veṭeṇḍū". One is called Viṭucca and one is called Viṭuṭo. "Sahā" means that Viṭuṭo also arrived together with them.
281:
They are the deity Candana, the deity Kāmaseṭṭha, the deity Kinnighaṇḍu, and the deity Nighaṇḍu. There is also another servant named Kinnighaṇḍu. In the Pali text, however, they write "Kinnughaṇḍū". There is another servant named Nighaṇḍu. These many individuals are the servants of the four Great Kings. Apart from these, there are:

The deity Panāda and Opamañña, Devasuta and Mātali,
the Gandhabba Cittasena, King Naḷa and Janesabha,
Pañcasikha also arrived, as well as Timbarū and Suriyavacchasā.

These are celestial kings. Among them, Devasuta is the charioteer of the gods. Cittasena refers to the deities Citta, Sena, and Cittasena. "Gandhabba" means this Cittasena is a deity belonging to the Gandhabba host. Not only he, but all those such as Panāda are also Gandhabbas. "Naḷo rājā" is a certain deity named Naḷakāra because he was formerly a reed-worker. "Janesabho" is the deity Janavasabha. "Āguṃ Pañcasikho ceva" means that the deity Pañcasikha also arrived. "Timbarū" is the Gandhabba king of that name. "Suriyavacchasā" is the daughter of that King Timbarū.

These Gandhabba kings mentioned by name, along with many other Gandhabbas, arrived at this forest, the assembly of the community of monks, with joyful and delighted minds.

Then the Nāgas living in Lake Nāgasada and the Nāgas living in the city of Vesālī arrived together with the retinue of Tacchaka Nāgas. "Kambalassatarā" refers to the Nāga Kambala and the Nāga Assatara. It is said that these Nāgas live at the foot of Mount Sineru. They are highly powerful Nāgas whom even Garuḍas cannot carry away. The Nāgas living at the Payāga ferry also arrived together with their assembly of kinsmen.

The Nāgas living in the Yamunā River and the Nāgas born in the Dhataraṭṭha lineage, as well as the deity named Erāvaṇa, arrived. Erāvaṇa is not a Nāga by birth; however, he is referred to by the designation "Nāga" (elephant). That deity Erāvaṇa also arrived.
282:
“Ye nāgarāje sahasā harantīti” refers to the Garuḍa kings who, overcome by greed for food, forcibly seize and carry away the various types of Nāgas mentioned above, other than the Kambala and Assatara. These Garuḍas are called “Dibba” because they possess power similar to that of the devas. They are called “Dija” because they are born twice—once from the mother’s womb and once from the eggshell. They are called “Pakkhī” because they are endowed with wings. They are called “Visuddhacakkhu” because they have eyes capable of seeing Nāgas within a range of a hundred or a thousand yojanas. These Garuḍa kings arrived at this Mahāvana forest only by way of the sky. They are named “Citrasupaṇṇa” because they have variegated wings.

At that time, the Buddha made the Nāga kings safe from the danger of the Garuḍas. Therefore, all those Nāgas and Garuḍas, calling to each other with pleasant words, greeting each other like friends and relatives, were joyful and happy, embracing, holding hands, and placing hands on each other’s shoulders. The Nāgas and Garuḍas took refuge only in the Buddha.

“Jitā vajirahatthena” refers to those conquered by Sakka, the king of devas, who holds the thunderbolt. They are the powerful Asuras who live in the great ocean and are the brothers of Sakka because of the Asura princess Sujātā. Among those Asuras, the Kālakañja Asuras came, having created large and terrifying forms. Other archer Asuras named Dānaveghasa also came. Along with Vepacitti and Sucitti Asuras, the deity Māra named Namuci also came. Why did Māra, who lives in the Paranimmita-vasavatti heaven, come together with these Asuras who live in the great ocean? Because of the lack of desire for merit. Those Asuras are incapable of liberation, and Māra is the same. Therefore, they came together due to their similar natures.

The hundred sons of the great Asura king Bali also came. All of them are named “Virocana” after their maternal uncle Rāhu. They gathered and prepared their own Bali army and approached Rāhu, the lord of Asuras.
283:
“May there be good fortune to the Lord Asura; now is the time for the Lord Asura to approach the Mahāvana forest, the meeting place of the monks, to see the Saṅgha of monks,” is the meaning.

“The Devas of Water, Earth, Fire, and Wind also came” means the Devas named Āpo, Pathavī, Tejo, and Vāyo, who were born by practicing the preparatory meditation on the water-kasiṇa and so forth, have arrived. “Varuṇa, Vāraṇa, and Soma Devas came with their retinues” means the Devas named Varuṇa, Vāraṇa, and Soma arrived together with the Deva named Yasasa. “Mettā-karuṇā-kāyika Devas” are those born by practicing meditation on loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā). “The Devas with great retinues arrived” means those Devas of great fame and retinue have also arrived.

“These ten groups of Devas in ten ways, all of various colors” means those ten groups of Devas, standing in ten ways, arrived with various colors such as blue and so forth.

The Veṇḍu Devas, the Sahali Devas, the Asama Devas, and the two Yamaka Devas also arrived. The Devas who depend on the Moon Deva arrived, placing the Moon Deva at the front. Similarly, the Devas who depend on the Sun Deva arrived, placing the Sun Deva at the front. The Devas who depend on the constellations arrived, placing the constellations at the front. “The Manda-valāhaka Devas arrived” means the Vāta-valāhaka Devas (causes of wind), the Abbha-valāhaka Devas (movers of clouds), and the Uṇha-valāhaka Devas (causes of heat)—all these groups of Valāhaka Devas are called “Manda-valāhaka.” They also arrived. Vāsava, the chief of the Vasu Devas, who is also called Sakka and Purindada, also arrived.

These ten groups of Devas also arrived in ten ways. All of them have various colors such as blue and so forth.

Furthermore, the Devas named Sahabhū arrived. They were shining like flames of fire. It is also said that “Jalamaggi” and “Sikhāriva” are the names of these Devas. The Ariṭṭhaka Devas and the Roja Devas also arrived. These are called the Umāpuppha Devas, who have the color of the flax flower.
284:
Because the radiance of the bodies of the devas Ariṭṭha and Roja is like the Umā flower (flax flower), they are called the 'Umāpupphanibhāsin' devas.

The two devas Varuṇa and Sahadhamma, as well as the devas Accuta and Anejaka, have arrived. The Suleyya and Rucira devas have also arrived. Devas named Vāsavanesī have arrived. These ten groups of devas have arrived in ten ways.

The Samāna and Mahāsamāna devas, as well as the Mānuṣa and Mānuṣuttama devas, have arrived. The Khiḍḍāpadosika and Manopadosika devas have also arrived.

Then, the devas named Hari arrived. The devas named Lohitavāsī also arrived. These two types, the Pāraga and Mahāpāraga devas, have arrived. These ten groups of devas have arrived in ten ways.

The Veghanasa devas arrived together with these three types of devas: Sukkā, Karambhā, and Aruṇā. The leading devas named Odātagayhā arrived. The devas named Vicakkhaṇa arrived.

The Sadāmatta and Hāragaja devas, as well as the glorious Missaka devas, have arrived. The king of devas, Pajjunna, also arrived thundering. Wherever that rain-god goes, he causes rain to fall there. These ten groups of devas have arrived in ten ways.

The Khemiya devas, the inhabitants of the Tusita heaven, and the inhabitants of the Yāma heaven have arrived. The glorious Kathaka devas also arrived. (In the Pali text, however, they are written as 'Kaṭṭhaka'). There were also the Lambitaka and Lāmaseṭṭha devas. There were also the Joti devas, who shine like a bonfire lit on a mountain top. Those Joti devas and the Āsa devas have arrived.
285:
In the Pali text, however, it is written as 'Jātināma'. The devas named Āsā are called 'Āsā' due to the power of desire (chanda). The Nimmānarati devas have arrived, and then the Paranimmitavasavatti devas arrived. These ten groups of devas also arrived in ten ways.

These sixty groups of devas, starting with the Āpo devas, have various colors according to the power of their hues, such as blue and so on. They arrived according to their names and categories. Devas from the remaining world systems who are similar to them in color and name have also arrived. Thus, with a single term, [the Buddha] points to all the devas as if making a collection or a bundle.

Having thus pointed out the groups of devas in the ten thousand world systems, he now spoke the verse beginning with 'Pavuṭṭhajātiṃ' to show the reason for their arrival. The meaning of that verse is: The Noble Saṅgha is called 'Pavuṭṭhajāti' because birth has been abandoned. We shall see the Noble Saṅgha, who are called 'Akhīla' because they are free from the spikes of lust, hatred, and delusion; 'Oghatiṇṇa' because they have crossed over the four floods and remain firm; and 'Anāsava' because they are free from the four taints.

We shall also see the Buddha of Ten Powers (Dasabala), who is called 'Oghatara' because he has crossed those same four floods; 'Nāga' because he does no evil; and who shines with glory like the moon, having transcended the impurity of evil. For this purpose, all those devas arrived according to their names. Furthermore, devas from other world systems who are similar in color and name arrived together.

Now, wishing to show the Brahmas, he spoke the words beginning with 'Subrahmā Paramatto ca'. There, Subrahmā is one Brahma. Paramatta is also a Brahma. The Noble Brahmas, who are the sons of the Blessed One possessed of great psychic power, arrived together. Sanatkumāra and Tissa Mahābrahmā also arrived. That Brahma also arrived.

It means: 'From a thousand Brahma worlds, the Mahābrahmās have arrived; that Mahābrahmā stands surpassing other Brahmas. That Mahābrahmā, who was born in the Brahma world, who is possessed of majesty, who has a great body, and who is endowed with fame and retinue, has arrived.'
286:
In this verse, "a thousand Brahma worlds" means a thousand Mahābrahmas have arrived, who are capable of spreading light over a thousand world systems with one finger, and over ten thousand world systems with ten fingers. "The Great Brahma stands surpassing" means each Mahābrahma stands surpassing other Brahmas in terms of appearance, retinue, and longevity. "Upapanno" means one who is born in the Brahma world. "Jutimanto" means one who is endowed with majesty. "Bhismākāyo" means one who has a huge body, having a physical form about the size of two or three village fields in the Magadha country. "Yasassī" means one who is endowed with fame, which is the splendor of the physical form.

Among these thousand Brahmas, ten such lords, Mahābrahmas who each exercise individual authority, have arrived. In the midst of those Brahmas, the Mahābrahma named Hārita has arrived, accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand Brahmas.

Māra’s army arrived to overwhelm all those hosts of devas who came with Sakka, the king of devas, as their leader, and those hosts of Brahmas who came with Hārita Mahābrahma as their leader. He said, "Look at the foolishness of the Dark One (Kaṇha), the one of evil unwholesome deeds."

"Come, seize them, bind them!" Thus he commanded his own assembly. He said, "May this entire circle of devas and Brahmas be bound by lust (rāga)." He said, "Surround them from all sides; let not even a single one of them escape." The variant reading "Mā vo muñcetha" has the same meaning.

Thus, at that Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya), Māra, who has a great army, dispatched the army of Māra. Striking the surface of the earth with his hand, he made a terrifying sound to show Māra's intimidation.

While roaring a great roar like a heavy rain cloud accompanied by lightning, at that time, that Māra, having shown that terror, retreated.
287:
Māra retreated. Being extremely furious and angry, unable to bring anyone under his control, and being unable to make them follow his will, he retreated against his own will. The Blessed One knew, "This Māra, seeing this great assembly of devas and Brahmas, is thinking, 'I will create an obstacle to the realization of the Truths (abhisamaya),' and is showing Māra's intimidation by sending Māra's army at intervals." This is the nature of the Blessed One: in an assembly where the realization of the Truths will not occur, He does not prevent Māra from showing intimidation. However, in an assembly where the realization of the Truths will occur, He resolves (adhiṭṭhāna) in such a way that the assembly neither sees Māra's form nor hears his voice. In this assembly of devas and Brahmas, many devas and Brahmas will realize the Truths. Therefore, He resolved so that the devas would neither see Māra's form nor hear his voice. Thus, it was said, "At that time, that Māra, being extremely furious and unable to have his way, retreated."

"The One with Vision (Cakkhumā), having known and discerned all that with higher knowledge," means the Blessed One, having known and discerned all the actions of that Māra, said, "Monks, the army of Māra has approached; recognize them." This means He said, "Monks, the army of Māra has approached; recognize those Māra's soldiers appropriately for yourselves, and enter the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti)." "They made an effort" means they initiated energy to enter the attainment of fruition. "They departed from the passion-free ones" means Māra and his army departed far away from the Noble Ones (Ariyas) who are free from passion. "Not even a single hair of theirs stirred" means they could not make even the hairs of those passion-free Noble Ones move. Then, Māra recited this verse concerning the Saṅgha of monks:

"All your disciples, who have conquered the battle, surpassed fear, are famous, and are well-known among the people, rejoice together with the Noble Ones who have arisen in the Dispensation."

In that verse, "rejoice together with the Noble Ones who have arisen in the Dispensation" means they rejoice, they greatly rejoice together with the Noble Ones who have well arisen in the Dispensation of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala). "Well-known among the people" means those who are famous, well-known, and specially recognized among the people.

This Mahāsamaya Sutta is dear and pleasing to the devas; it increases the joy of the heart. Therefore, a person speaking auspicious words should recite this very Sutta at new places or during renovations. It is said that devas wander about with their ears inclined, thinking, "We will listen to this Sutta." At the conclusion of the teaching...
288:
At the end of this Mahāsamaya Sutta, one hundred thousand crores of deities attained the fruit of Arahatship. The number of noble disciples, such as Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) and others, is indeed beyond counting.

Regarding the fact that this Sutta is dear and pleasing to the deities and causes their hearts to flourish, there is this illustrative story: It is said that a certain goddess lived in a Naga tree (ironwood tree) at the entrance of the Naga Cave in the Koṭipabbata Monastery. A young monk was reciting this Mahāsamaya Sutta inside the cave. Having heard it, the goddess uttered a loud 'Sādhu' at the conclusion of the Sutta. The monk asked, "Who is this?" She replied, "Venerable sir, I am a goddess." "Why did you say Sādhu?" he asked. "Venerable sir, I heard this Sutta on the day the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) sat in the Mahāvana forest and preached it, and only today have I heard it again. You, venerable sirs, have well-preserved this Dhamma, without losing even a single syllable from the Pali text preached by the Blessed One," she replied.

"Did you hear it yourself when the Ten-Powered One was preaching?" he asked. "Yes, venerable sir," she replied. "I have heard that the assembly of deities and Brahmas was very large then; where were you standing when you heard it?" he asked. "Venerable sir, I was a goddess residing in the Mahāvana forest. However, when the powerful deities arrived, I found no space in Jambudīpa. Thus, I came to this island of Tambapaṇṇi and attempted to listen while standing at the port of Jambukola. As more powerful deities arrived there as well, I gradually moved back until I stood in the sea, in water up to my neck, behind the village of Mahāgāma in the Rohaṇa region, and listened from there," she replied.

"Goddess, your standing place was very far; did you see the Teacher?" he asked. "Venerable sir, what are you saying? While the Teacher was preaching the Dhamma in the Mahāvana forest, I felt as if He was looking only at me, and with a heart full of devotion and respect, I remained submerged among the waves," she replied.

"It is said that on that day, one hundred thousand crores of deities attained the fruit of Arahatship; did you also attain Arahatship then?" he asked. "No, venerable sir," she replied. "I suppose you attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi)?" "No, venerable sir." "I suppose you attained the fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi)?" "No, venerable sir." "I have heard that the deities who attained the three paths are beyond counting; I suppose you became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna)?" Since the goddess had only attained the fruit of Stream-entry on that day, she felt shy and said, "The venerable one asks what should not be asked." Then the monk asked, "Goddess, can you show your form to us?" "Venerable sir, I am unable to show it," she replied.
289:
"I cannot show my entire body, but I will show the venerable sir just a finger joint." Saying this, she pointed her finger through the keyhole toward the inside of the cave. It became as bright as the rising of a thousand moons and a thousand suns. The goddess said, "Venerable sir, be diligent (appamāda)," paid homage to the young monk, and departed. In this way, this Mahāsamaya Sutta is dear, pleasing, and delightful to the deities; the deities cherish this Sutta.

## The Commentary on the Mahāsamaya Sutta is finished.
290:
## 8. Sakkapañhasutta-vaṇṇanā
## Commentary on the Introduction (Nidāna)
This Sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Sakkapañha Sutta.
