In this Sakkapañha Sutta, the explanation of the obscure terms is as follows: The Brahmin village named "Ambasaṇḍā" is so called because it was situated near mango groves (amba-saṇḍa). "Vediyake pabbate" means that the mountain was surrounded on all sides by a dark-green forest, which grew at the foot of the mountain and resembled a jeweled pedestal (maṇi-vedikā) made of blue sapphires; therefore, it came to be known as "Vediyaka Mountain". "Indasālaguhāyaṃ" means that since ancient times, that cave was located between two mountains, and there was an Indasāla tree (Sal tree) at its entrance; thus, it came to be known as the "Indasāla Cave". Later, people enclosed the cave with walls, fitted it with main doors and windows, and having made it an exquisite cave adorned with well-finished plasterwork, floral designs, and creeper motifs, they offered it to the Blessed One. However, people still recognized it by its former name, "Indasāla Cave". It is in reference to that exquisitely prepared cave that "Indasālaguhāyaṃ" is said.

"Ussukkaṃ udapādi" means that a righteous zeal (effort) arose. One might ask: Does this Sakka, King of Devas, not see the Blessed One frequently? There is no assembly of deities where he has not gone before. There is no son of the gods who dwells in diligence like Sakka. Why, then, did zeal arise in him to see the Buddha, as if he had never seen Him before? It was because he was terrified and threatened by the fear of death. At that time, his life span was exhausted, and having seen the five prior omens (pubbanimitta), he knew, "Now my life span is exhausted." Among the sons of the gods in whom the omens of death appear, those who were reborn in the deva world through meager meritorious deeds fall into fear and trembling, wondering, "Where will we be reborn now?" But those who were reborn after performing many meritorious deeds that provide refuge from fear do not fear, relying on the gifts they have given, the virtue they have guarded, and the meditation they have practiced, thinking, "We shall experience prosperity in the higher deva worlds."

Sakka, the King of Devas, however, saw the prior omens and looked upon the city of the gods ten thousand yojanas in extent, the Vejayanta Palace one thousand yojanas high, the Sudhammā Hall of the Gods three hundred yojanas in extent, the Pāricchattaka tree one hundred yojanas high, the Paṇ膽ukambala stone seat sixty yojanas in extent, the assembly of thirty-five million celestial dancers in the two deva worlds, the Nandana Grove,
291:
Sakka, the king of devas, looked upon all his splendors—the Paṇḍukambala silken stone seat, the three crores of dancers, the celestial assemblies, and the gardens of Nandavana, Cittalatā, Missaka, and Phārusaka—and was overcome by fear, thinking, "Alas, this prosperity of mine will surely perish."

Then he looked around, thinking, "Is there any recluse or brahmin, or even the Great Brahmā, the grandfather of the world, who can thoroughly extract this arrow of sorrow rooted in my heart and make this prosperity of mine permanent?" Seeing no one, he thought again, "Only the Fully Enlightened Buddha is capable of extracting the arrow of sorrow that has arisen even for a hundred thousand like me." While he was thus reflecting, at that time, the effort to see the Blessed One arose in Sakka, the lord of devas.

"Where is the Blessed One staying now? In which district, depending on which town is he dwelling? Whose requisites is he using, and to whom is he preaching the Dhamma that grants the Deathless?" (he pondered). "Addasā kho" means he saw, he realized through penetration. "Mārisā" is a term of endearment, a specific mode of address among the devas. It also means "dear one who is free from suffering." Why did he call the devas? He called them for the sake of companionship. It is said that previously, when the Blessed One was staying at the Saḷalaghara monastery, Sakka went alone to see him.

The Teacher thought, "This Sakka's knowledge is not yet mature. After a few days, when I am staying in the Indasāla Cave, he will see the five omens [of death] and, fearing the danger of death, will approach me together with the devas from the two celestial realms. He will ask fourteen questions, and at the conclusion of the explanation of the questions on equanimity, he, along with eighty thousand devas, will be established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala)." Thus, the Teacher did not grant him an opportunity.

Sakka thought, "Because I went alone before, the Teacher did not grant me an opportunity. Surely, I do not have the strong supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruit. However, if even one person has the supporting condition, the Blessed One will surely preach the Dhamma to the assembly as far as the limits of the world-system. There will surely be some deva in the two celestial realms who has the supporting condition; the Teacher will preach the Dhamma with reference to that deva. By listening to that Dhamma, I too shall appease my own distress." Thinking thus, he called the devas for the sake of companionship.

"Evaṃ bhaddaṃ tavāti kho devā tāvatiṃsā" means: "O Great King, let it be so. Let us go to see the Blessed One. The arising of a Buddha is rare. May it be a blessing to you, who, instead of saying 'Let us go to play on the mountain top or in the river,' urges us toward such a meritorious occasion." Thus they consented. "Paccassosuṃ" means they accepted his words with great respect, placing them on their heads.
292:
Sakka, the king of devas, called Pañcasikha, the son of the Gandhabba devas. Even though he had already called the devas, why did he call this Pañcasikha separately? It was for the purpose of obtaining permission. It is said that this thought occurred to him: "It is not appropriate to approach the Teacher by bringing a host of devas from the two celestial realms as if striking him with a heavy burden. But this Pañcasikha is an attendant of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) and is a favorite; he goes at any desired moment to ask questions and listen to the Dhamma. I will send this Pañcasikha ahead to request permission, and only after he has obtained permission will I approach and ask my questions." Thus, he called him for the purpose of obtaining permission.

"May it be a blessing to you," said Pañcasikha, consenting: "O Great King, let it be so. May it be a blessing to you, who, instead of saying to me, 'Come, dear friend, let us go to see the garden-play or the dancers' festival,' says, 'We shall see the Buddha, we shall hear the Dhamma.'" Supporting Sakka's words very firmly and consenting to them, he followed him, going together in company.

In that context, "Beluvapaṇḍu" refers to a lute that has a pale yellow color like a ripe wood-apple. It is said that its bowl was made of gold, its neck of sapphire, its strings of silver, and its pegs of coral. The bowl was one gāvuta in size, the place where the strings are tied was one gāvuta, and the upper part of the neck was one gāvuta; thus the lute was three gāvutas in length. Thus, taking that lute, he tuned it to the fifty-fold melodies, struck it with his fingertips, and produced a sweet song. Signaling to the remaining devas the time of Sakka's departure, he stood to one side. When the host of devas had assembled by this signal of song and music, then Sakka, the lord of devas... appeared on Mount Vediyaka.

"Atiriva obhāsajāto" means that on other days, the place would be illuminated by the radiance of just one deva, or a Māra, or a Brahmā; but on that day, because of the radiance of the devas from the two celestial realms, it was exceedingly brilliant. It was like a single great lamp, similar to the time when a thousand moons and a thousand suns have risen. It is said that the people in the surrounding villages saw this at the time they usually had their evening meal, while children were playing in the middle of the village as Sakka went to that mountain. Therefore, the people saw it and said: "Indeed, devas usually approach the Blessed One at the middle watch of the night. Why has this one come even in the early part of the evening?" Thus they questioned.

The answer is that he came because he was threatened by the fear of death. "Ko nāma" means: "Friends, what is the name of that radiance? Who is this that approaches the Blessed One to ask questions and hear the Dhamma? Is it Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā? Friends, how will the Blessed One answer the questions, and how will he preach the Dhamma?" This is the meaning.
293:
Why did he come even in the early part of the first watch? Because he was threatened by the fear of death. "Friends, what is the name of this radiance? What powerful deva or Brahmā approaches the Blessed One today to ask questions and listen to the Dhamma? How will the Blessed One answer the questions and teach the Dhamma? It is a gain for us that the Teacher, the dispeller of doubts for devas like us, dwells in a monastery not far away, where we get the opportunity to give even a bowlful or a spoonful of almsfood." Thinking thus, they stood saluting with hands raised to their heads, glowing with the union of ten fingernails, being agitated and having their hair standing on end.

"Difficult to approach" means hard to attend upon. "I am with lust, hatred, and delusion; the Teacher is free from lust, hatred, and delusion. Therefore, the Tathāgata is difficult to be attended upon by one like me." "Meditating" means meditating through both lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna (meditation on characteristics) and ārammaṇūpanijjhāna (meditation on objects). Because he delights in that very meditation, he is called "one who delights in meditation." Immediately after that, he is secluded in a good object or is currently meditating. Therefore, he is difficult to approach not only because he is meditating and delighting in meditation, but also because he is currently in seclusion. "Please please him" means "Please win him over" or "Please make an opportunity for me." In the phrase "taking the Beluva lute," was it not already taken? Yes, it was. But while traveling, it was hung on the shoulder; now, placing it in the left hand and preparing it for playing, he held it up. Thus it is said, "taking."

## Pañcasikhagītāgāthāvaṇṇanā
"Made to hear" means caused to know. "Inspired by the Buddha" means occurring with the Buddha as the cause or basis. The same method applies to the remaining words.

"Sūriyavacchasā" refers to one who has a body radiance like the sun. It is said that radiance rises from the toes of that goddess up to the tips of her hair, making her appear like the orb of the rising sun; thus they know her as "Sūriyavacchasā." Referring to her, he said: "Auspicious Sūriyavacchasā, I salute your father Timbaru, the king of the Gandhabba devas." By whom you were born, O beautiful one, endowed with all beautiful limbs. Just as wind is desired and dear to those who are sweating so that the sweat may disappear, so are you dear to me. Just as one who is oppressed by thirst desires water to drink...
294:
By which cause, depending on which Timbaru, the king of devas, you were born, O beautiful one, fair in all your limbs. You are the one who increases my joy and happiness. Just as wind is desired, dear, and pleasing to those who are sweating in order to remove the sweat, so are you dear to me. Just as water is desired by one who wishes to drink, being overcome by thirst, and just as the nine supramundane states (nava-lokuttara-dhamma) are desired, dear, and pleasing to the Arahants, so are you desired by me. O Aṅgīrasī (Sūriyavacchasā), who has radiance from your limbs, just as food is desired by one who wishes to eat, being overcome by hunger, so are you desired by me. Just as someone would extinguish a blazing fire with a pot of water, so extinguish the fever of sensual lust that has arisen in me because of you. Just as a bull elephant smeared with lotus pollen, oppressed and distressed by the heat of the sun, having plunged into a lotus pond and drunk, remains submerged with only the tip of its trunk visible and experiences happiness and pleasure, even so, when shall I descend between your breasts and belly and obtain happiness and pleasure?

"Like an elephant beyond the hook, I have conquered the goad (tutta) and the spear (tomara); I know no reason, intoxicated by your beautiful thighs." Here, 'tutta' refers to the iron rod used for piercing the base of the ears. 'Tomara' refers to the handled spear used for piercing the feet, etc. 'Aṅkusa' refers to the curved hook used for piercing the head. An elephant in rut that is beyond the hook, having surpassed the hook, does not come under control even when pierced by the hook; thinking "I have conquered the goad and the spear, I no longer follow the hook," he knows no reason due to pride and intoxication. Just as that elephant beyond the hook knows no reason, thinking "I have conquered the goad and the spear," even so, I too, being intoxicated by your thighs which are endowed with auspicious marks—intoxicated, negligent, like a madman—know no reason. Or, like an elephant beyond the hook, I too am negligent because of you, and regarding the cause for the fading of lust from you, not even one...
295:
Furthermore, I do not know the cause of detachment (from you). Why? Just as that elephant, though conquered by the goad and pike (tutta-tomara), does not heed the words of any trainer, so I, being infatuated with you, do not heed the words of any advisor; thus, I do not know the cause of detachment.

"I have a mind infatuated with you" means: O lady with auspicious thighs, I have a mind bound to you by passion. "Gedhitacitto" means having a mind that has approached infatuation. "The mind is transformed" means it has abandoned its natural pure state and remains so. "Unable to turn back" means unable to retreat from infatuation with you. "Like a fish that has swallowed a hook" means like a fish that remains having swallowed the hook. There is also a variant reading "ghaso," which has the same meaning as stated above.

"Vāmūrū" means a goddess with thighs shaped in a beautiful manner, or it means a goddess with thighs like banana trunks. "Sajā" means to embrace (clasp the neck). "Mandalocane" is used because women do not look harshly but look gently and softly; therefore, they are called "mandalocanā." "Palissajā" means to embrace completely from all sides (clasp the neck). "I have always desired this embrace" means I have desired this clasping of the neck repeatedly.

"My peace is indeed small" means it is small by nature. "Vellitakesiyā" is used because when that goddess's hair is loosened and let down her back, it moves in curls like a snake; thus she is called "Vellitakesī." It refers to you, the goddess with such snake-like curling hair. "It has many aspects" means it has become manifold. There is also a variant reading "anekabhāgo." "Like an offering given to an Arahant" means it arises in many various ways, just like a gift given to an Arahant.

"Whatever merit I have performed" means whatever merit has been done by me. "Towards Arahants who have attained the quality of tādi" means merit performed towards Arahants who have reached the state of equanimity (tādi-lakkhaṇa). "May it ripen together with you only" means may all that merit yield its result only together with you.

"Ekodī" means reaching a state of oneness. In the phrase "nipako sato," wisdom is called "nepakka"; being endowed with that wisdom, one is "nipako." Being endowed with mindfulness, one is "sato." "Amataṃ muni jigīsāno" means just as that Buddha Sage seeks the Deathless Nibbāna, so too, O Sūriyavacchasā, do I seek you. Or, it means just as that Sage wanders seeking and searching for the Deathless, so do I wander seeking and searching for you.

"Just as the Sage rejoices upon reaching supreme Enlightenment" means just as the Buddha Sage, sitting on the Bodhi-throne, rejoices and is delighted upon attaining Omniscience. So too...
296:
"Nandeyyaṃ" means: in this way, if I were to attain union with you and rejoice, if I were to become filled with joy and happiness. In the phrase "tāhaṃ bhadde vareyyāhe," "ahe" is a form of address. O lady Sūriyavacchasā, if Sakka, the king of gods, were to offer a boon: "Will you take the kingship of the devas in the two deva worlds, or will you take Sūriyavacchasā?", I would reject the kingship and say "I will take only Sūriyavacchasā"; thus would I desire, long for, and take you.

"Like a Sal tree in full bloom" refers to a Sal tree at your father's city gate that blooms constantly. That Sal tree is very delightful. Like that constantly blooming Sal tree, I praise and worship your father, who possesses great glory through such beauty. I worship the father who has such a daughter.

Regarding the phrase "saṃsandatīti," why did the Buddha praise the quality of the song and the sound of the lute? Did the Buddha have strong passion for those sounds? No. The Buddha remains equanimous with "six-factored equanimity" (chaḷaṅgupekkhā) regarding the six sense objects. In such matters, He merely knows the pleasant and unpleasant objects, but has no attachment to them. As it is said: "Friends, the Blessed One has the eye-faculty, He sees forms with the eye, but the Blessed One has no desire or passion; the Blessed One has a well-liberated mind. The Blessed One has the ear-faculty..." etc. (Saṃyutta Nikāya). If He did not speak of the merits, the deva Pañcasikha would not know "The Blessed One has given me the opportunity." Then Sakka would think "The Blessed One has not given Pañcasikha the opportunity," and would take the devas and return from there. If they returned, it would be a great loss. Only when the merits were spoken did they know "The Blessed One has given Pañcasikha the opportunity," and approached with the devas to ask questions. The Buddha spoke the praise knowing that at the end of the answers, eighty thousand devas would be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

In that context, "kadā saṃyūḷhā" means when was it composed or combined? "At that time, Bhante" refers to the eighth week after Your attainment of Omniscience. "Named Bhaddā Sūriyavacchasā" means she is named Bhaddā by name, and called Sūriyavacchasā because of her physical perfection. "Sister" (bhaginī) is just a mode of address, meaning a goddess (devadhītā). "Parakāminī" means desiring or longing for another deva.
297:
'Upanaccantiyā' means one who is dancing. It is said that at one time, she went with the Four Great Kings to perform a dance for Sakka, the king of gods. At that moment, Sakka proclaimed the eight true qualities of the Tathāgata. That goddess, who went and danced on that day, heard those qualities.

## Commentary on Sakka's Approach
'Paṭisammodati' means the Blessed One, saying 'Your words and mine agree,' etc., greets him joyfully. Pañcasikha the gandhabba also rejoices in return. When reciting the verses, Pañcasikha rejoices, and the Blessed One rejoices in return. 'Āmantesi' means he made it known. It is said that Sakka had this thought: 'This Pañcasikha, sent by me for my business, is doing his own business. Standing in the presence of such a Teacher, he speaks inappropriate words connected with sensual pleasures. Dancers are indeed shameless; when speaking, they might even show improper behavior. Let me now make my business known to this Pañcasikha.' Thinking thus, he called and spoke to him.

'Evañca pana tathāgatā' etc. are the words placed by the Elders who performed the Recension (Saṅgāyana). 'Abhivadanti' means speaking words of prosperity as a way of accepting a salutation. 'Abhivadito' means addressed with words of prosperity.

'Urundā samapādī' means it became wide and open. The darkness within the cave disappeared. 'Āloko udapādi' means the darkness that was naturally in the cave disappeared and light arose. All these are the words of the Elders of the Recension.

'Venerable Sir, I have desired to see you for a long time' is the meaning. (I have been delayed) due to various small and large matters. Sons and daughters of the gods are born on the laps (of deities); goddesses who serve at the feet are born on the beds; deities who perform the task of decorating those goddesses are born surrounding the beds; those who perform various services are born within the mansion. For these deities, there is no such thing as a legal judgment. However, for those born in the boundary between two mansions, being unable to decide 'Is this yours or mine?', they undergo a legal judgment and ask Sakka, the king of gods. Then Sakka usually says: 'To whichever mansion it is closer, let it belong to that person.'
298:
If both are at an equal distance, he says, "To whichever mansion the deity stands looking at, it belongs to that person." If the deity does not look at either, he takes it as his own property to cut off the quarrel between the two. Activities such as playing are also duties to be performed. Referring to such duties, he said, "due to various duties and affairs."

"Salalāgārake" means in a scented hut (gandhakuṭi) made of salala wood. "Aññatarena samādhinā" means at that time, the Blessed One, knowing that Sakka's knowledge was not yet mature and wishing to grant him an opportunity later, sat in the dwelling of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Sakka, not knowing this, said "by some concentration." "Bhūjati ca nāma": Bhūjati is the name of that goddess. "Paricārikā" means a goddess who serves at the feet. It is said that she had attained two fruits (of the path). Therefore, she no longer had any delight in the deva world. She would always come to serve the Blessed One, placing her joined palms on her head and standing in worship of the Blessed One.

Regarding the phrase "He emerged from that concentration due to the sound of the chariot wheel," it should not be said that "one who has entered an attainment hears sound." Did the Blessed One not say to Sakka, the lord of devas, "Indeed, I emerged from that concentration due to the sound of the chariot wheel of the venerable one"? Let alone the sound of a chariot wheel, one who has entered an attainment does not hear the sound of a pair of conch shells being blown near the ear, nor even the sound of a thunderbolt, while within that attainment. In truth, the Blessed One entered the attainment of fruition for a determined duration, thinking, "I will not grant Sakka an opportunity for this much time." Sakka, thinking "The Teacher does not grant me an opportunity now," circumambulated the scented hut to the right, turned the chariot back, and headed toward the deva world.

The sound of the chariot within the precinct of the scented hut became like the sound of a five-piece musical ensemble. For the Blessed One, who emerged from the attainment according to the predetermined time, the first advertence (āvajjana) arose along with the sound of the chariot. Therefore, he spoke in this way.

## Commentary on the Story of Gopaka

"Sīlesu paripūrakārinī" means one who practices the five precepts to fulfillment. "Itthittaṃ virājetvā" means that womanhood is of no benefit. This is because while remaining in the state of a woman, it is not possible to enjoy the glory of a Universal Monarch, nor the glory of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā, nor is it possible to reach Paccekabodhi or Samma-sambodhi. Thus, one becomes disenchanted with womanhood. Manhood alone is great, noble, and supreme; only by standing in this state of manhood can one attain those successes...
299:
In this manner, she is said to have developed the state of manhood. That Princess Gopikā also did the same. Therefore, it is said: "Having discarded the state of a woman and developed the state of a man." The phrase *hīnaṃ gandhabbakāyaṃ* refers to the low host of Gandhabbas.

If it is asked why those who possessed pure virtue were reborn in that low host of Gandhabbas, it is because of their previous attachment. It is said that in the past, that very Gandhabba realm had been their dwelling place; therefore, through the power of attachment, they were reborn there. *Upaṭṭhānaṃ* refers to the Sudhamma assembly hall where they serve. *Pāricariyaṃ* refers to the state of providing service. They come with the thought, "We shall serve you with song and music."

*Paṭicodesi* means he reminded them (made them remember). It is said that upon seeing those three devas, he reflected: "These young devas are exceedingly radiant and beautiful; by what meritorious deed have they come here?" and he saw that "they had been monks." Then, investigating further, "If they were monks, did they fulfill the virtues?" he saw that "they were fulfillers of virtue." Investigating further, "If they were fulfillers of virtue, did they have any other special qualities?" he saw that "they were attainers of jhāna." Investigating further, "If they were attainers of jhāna, where did they reside?" he saw that "they were the monks who frequented my house."

Those with pure virtue can be reborn wherever they wish among the six deva worlds. However, these individuals were not reborn in the higher deva worlds. Those who attain jhāna are reborn in the Brahma world, yet these individuals were not reborn in the Brahma world either. [He thought:] "As for me, by standing in their admonition, I was reborn as a son in the lap of Sakka, the lord of devas; but these individuals were reborn in the low Gandhabba realm. Such persons should be reproached again and again and pierced deeply." Thinking thus, he reproached them with words such as "*Kutomukhā*" and so on.

In that context, *kutomukhā* means: "While the Blessed One is preaching the Dhamma directly in front of you, where are your faces turned as you listen? Are your minds elsewhere? Are you looking here and there, or are you nodding off?" *Duddiṭṭharūpaṃ* refers to an ill-favored nature, a physical form that is improper to look at. *Sahadhammike* refers to those who have well-practiced the Dhamma and performed meritorious deeds within the dispensation of the same Teacher. Regarding *tesaṃ bhante*: after the deva Gopaka spoke thus and reproached them again with words such as "Oh, you are shameless and without conscience," two of those three devas regained mindfulness in that very life.

*Kāyaṃ brahmapurohitaṃ*: It is said those two devas reflected thus—"Dancers, singers, and musicians should receive a reward upon coming here. But this deva Gopaka, from the moment he saw us, has been crackling like a furnace sprinkled with salt. Why is there such reproach?" When they reflected, they saw their own former state as monks, their possession of pure virtue, their attainment of jhāna, and the fact that the deva Gopaka had been their lay supporter. They realized: "Those with pure virtue are reborn in whatever place they desire among the six deva worlds; those who attain jhāna are reborn in the Brahma world. We, however, were unable to be reborn in the higher deva worlds or the Brahma world."
300:
However, from the moment this deva Gopaka saw us, he has been crackling like a furnace sprinkled with salt. Reflecting, "Why is this?", they saw their own former state as monks, their pure virtue, their attainment of jhāna, and that this deva Gopaka had been a lay devotee who frequented their house. They realized: "Those with pure virtue are reborn in whatever place they desire among the six deva worlds; those who attain jhāna are reborn in the Brahma world. We were unable to be reborn in the higher deva worlds or the Brahma world. By standing in our admonition, this woman has been reborn in a higher realm; but we, though being monks and having practiced the holy life under the Blessed One, have been reborn in the low Gandhabba host. This is why this deva Gopaka is thus rebuking (reproaching) us."

While listening to the words of that deva Gopaka, two among those three individuals regained mindfulness of the first jhāna. Using that jhāna as a basis, they contemplated formations (saṅkhāra) and were established in the fruit of Non-Returning (anāgāmī-phala). At that moment, their meager sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) existence could no longer persist. Therefore, they passed away immediately and were reborn in the Brahmapurohita realm. That Brahma body of theirs arose while they were still in that Gandhabba realm. Thus it was said: "Venerable Sir, of those devas reproached by the deva Gopaka, two regained mindfulness in this very life and reached the Brahmapurohita host."

In that passage, "in this very life" (diṭṭheve dhamme) means they regained mindfulness of jhāna in that very existence. It should be understood that they passed away while remaining in that state and then obtained the Brahmapurohita body, the physical form of a Brahmapurohita. As for "one deva" (eko pana devo), it refers to the one deva who, being unable to cut off attachment, remained settled in sense-pleasures and became a permanent inhabitant of that Gandhabba realm.

*Saṅghañcupaṭṭhāsiṃ* means I served and attended to the Saṅgha.

*Sudhammatāya* means because of the excellence of the Dhamma. *Tidivūpapanno* means one who is reborn in Tidiva, the city of the Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa). *Gandhabbakāyūpagate vasīne* refers to those who have arrived as inhabitants of the Gandhabba realm. The phrase *ye ca mayaṃ pubbe manussabhūtā* should be understood by connecting it with the words: "We who were formerly human beings served with food and drink."

*Pādūpasaṅgayha* means clasping the feet, honoring them (by providing water for washing the feet and oil for anointing the feet), and paying homage. *Sake nivesane* means in one's own house; this phrase should also be connected with "served."

*Paccattaṃ veditabbo* means it is to be personally known and experienced. *Ariyāna subhāsitāni* refers to the well-spoken words of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, which are being spoken by you.
301:
“Tumhe pana seṭṭhamupāsamānā” means approaching the noble Buddha or the unsurpassed Dispensation of the Buddha. “Brahmacariyaṃ” is the noble practice. “Bhavatūpapatti” is the rebirth or arising of the venerable ones.

“Agāre vasato mayhaṃ” means of me living in the midst of the house.

“Svajjā” means that ‘I’ now. In this context, “Gotamasāvakena” refers to the Gopaka deva as a disciple of Gotama. “Samecca” means having gone in harmony.

“Handa viyāyāma byāyāma” means “Come, let us strive, let us strive especially.” In the phrase “Mā no mayaṃ parapessā ahumhā,” “no” is merely a particle. The meaning is: “Let us not be those who are merely the servants of others.” “Gotamasāsanāni” here refers to the first jhāna, which is naturally penetrated, as the teaching of Gotama. “Anussaraṃ” means recollecting that first jhāna.

“Cittāni virājayitvā” means having detached the mind from the five cords of sensual pleasure. “Kāmesu ādīnavaṃ” means they saw the danger in sensual pleasures through the power of suppression by the first jhāna, and through the power of total eradication by the third path (Anāgāmī-magga). “Kāmasaṃyojanabandhanāni” refers to the fetters of sensuality and the bonds of sensuality. “Pāpimayogāni” means the bonds of the Evil One (Māra), which are things that bind. “Duraccayāni” means difficult to overcome. “Sa-indā devā sapajāpatikā” means the devas who are established with Indra as their leader are called “Sa-inda,” and those with the deva king Pajāpati as their leader are called “Sapajāpatika.” “Sabhāyupaviṭṭhā” means established or seated in the assembly.

“Vīrā” means the brave ones. “Virāgā” means those free from passion. “Virajaṃ karontā” means producing the stainless path of Non-returning. “Nāgovā sannāni guṇāni” means having cut the bonds of sensual fetters like a great elephant, they surpassed the Tāvatiṃsa devas. “Saṃvegajātassa” means of Sakka, in whom a sense of urgency had arisen.

“Kāmābhibhū” is one who overcomes both types of sensuality (objective and subjective). “Satiyā vīhīnā” means those devoid of mindfulness associated with jhāna.

“Tiṇṇaṃ tesaṃ” means among those three devas. “Āvasinettha eko” means only one remained as a resident in that lower Gandhabba realm. “Sambodhipathānusārino” means those who follow the path to enlightenment (the path of Non-returning). “Devepi hīḷenti” means the two devas were disparaging and looking down upon...
302:
Disparaging and looking down upon (the devas) in the deva realm, with minds well-concentrated through access concentration and absorption concentration, they flew up into the sky, scattering the dust from their feet onto the heads of the devas.

“Etādisī dhammapakkāsanettha” refers to the proclamation of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths in this Dispensation; through that Dhamma, the disciples are endowed with these qualities. “Na tattha kiṃ kaṅkhati koci sāvako” means among those disciples, not even a single disciple has doubt regarding the Buddha and so forth, or regarding the state of the Triple Gem which is unobstructed in the four directions. It means “He dwells without attachment or clinging in all directions.” Now, wishing to praise the virtues of the Blessed One, he says: “We pay homage to the Buddha, the Conqueror, the Lord of people, who has crossed the fourfold flood, who has cut off doubt.” In that verse, “Vicikicchasinnaṃ” means one who has cut off doubt, and “Janindaṃ” means the one supreme over all the world.

“Yaṃ te dhammaṃ” means that Dhamma of yours. “Ajjhagāṃsu te” means those devas have attained. “Kāyaṃ brahmapurohitaṃ” means they attained the body of a Brahma’s Retainer even while we were looking. The meaning is: “Venerable Sir, having known your Dhamma, among those three persons, those two who reached distinction attained the path and fruit of Non-returning, and even while we were looking, they attained the Brahma’s Retainer body and reached the distinction of the path and fruit. We too have come to attain that Dhamma.” “Āgatamhase” means we have arrived. “Katāvakāsā bhagavatā, pañhaṃ pucchemu mārisā” means “Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One grants us the opportunity, being those who have received permission from the Blessed One, we wish to ask a question.”

## Maghamāṇavavatthu

“Dīgharattaṃ visuddho kho ayaṃ yakkho” means he has been pure (or desired to be pure) for a long time. How long? Since the time he was the youth Magha in the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha, before the Buddha had arisen. At that time, it is said that this Sakka, having risen early one day, went to the place in the middle of the village where people gathered for village work. He cleared the rubbish from the spot where he was to stand with the tip of his foot, making it pleasant. Another person came and stood there. With just that much action, he gained mindfulness, cleared a space about the size of a threshing floor in the middle of the village, scattered sand, brought wood, and made a fire during the cold season. Young and old came and sat by that fire. Then one day, this thought occurred to the youth Magha: “We go to the city and see the King, the King’s ministers, and so on. In these mansions of the moon and sun, the deva named Canda...”
303:
One day, this thought occurred to the youth Magha: "We go to the city and see the King, the King's great ministers, and so on. Regarding these Moon and Sun deities, people say, 'There is a deity named Canda, a deity named Suriya.' By doing what did they attain such prosperity?" Then he thought, "It is not by any other means; they attained it only by performing meritorious deeds." He further reflected, "I too should perform only those meritorious deeds that grant such prosperity."

Magha rose early, drank gruel, and taking an adze, an axe, a hoe, and a pestle in his hand, went to a crossroads. He used the pestle to lift and roll away stones from the path. He removed trees that might strike the axles of carts and carriages. He leveled uneven ground. He built a rest-house at the crossroads. He dug a pond. He constructed a bridge. Having worked all day in this manner, he returned home at sunset. Someone asked him, "Friend Magha, you go out early in the morning and return from the forest only in the evening; what work do you do?" He replied, "I am performing meritorious deeds; I am clearing the path leading to the heavenly realm." When asked, "Friend, what is this thing called merit?" he said, "Do you not know?" "Indeed, I do not know," the man replied. Magha asked, "When you went to the city, have you ever seen the King, the King's great ministers, and others?" "Yes, I have seen them," he replied. "They attained that status by performing meritorious deeds. I, too, am performing meritorious deeds that grant such prosperity."

"Have you ever heard that there is a deity named Canda and a deity named Suriya?" Magha asked. "Yes, I have heard so," the man replied. "I am clearing the path that leads to the heavenly realm, the abode of that Moon and Sun," Magha said. The man asked, "Is this meritorious work suitable only for you, or is it also fit for others?" Magha replied, "This merit is not forbidden to anyone." "If that is so, when you go to the forest tomorrow, please give me a signal (call me)," the man said. The next day, Magha took him along. In this way, thirty-three young men in that village became followers of Magha. Being of one mind, they went about performing meritorious deeds. Wherever they went, they leveled the roads, completing the work in a single day. They also finished digging ponds, building rest-houses, and constructing bridges in a single day.

Then the village headman thought: "In the past, when these men were drinking liquor and committing acts such as killing living beings, I obtained wealth through coins, fines, and taxes. Now, since the time they began performing merit, there is no such income. I shall now slander them at the royal court." He approached the King and said, "Great King, I see thieves." "My dear man, where do you see them?" the King asked. "In my village," he replied. "What kind of thieves are they?" the King asked. "They are rebels against the King, Your Majesty," he replied. "Of what class are they?" "They are of the householder class, Your Majesty." "What will householders do? Why did you not report this to me even though you knew?" the King asked. "Great King, I did not dare to report it out of fear. Now, please do not punish me," he replied. Then the King, believing that the village headman was making a serious accusation, said, "If that is so, go; arrest those thieves yourself." Giving him authority, the King sent him away. The village headman went, and after the men had worked in the forest all day and eaten their evening meal...
304:
When asked, 'Why did you not tell me, knowing this?' he replied, 'Great King, I did not speak out of fear. Now, please do not be angry with me.' Then the King, believing that 'This man is reporting a great matter to me,' gave him forces and sent him, saying, 'If so, go; bring them yourself.'

The village headman went and worked in the forest all day. After eating his evening meal, he sat in the middle of the village. While they were consulting, 'What work shall we do tomorrow? Which road shall we level? Shall we dig a pond or build a bridge?' he surrounded them and bound them, saying, 'Do not move! It is the King's command!' and led them away. Then their wives, hearing that 'Your husbands are being led away bound as thieves guilty of offenses against the King,' said, 'For a long time these deceitful ones have stayed in the forest every day saying "We are doing meritorious deeds." All work has been ruined; there is no progress at home. They are well-bound indeed! They are well-caught indeed!'

The village headman led them and presented them to the King. Without investigating or reflecting, the King commanded, 'Have them trampled by an elephant.' While they were being led away, the youth Magha asked the others, 'Friends, will you be able to follow my word?' They replied, 'It is only because we followed your word that we have encountered this danger. Nevertheless, we will follow your word. Tell us, what shall we do?' He said, 'Friends, for those wandering in this cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra), such danger is constant. Are you thieves?' They answered, 'We are not thieves.' He said, 'In this world, the Act of Truth (Saccakiriya) is the only refuge. Therefore, all of you perform an Act of Truth: "If we are thieves, let the elephant trample us; if we are not thieves, let it not trample us."' They did so.

The elephant could not even approach them but fled trumpeting. Even when they struck the elephant with iron rods, forks, and goads, they could not bring it near. They reported to the King, 'We cannot bring the elephant near.' He commanded, 'If so, cover them with mats and have them trampled.' When they were covered with mats, the elephant fled, trumpeting twice as loudly.

The King, hearing this, summoned the slandering village headman and asked, 'Dear man, why does the elephant not wish to trample them?' He replied, 'Your Majesty, the leading youth knows a mantra; this is the power of that mantra.' The King summoned the youth Magha and asked, 'Do you have a mantra?' He replied, 'Your Majesty, I have no mantra. However, we performed an Act of Truth: "If we are the King's thieves, let it trample us; if we are not thieves, let it not trample us." This is the power of the Act of Truth.'

'Dear men, what work do you do?' he asked. They replied, 'Your Majesty, we level the roads, we build rest-houses at crossroads, we dig ponds, and we build bridges. We go about performing such meritorious deeds.' Then the King asked the village headman, 'Why did you slander these men?' He replied, 'When they were negligent, I received such wealth; when they were not negligent, I did not receive it. For that reason, I slandered them.' The King said, 'Dear men, although this elephant is an animal, it knows your virtues even while being your enemy. I, though a human, did not know. I grant you the village where you live repeatedly. Let this elephant also be your elephant. Let the slandering village headman be your slave. From this day forward, perform meritorious deeds on my behalf as well.' Saying this, he gave them wealth and released them.
305:
“We are traveling about performing such meritorious deeds as leveling roads, digging ponds, and building bridges,” they reported.

The King asked, “My man, for what purpose did you slander these people?” “When we are negligent, I obtain such and such wealth; when we are diligent, I do not. For that reason, I slandered them,” he replied. “My men, even this elephant, though an animal, knows your virtues. I, though a human, did not know. I return your home village to you alone. Let this elephant also be yours. Let this slandering village headman also be your slave. From this day forward, perform meritorious deeds dedicated to me as well,” the King said, and after giving them wealth, he dismissed them.

Taking the wealth and riding the elephant in turns, they discussed: “Friends, although it is true that merit is performed for the sake of future lives, our merit has borne fruit in this very life, like a blue lotus blooming in the water. Now, let us perform even greater merit.” “What kind of merit shall we perform?” they pondered. “Let us build a sturdy rest-house at the four-way crossroads for the public to rest. However, let us do it by ourselves, without involving women. For when we were being led away as thieves, not even one of the women felt the slightest bit of sorrow; instead, they stood up saying, ‘They are well-bound, well-captured.’ Therefore, we shall not give them a share of the merit.” Returning to their homes, they gave the elephant thirty-three lumps of rice and thirty-three handfuls of grass, so that the elephant's belly was full. They entered the forest and felled trees, and the elephant dragged the felled trees to the cart-track. They planed the wood and began the work on the rest-house.

In Magha the youth's house, there were four wives: Sujātā, Sudhammā, Cittā, and Nandā. Sudhammā asked the carpenter, “Father, these friends go early and return in the evening; what work are they doing?” “Mother, they are building a rest-house,” he said. “Father, please let me have a share in the merit of the rest-house,” she said. “They say they will do it without involving women,” he replied.

Then Sudhammā gave the carpenter eight kahāpaṇas and said, “Father, by some means or other, make it so that I get a share of the merit.” The carpenter agreed, saying, “Very well, mother.” He first took his adze and axe, stood in the middle of the village, and shouted loudly, “Friends, why have you not come out even at this time today?” Knowing that all had reached the road, he said, “You go on ahead; I have some delaying work to do,” and sent them off. Then, going by another path, he felled a tree suitable for a pinnacle, planed it, made it smooth, and kept it in Sudhammā's house. “When I ask for it, bring it out and give it to me,” he instructed. Later, when the timber construction was finished, they performed the leveling of the ground, laying the foundation, erecting the pillars, placing the crossbeams, and setting up the scaffolding for the pinnacle. The carpenter, staying on the scaffolding for the pinnacle, lifted the rafters from the four directions and said, “Friends, there is one part of the structure that was forgotten and not prepared.”
306:
The carpenter had sent those men ahead, then went by another path, cut a tree suitable for a pinnacle, planed it, made it smooth, brought it, and kept it in Sudhammā's house. “On the day I say ‘Give it to me,’ bring it out and give it,” he had instructed.

Then, when the timber work was finished, and after they had completed the leveling of the ground, laying the foundation, erecting the pillars, placing the crossbeams, and setting up the scaffolding for the pinnacle, the carpenter sat on the scaffolding for the pinnacle, lifted the rafters from the four directions, and said, “Friends, there is one thing that was forgotten and not prepared.” “Friend, what was forgotten? Did you forget everything?” they asked. “Friends, where will these rafters rest? It is necessary to obtain what is called a pinnacle,” he said. “Friend, where can we get one now?” they asked. “It might be found in the houses of the families; go around and ask,” he said.

They entered the village and inquired, and at the door of Sudhammā's house, they asked, “Is there a pinnacle in this house?” Sudhammā said, “There is.” “Then take the price for it,” they said. “I will not take the price. If you will share the merit with me, I will give it,” she said. “Friends, come away; we cannot give a share of the merit to a woman. Let us go to the forest and cut a tree,” they said and departed.

Then the carpenter asked, “My men, did you not get the pinnacle?” They told him the matter. The carpenter, still sitting on the scaffolding for the pinnacle, looked up at the sky and said, “Friends, today the constellation is good. Such a constellation can only be found again after another year. The timber you have brought with great hardship will rot right here during the whole year. When you are reborn in the deva world, let there be a rest-house for that Sudhammā in one corner as well. Just bring that pinnacle.”

Sudhammā, before they came again, had the words “This rest-house is named Sudhammā” carved on the lower surface of the pinnacle, wrapped it in a brand-new cloth, and kept it. The workers came and said, “Hey Sudhammā, give us the pinnacle. Let happen what may; we will share the merit with you.” Sudhammā brought out the pinnacle and said, “My men, do not unwrap this cloth until the eight or sixteen rafters have been mounted,” and gave it to them. They agreed, saying “Very well,” took it, and as soon as they had mounted the rafters, they unwrapped the cloth.

A man who was the village headman looked up, saw the letters, and said, “Friends, what is this?” He called a man who could read and showed it to him. That man...
307:
"This rest-house shall be named Sudhammā," he said. "Friends, take it away! Even though we have been working on this rest-house from the start, we have not even obtained a name for it. This Sudhammā, with a pinnacle timber as precious as a jewel (and as large as a mountain), is having the rest-house built in her own name," they lamented. While they were still lamenting, the carpenter inserted the rafters, fixed them with pins, and completed the work on the rest-house.

They divided the rest-house into three sections: one section was made as a dwelling for the rulers, one for the poor, and one for the sick. The thirty-three men laid out thirty-three planks and gave a signal to the elephant: "When a guest arrives and sits upon the plank spread by a certain person, take that guest and establish him only in the house of the owner of that plank. The responsibility for massaging his feet and back, and providing all food, snacks, and bedding shall rest solely upon the owner of that plank." The elephant would take every guest who arrived and lead them to the house of the plank-owner, who would then perform the necessary duties for the guest for that day.

Magha the youth had a Kovilāra tree planted in a place not far from the rest-house, and at the foot of that tree, he had a stone slab spread. His wife, named Nandā, had a pond dug nearby. Cittā had small flowering plants cultivated. However, Sujātā, the eldest of all, wandered about merely decorating herself while holding a mirror. Magha said to Sujātā, "Lady, Sudhammā has become a sharer in the merit of the rest-house; Nandā has had a pond dug; Cittā has planted flowering trees. But as for you, you have no meritorious deed yet. Lady, perform at least one good deed." She replied, "For whose sake are you doing this? Is not the merit you perform mine as well?" and continued to occupy herself only with decorating her person.

Magha the youth remained until the end of his life, and after passing away from there, he was reborn as Sakka, the King of Gods, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Those thirty-three villagers also passed away and were reborn as thirty-three deities in the presence of that same Sakka. For Sakka, a palace named Vejayanta arose, seven hundred yojanas in height. Its banner rose three hundred yojanas. As a result of planting the Kovilāra tree, the Pāricchattaka tree appeared, with a circumference of three hundred yojanas and a trunk fifteen yojanas in girth.
308:
Due to the merit of the stone slab, the Paṇḍukambala stone slab, sixty leagues in size, appeared at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree. Due to the merit of Sudhammā’s pinnacle-wood, the assembly hall of the gods named Sudhammā, three hundred leagues in size, appeared. Due to the merit of Nandā’s pond, a pond named Nandā, fifty leagues in size, appeared. Due to the merit of Cittā’s flower garden, a garden named Cittalatāvana, sixty leagues in size, appeared.

Sakka, the king of gods, was seated on a golden throne one league in size in the Sudhammā assembly hall, with a white parasol three leagues in size being held over him. Surrounded by those devas, those goddesses, thirty million dancers, and deities from the two deva worlds, he looked upon his great glory. Seeing those three women, he thought, “These women are clearly visible; where is Sujātā?” Searching, he saw, “This Sujātā, not following my words, has been reborn as a female crane in a mountain cleft.” He descended from the deva world and went to her. Upon seeing him, the crane recognized him as Sakka and lowered her head.

“You foolish crane, why do you not lift your head now? You did not follow my words and spent your time only adorning yourself. Great glory has arisen for Sudhammā, Nandā, and Cittā. Come and see our glory!” So saying, he took her to the deva world, placed her by the Nandā pond, and sat on his throne.

The celestial dancers asked, “Great King, where did you go?” Although he did not wish to tell them, he was pressed by those goddesses and said, “I went to Sujātā.” “Great King, where was she reborn?” they asked. “In a mountain cleft,” he replied. “Where is she now?” they asked again. “I have left her at the Nandā pond,” he said. “Friends, come, let us see our lady!” they said, and all the goddesses went there. In her previous life as a human, she had been the eldest of all the wives and had looked down on them. Now, those young goddesses, seeing the crane, mocked her, saying, “Friends, look! Our lady’s face is just like a needle for piercing crabs!” and so on.

The crane was extremely ashamed and said to Sakka, “Great King, what use are these mansions made of gold, silver, and gems, or the Nandā pond to me? Great King, for beings, their own birthplace is the only place of happiness. Please send me back to that mountain cleft.” Sakka sent her back to the mountain cleft and asked, “Will you follow my words?” “I will, Great King,” she replied. “Then take the Five Precepts and keep them unbroken. In a few days, I will make you the leader of these goddesses,” he said. The crane did exactly as Sakka said.
309:
After a few days, Sakka, wanting to test her by thinking, "Will she be able to guard her virtue (sīla)?", went and took the form of a dead fish, lying belly-up and floating on the surface of the water in front of the crane. The crane, thinking "It must be a dead fish," went and grabbed it by the head. The fish wiggled its tail. Thinking "It seems to be alive," she released it back into the water. Sakka, standing in the sky, said, "Sādhu, sādhu! You are indeed guarding the precept. Guarding it thus, I shall make you the chief of the celestial dancers within a few days." Although she lived for five hundred years, she never had a full stomach even for a single day; though her body became dry and withered, she kept her virtue unbroken and, after passing away, was reborn in the house of a potter in Bārāṇasī.

Sakka, looking for where she was reborn, saw her and thought, "It is not yet possible to bring her from there to this heaven. I will make her livelihood easy for her." Disguising himself as an old man with a small cart full of golden melons, he sat in the middle of the village and cried out, "Take these melons!" The villagers from all around came and said, "Grandfather, give us some." He replied, "I give only to those who keep the virtue; you should keep the virtue." The villagers said, "Grandfather, we do not even know what 'virtue' is like; sell them to us for money." He repeated, "I give only to those who keep the virtue." They all turned back, saying, "Hey people, who is this old melon-man?"

The potter's daughter asked, "Mother, you went for melons but came back empty-handed?" They replied, "Yes... that old melon-man says 'I will give only to those who keep the virtue.' Perhaps his own daughters live by eating virtue; we don't even know what virtue is." The potter's daughter thought, "He must have brought them for me," and went to him, saying, "Grandfather, please give me some melons." He asked, "Daughter, do you keep the virtue?" She replied, "Yes, grandfather, I do." He said, "Then I brought these melons just for you," and left the cart at her door before departing. She kept the virtue for the rest of her life and, after passing away, was reborn as the daughter of Vepacitti, the Asura. Due to the merit of her virtue, she became exceedingly beautiful. Vepacitti, saying "I will hold a marriage ceremony for my daughter," gathered all the Asuras. Sakka, looking for where she was reborn, saw, "She is reborn in the Asura realm, and today they will marry her off." Thinking "Now I must go and get her by some means," he disguised himself as an Asura and stood among them.
310:
"I will perform the marriage ceremony for my daughter," he said, and gathered the Asuras. Sakka looked to see where she was born and, seeing she was in the Asura realm, thought, "I shall take her now by creating an incidental cause." He disguised himself as an Asura, went there, and stood among the Asuras. The father gave a garland into the hand of the Asura maiden and said, "Proclaim your husband. Throw it upon the one you desire." Looking around, she saw Sakka and, due to the affection born from living together in previous lives, she thought, "This is my husband," and threw the garland upon Sakka. Sakka took her by the arm and flew up into the sky. At that moment, the Asuras realized what had happened. They pursued them, shouting, "Seize him! Seize him! The old Sakka! He is our enemy! We will not give the young girl to this Sakka!" Vepacitti asked, "Who took her?" They replied, "Great King, the old Sakka took her." He said, "Among the rest of the gods, this Sakka alone is the best. Let them go." Sakka took her and placed her in the position of the chief of two and a half crores of celestial dancers. That Asura maiden, Sujitā, made a request to Sakka: "Great King, I have no mother, father, brother, or sister in this deva realm. Great King, wherever you go, please take me with you." Sakka gave his word, saying, "Very well."

Thus, seeing the purity of Sakka from the time he was the youth Magha in the small village of Macala, the Blessed One said, "This Yakkha has been pure for a long time." *Atthasañhitaṃ* means depending on one's own benefit and the benefit of others, or depending on the cause of welfare and happiness.

## Pañhaveyyākaraṇavaṇṇanā

*Kiṃ saṃyojanā* means having what kind of fetters, or being bound by what kind of bond. *Puthukāyā* means many people. *Averā* means being without anger. *Adaṇḍā* means being free from the punishment of weapons and the punishment of wealth (fines). *Asapattā* means being without enemies. *Abyāpajjā* means being free from mental distress. *Viharemu averino* means they aspire, performing acts of giving and worship, thinking: "Oh, it would be good if we could live without enmity with anyone! It would be good if, without giving rise to anger in anyone, we could enjoy the wealth obtained in a snap of the fingers along with a thousand attendants!" *Iti ca nesaṃ hoti* means "thus this aspiration occurs to them." *Atha ca panā* means "and yet, despite having such an aspiration."

*Issāmacchariyasaṃyojanā* means those who have the fetters of envy and stinginess; envy (*issā*) having the characteristic of begrudging the prosperity of others, and stinginess (*macchariya*) having the characteristic of not being able to endure sharing one's own prosperity with others. This is the summary here. In detail, envy and stinginess have already been explained in the Abhidhamma.
311:
In this context, due to stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsa-macchariya), one is reborn as a yakkha or a peta, wandering about carrying the refuse of that dwelling on one's head. Due to stinginess regarding families (kula-macchariya), upon seeing others giving gifts and so forth to that family and thinking, "Alas, this family of mine is ruined," blood flows from the mouth, diarrhea occurs, and the large and small intestines come out in pieces. Due to stinginess regarding gains (lābha-macchariya), being stingy with gains belonging to the Saṅgha or a group and using them as personal property, one is reborn as a yakkha, a peta, or a great python. Due to stinginess regarding physical appearance and qualities (vaṇṇa-macchariya) and stinginess regarding the learned Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma-macchariya), praising only one's own appearance and qualities while disparaging others' by pointing out various faults, saying, "What beauty does this person have?" and not giving even a little of the learned Dhamma to anyone, one becomes ugly and mute.

Furthermore, due to stinginess regarding dwellings, one is cooked in the Iron House (Lohageha) hell. Due to stinginess regarding families, one becomes a person of few gains. Due to stinginess regarding gains, one is reborn in the Dung (Gūtha) hell. Due to stinginess regarding appearance, wherever one is reborn in existence, one lacks beauty. Due to stinginess regarding the Dhamma, one is reborn in the Hot Ashes (Kukkula) hell. This fetter of envy and stinginess (issā-macchariya-saṃyojana) is abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). As long as that fetter is not abandoned, even though gods and humans may wish for freedom from enmity and so forth, they cannot escape from the danger of enmity and the like.

In the phrase "crossed over doubt in this problem," the statement "I have crossed over doubt by hearing the words of the Exalted One" is meant; it does not indicate the removal of doubt by the power of the Path. "Free from hesitation" means that such hesitation as "How is this? How is that?" has disappeared.

Terms such as "origin" (nidāna) have the meanings already mentioned. "Having pleasant and unpleasant as their origin" means that stinginess (macchariya) has pleasant beings and formations as its origin, while envy (issā) has unpleasant beings and formations as its origin. Alternatively, both have both as their origin. Indeed, for a monk, fellow-residents and others, and for a householder, children and others, or animals such as elephants and horses, are pleasant beings who are cherished and considered "mine." If they do not see them even for a moment, they cannot endure it. When such a person sees another obtaining such a pleasant being, they feel envy (issā). When others ask for that pleasant being, saying, "We have some business with this person; please give him to us for a moment," they feel stinginess (macchariya), saying, "I cannot give him; he will be tired or he will be distressed," and so forth. Thus, first of all, both have pleasant beings as their origin. For a monk, requisites such as the bowl and robes, and for a householder, items such as ornaments, are pleasant and delightful things. That person—
312:
—seeing such an object arising for another, feels envy (issā), thinking, "Oh, may such a thing not happen to him!" Or when asked by others, one feels stinginess (macchariya), saying, "We too cherish this so much that we do not use it; we cannot give it." Thus, both envy and stinginess have pleasant formations (piya-saṅkhāra) as their origin.

Even when obtaining the aforementioned unpleasant beings and formations, although they are disagreeable to that person, due to the perverted nature of the defilements, one feels envy, thinking, "Who else besides me can obtain such a thing?" Or when asked, one feels stinginess, not wishing to give it even temporarily. Thus, both envy and stinginess have unpleasant beings and formations as their origin.

In the context of "having desire (chanda) as its origin," there are five types of desire: the desire for seeking (pariyesana-chanda), the desire for obtaining (paṭilābha-chanda), the desire for consumption (paribhoga-chanda), the desire for hoarding (sannidhi-chanda), and the desire for spending (vissajjana-chanda).

What is the desire for seeking? Here, a certain person, being insatiable and full of desire, seeks visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and wealth. This is called the desire for seeking.

What is the desire for obtaining? Here, a certain person, being insatiable and full of desire, obtains visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and wealth. This is called the desire for obtaining.

What is the desire for consumption? Here, a certain person, being insatiable and full of desire, consumes visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and wealth. This is called the desire for consumption.

What is the desire for hoarding? Here, a certain person, being insatiable and full of desire, hoards wealth, thinking, "It will be useful when dangers arise." This is called the desire for hoarding.

What is the desire for spending? Here, a certain person, being insatiable and full of desire, spends wealth on elephant-riders, horse-riders, charioteers, and archers, thinking, "These people will protect me, guard me, cherish me, and surround me." This is called the desire for spending. These are the five types of desire. In this context, only craving (taṇhā) is intended; it is in reference to that craving that this was spoken.

In the context of "having thought (vitakka) as its origin," the decisive thought (vinicchaya-vitakka) described as "decision based on gain" is called thought (vitakka). Regarding "decision," there are two kinds of decision—
391:
Desiring to show [this], [the Blessed One] said: "In the world, the eye is of a pleasant nature and a delightful nature; here this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; here, when ceasing, it ceases," and so forth.

## Explanation of the Exposition of the Truth of the Path

The word "Ayam-eva" (This alone) is a restriction for the purpose of excluding any other path. "Ariya" (Noble) is the noble path because it is far from the defilements to be killed by each respective path, and because it makes one a Noble One (ariya). By the words "knowledge in suffering" and so forth, the meditation subject of the Four Truths is shown. Among those Four Truths, the first two truths are the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), and the latter two truths are the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa). Among these, for a monk, there is an intensive application of the meditation subject to the round, but there is no such intensive application to the ending of the round yet. This is because, having learned the first two truths from a teacher—both in brief as "The five aggregates are suffering, craving is the origin" and in detail by the method of "What are the five aggregates? The aggregate of form..." and so forth—the practitioner (yogāvacara) performs the work while repeatedly reciting them verbally. However, regarding the other two truths, he performs the work merely by hearing that "The Truth of Cessation is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; the Truth of the Path is desirable, lovely, and pleasing." One who practices in this way penetrates the Four Truths with a single penetration and realizes them with a single breakthrough (abhisamaya). He penetrates suffering through the penetration of full understanding (pariññā-paṭivedha), the origin through the penetration of abandoning (pahāna-paṭivedha), cessation through the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha), and the path through the penetration of development (bhāvanā-paṭivedha). He realizes suffering through the breakthrough of full understanding... (and so forth)... and the path through the breakthrough of development. Thus, for him, in the preliminary stage, there are learning, questioning, hearing, retaining, reflecting, and penetrating regarding the first two truths; but regarding the latter two truths, there are only hearing and penetrating. In the subsequent stage, there is penetration by way of function (kicca) regarding the three truths, while in the Truth of Cessation, there is penetration by way of object (ārammaṇa). Reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā), however, occurs only for one who has reached the truths. Since this person is a beginner (ādikammika), that reviewing is not mentioned here.

For this monk, in the earlier stage while grasping the Dhamma, there is no reflection through concern (ābhoga), bringing to mind (samannāhāra), and attention (manasikāra) such as "I fully understand suffering, I abandon the origin, I realize cessation, I develop the path"; it only arises starting from the time of grasping. In the subsequent stage, however, suffering is indeed fully understood... (and so forth)... the path is indeed developed. Among those truths, two truths are deep because they are difficult to see, and two truths are difficult to see because they are deep. The Truth of Suffering is evident because of its occurrence; it reaches the point where one might say "Oh, what suffering!" when struck by a stump or a thorn, etc. The Origin is also evident because of its occurrence by way of the desire to eat, the desire to consume, and so forth. However, in terms of penetrating their characteristics, both are deep. Thus, they are deep because they are difficult to see. The effort to see the remaining two truths is like the effort to grasp the peak of existence (bhavagga)...
